1. From AI-Assisted Coding to Spec-Driven Development

1.1 Starting with a prompt

More software work now begins with a description than with a blank file. You describe the behaviour you want, and a model returns code, a test, a documentation draft, or a refactoring suggestion. The request can be a sentence or a page; the response can be pasted into the project and tried. That is the new starting point, and it changes how quickly a first result appears.

The effect is largest when the task is bounded. A prototype, an isolated utility, a converter, or a small feature with a clear input and output gives the model enough context to produce something useful. The cost of trying an approach falls, so you try more approaches. That is a real gain, and it is not limited to trivial work. It is simply strongest where the boundaries are visible.

Speed is not the same as quality. Code that arrives quickly can still ignore the project's conventions, duplicate an abstraction that already exists, or solve the immediate request in a way that fits badly with the surrounding design. It may run and still be hard to maintain. Running is a low bar; whether the result is right is a separate question.

The first workflow is simple. You explain the feature, ask for an implementation, paste the result into the project, and try it. If it fails, you describe the failure and ask for another attempt. If it passes, you may keep it and move on. The loop is prompt, generate, paste, test, and repeat, and it is often enough to get a first version into view.

That loop is genuinely useful. It gives fast feedback and makes it easy to explore a library or an API before committing to a design. It is a good way to build a throwaway prototype, a small script, or a rough feature that you intend to rewrite.

The limitation is in the input. The result is only as good as the request and the assumptions the model brings to it. A missing behaviour is inferred rather than asked about. An unsuitable architecture is chosen because the model has no knowledge of the project's architecture, so it guesses from what it does know. Project conventions are ignored because they were never in the prompt. Nothing in the result distinguishes a guess from a decision. None of this requires the model to be careless; it follows from working with an incomplete description. Not all of the missing information is context that someone forgot to provide. A requirement can be correctly silent about things that are not requirements — the order of operations, the wording of a message, the internal structure of a component — and those silences are decisions waiting to be made. When a model fills one, the result is a guess embedded in code.

1.2 Talking before code

Direct generation remains legitimate, but it leaves no durable statement of intent. When the first result survives, the next improvement is a conversation about the implementation before any code is requested. You and the model discuss what the change should do, what it must fit into, and which trade-offs are acceptable. No code is written yet. The request becomes a shared proposal rather than a single instruction.

The conversation covers the decisions that code would otherwise make silently:

  • what problem the change solves and what behaviour it should produce;
  • what existing code, interfaces and constraints it has to fit;
  • which design options exist and what each one trades away;
  • which edge cases, failure modes and security concerns matter;
  • what tests or acceptance criteria will show that it works;
  • how the work should be sequenced into steps.

Discussing those decisions first turns a vague request into shared understanding. The point is to close the information gaps that would otherwise become guesses before the model fills them in. Ambiguity is exposed while it is still cheap to resolve. Assumptions can be challenged before they are embedded in source, and rework falls because the shape of the change is agreed before it is built. The gain depends on the quality of the conversation; a discussion that never reaches a decision is just a longer prompt.

Consider a request as ordinary as "add CSV export". Which records should be exported? Which columns? Does the current filter apply, or does export ignore it? How should dates, numbers and text be formatted? Who is allowed to export what? What happens when the result is too large to build in memory? What should the file be called, and should the same request produce the same file twice? The request is one sentence; the implementation is a set of decisions. The quality labels people reach for — clear, testable, well-specified — are adjectives, not diagnostics. The test of a requirement is whether a concrete question about it can be answered, or only discussed.

1.3 What the conversation forgets

The conversation is better than the prompt, but it is still a conversation. Its value lives in the chat, and it usually disappears when the chat ends. You may have produced an excellent plan, but the plan is hard to retrieve later, and the conversation is not a project artifact. The next person sees the code, not the reasoning that produced it.

A later reader needs information that the conversation held:

  • why the change was made;
  • which alternatives were rejected, and why;
  • what was in scope and what was deliberately left out;
  • which constraints and project rules applied;
  • what must not break;
  • how the result was validated.

The same developer a week later is also a later reader. Memory is not a reliable interface.

Without a stable description, the system drifts. Drift is the slow divergence between what the system is supposed to do and what its code, tests and documents now say. Each change is made from a local understanding of the system, and local understandings accumulate. A specification can serve as the reference against which drift is detected and corrected, but a stale reference makes drift harder to see, not easier.

Review weakens under the same pressure. A reviewer sees a diff: lines added, lines removed, tests changed. What the reviewer does not see is the intent behind the change. Without a durable statement of purpose, they reconstruct it from the code, the commit message or memory. Deliberate exclusions are especially invisible: the reviewer cannot tell whether something was omitted on purpose or forgotten. The review becomes a check on the implementation rather than on the change. Recording the exclusion is the only way to make the difference visible, because an exclusion written into an artifact can be seen, challenged, and maintained.

Direct generation answers a narrow question: can we do this? It does not answer what should work, why it should work that way, how the work should be approached, which constraints apply, or what behaviour is acceptable and how it will be verified. Those answers are not a better prompt. They are a durable, reviewable record of intent. Different technologies and practices can supply that record, and the next paragraphs examine attempts to improve generation before asking what such a record must do.

1.4 Better context is not enough

Several techniques can improve the context available to direct generation:

  • retrieval over design decisions, specifications, code and past changes;
  • tool servers or protocols, such as MCP, that expose repositories, issue trackers, CI and monitoring;
  • persistent project instruction files, such as AGENTS.md, that are read at the start of a session;
  • repository search and dependency context;
  • automated tests, linters and type checks whose results are fed back into the loop.

Each technique gives the model more to work with. None of them, by itself, decides what the work should be.

These techniques are worth using. The instruction file is the one whose value is most often assumed. It tells an agent what the project expects, but where such files have been compared against none, the work has come out no better: what changed was how the agent worked, not what it produced. A context file passes on what a team already knows; it is not a lever on quality. Retrieval sees only what someone stored, and only in the form they stored it. Tool access gives current state, not durable intent. Session context is a selection, not the whole history. Files can preserve what the session loses, and written records are the foundation of the workflow that follows. But a hand-built collection of files will not match a framework that defines the artifacts, their relationships and their checks.

A specification is one such written reference. It is something tools, agents and people can work from, and it can be reviewed and corrected. A wrong specification is a defect to fix, not a truth to obey. The question is therefore not whether a document exists, but whether it preserves the intent the work needs and whether the team keeps it honest.

1.5 What the work needs

These failures suggest a set of needs, not a feature list. The first group is about preserving intent and context. A durable record should persist the intent of a change: why it is needed, what it should achieve, and what is excluded. It should make key information available later without requiring the old transcript. It should capture the general rules that apply to change, such as architecture, standards, testing, security, accessibility and error handling. It should describe the complete application, not only the part being changed. And it should separate current behaviour from the proposed change.

The second group is about how the work is reviewed, traced, delivered and validated. The record should be reviewable as an artifact, not only as a conversation. It should support traceability from a requirement to design decisions, tasks, tests and implementation. It should enable incremental delivery, so work can be split into reviewable changes. It should support validation, not just generation: acceptance criteria and tests need a basis for checking the result. The tests are not that basis on their own. A test can pass and still measure nothing that was asked for, because no test states which claim it is meant to decide. Only a requirement written down beforehand gives a test something to be measured against, and says what passing is supposed to mean. And it should remain lightweight and proportional, because a record that costs more than the change it describes will be abandoned.

1.6 From needs to spec-driven development

One family of practices responds to those needs by making intent explicit and treating the specification as an active artifact. In spec-driven development (SDD), requirements, constraints, acceptance criteria and validation are made explicit before and during implementation. The specification guides planning, implementation, testing and validation. It is a living reference rather than a project history, and it is expected to change when the work teaches something new.

One concrete implementation is OpenSpec. It organizes work as a change proposal, capability specifications, a design and a task list. Its specs/ directory holds the current behaviour of the system; its changes/ directory holds proposed modifications and the artifacts that describe them. Those are conventions, not requirements of spec-driven development.

The needs, not the tool, are the test. Another spec-driven tool or a team's own practice may use different names, different artifacts and a different file layout; what counts is whether it meets the needs of section 1.5, and the names matter less than the record. OpenSpec is replaceable in this argument.

1.7 What SDD costs

The cost of a record cannot be priced exactly, but its shape is not in doubt, and it arrives before anything is paid back. Planning takes time and tokens, and the attention it demands competes with the attention the rest of the work needs. The record is work of its own: it has to be read, reviewed and kept current, and every hour on it is an hour not spent on something else.

Most of the cost is not the writing. It is the deciding: the questions a record has to answer are the questions the work would otherwise have left to whoever implemented it, and answering them takes judgment. A page of prose is cheap; the hour spent settling what the page should say is the expensive part, and that hour is spent whether or not the page is ever written.

What it saves is rework that did not happen, which is why the saving is hard to see. A change that goes well leaves no trace of the version that would have gone wrong, so the benefit never appears as a line anyone can point at. The cost does: it sits in the session, in the review and in the record.

The bill is not small. Where the two routes have been run side by side on the same tasks, the one that wrote a specification, a plan and a task list before implementing spent many times the tokens and the elapsed time of a single free-form request, for a gain in passing tests that was real and far smaller than that multiple. A benchmark is not a team, so the comparison does not fix the price; it fixes the order of magnitude. This is a purchase with a visible bill, not a small extra step.

A record comes in sizes, and the size is what sets the price. It can be a paragraph in a change description, a specification kept beside the code, or the artifact from which the code is generated. Each size asks for more discipline than the one before and has to stay true for longer, so choosing a size is choosing what the work costs.

The person who pays for a record is usually not the person who gains by it. The effort falls on whoever writes it; the saving falls on whoever reads it later, who never sees the hour it cost. That is why a practice can be worth keeping for one person and still be resisted by the team around them. A team that wants the saving has to say what deserves a record: left to each person, the answers diverge and the record becomes a different thing in every change.

1.8 What it returns

In return, three things stop being lost. Rework is avoided: the decisions that implementation would have forced were settled before it. Review gains a subject: the reviewer sees the intent and the exclusions, not only the diff. And the next change gains a starting point, because it begins from a written reference rather than from someone's memory of the last conversation.

How large that return is cannot be measured from the outside, and it should be read as an estimate. Part of it comes from the record, part from the models being better at the same task than they were, and part from having stated the goal before delegating the work, which a careful conversation would produce as well. What remains is a judgment: the record is worth its cost to the people who keep it, and the size of the return is not established.

The measurements that exist are sobering. Where specifications have been compared against none across tens of thousands of changes, the difference in defects and in rework has been hard to find at all, and the association that does appear is explained by the difficulty of the work that gets specified. Such a comparison sees specification documents as they sit in repositories — a ticket reference, a page beside the code — and not the practice of writing one, which is what this chapter argues for. So it does not show that a record fails to help. It shows that the help has not been visible where it was expected to be easiest to see, which is an argument for choosing where to write a record rather than for abandoning the practice.

1.9 When SDD earns its cost

SDD is strong where intent, constraints and verification matter. Feature development, behavioural changes, integrations, refactors with risk, and security-sensitive work all benefit from a record that says what should happen and how it will be checked. So does collaboration among humans and agents, because the record is the shared reference they can both work from.

SDD is less useful when the cost of specification exceeds the value of the change. A quick experiment, a one-off script, an exploratory spike, a trivial fix, or an early prototype whose purpose is to learn what to build may need only a conversation. Writing a full record for such work can slow the learning that the work exists to produce. The list is not exhaustive, and simple work is not a defect.

None of this removes engineering judgment. A specification can also be incomplete, overly rigid or too abstract. The team still has to review the requirements, challenge the design, write meaningful tests, inspect the code and maintain the specification. SDD reduces guesswork; it does not transfer accountability to a document or a tool. The human remains responsible for the artifacts being right.

SDD does not replace direct AI coding or conversational exploration. The chapter has described three ways of working: direct generation, explain mode — the conversation before code — and spec-driven development. Each has legitimate uses, and the choice should follow the situation rather than an ideology. The table below gives a better default for several situations. Three questions generate it: how long the result has to live, how many people or agents will work on it, and what a wrong guess would cost. The three ways of working differ in whether a record is used; these questions decide how large that record should be. "Better default" does not mean the only option.

Situation Better default
Explore an idea or learn an API Direct generation or explain mode
Build a disposable prototype Direct generation; keep light notes if it survives
Fix a small isolated bug Explain mode; add a lightweight change record if the fix grows
Change user-facing behaviour SDD
Work on a critical workflow or integration SDD
Make an architectural decision SDD, especially with recorded rationale
Work across multiple sessions, people or agents SDD
Need reviewable intent and traceability SDD

These three ways of working are not stages to graduate from; they answer different durations. Direct generation is fastest when the result can be tried at once. Explain mode is better when the request has to be understood before code exists. Spec-driven development earns its cost when intent has to survive the session, be reviewed by someone else, or be traced from a requirement to a test.

The three ways differ in how they treat the information the model does not have. Direct generation leaves the model to guess. Explain mode resolves some of the gaps before code exists, but its answers stay in the conversation. A durable record keeps those answers where a later session, reviewer or agent can find them, so the next change does not start from a partial memory. The conversation is where understanding starts, but it is not where it stays. A specification, a change record and the tests that decide them are one way to keep that reference honest. The rule is therefore not "always specify" but "preserve enough context for the work": use the lightest process that keeps the model from having to guess about what matters, and that preserves the context needed to build, review and maintain the result.

2. The Cornerstones of Spec-Driven Development

The conversation in chapter 1 settled the intent, and when it ended, nothing had been written down. A good discussion is not a durable record. This chapter takes the next step: it names the principles that make a record durable enough to guide work. Spec-driven development (SDD) is a disciplined way to build software in which an explicit, versioned specification steers planning, implementation, testing and maintenance. It is not a programming language, and it does not replace engineering judgment. It is a way to make intent available to the people and tools that have to act on it.

2.1 What software development already solved

The gap between an idea and a working system is old, and software development has built practices to close it:

  • requirements engineering captures what a system should do, for whom, and under which constraints, and separates functional behaviour from quality attributes such as performance, security and usability;
  • architecture and design describe the system's structure, its components and responsibilities, its interfaces and its important trade-offs;
  • version control records how the code evolved, enables parallel work and makes a change reviewable;
  • issue trackers explain why work is needed, who owns it and which need it serves;
  • automated tests encode expected behaviour and guard against regressions;
  • code review brings a second pair of eyes to correctness, security and maintainability;
  • documentation carries knowledge beyond the conversation that produced it, though it often goes stale when it is written after implementation.

These practices remain valuable. SDD does not discard them or pretend to have invented them. It changes what organizes them: instead of a specification that is written once and then left behind, the specification remains active while the work is planned, implemented, tested and maintained. The change is in the organizing principle, not in the list of practices.

2.2 What AI changed

Chapter 1 described what happens when a model can turn a sentence into a plausible implementation. The consequence for this chapter is narrower. A human writing code carries a great deal of context implicitly: experience, project conventions, architectural constraints and a sense of the users. When a model generates code, that context has to be made explicit or the model will fill the gap with a guess. The faster the code arrives, the more expensive a wrong assumption becomes.

The guess is not made in a vacuum. A harness is everything around a language model that turns it into an agent: the loop that feeds results back to the model, the tools it can call, the context and instructions it receives, and the permissions that limit what it may do. In a coding agent, the model proposes an edit; the harness applies it, runs the tests and returns the output for the next step. People use the word more narrowly for a product, and more broadly for everything a team assembles around one; this chapter uses it for the whole runtime that couples the model to the work. What the harness supplies decides how much of the gap remains.

A single plausible answer is not the same as the right answer. A model can generate several, and it cannot know which one matches the team's intent unless that intent is available. Two sessions can follow different conventions: one may use the pattern the project already has, and the next may invent a new one. The response is not a better prompt. It is a shared, explicit reference: requirements, constraints, acceptance criteria and project context become first-class artifacts. The specification is that reference for intent.

2.3 Why the order of work changes

Traditional documentation often describes a system after it has been built, or it describes a plan that is never updated once implementation begins. In an AI-assisted workflow, that weakness is more visible: an agent may use outdated or incomplete context and produce code that fits the document rather than the system. The problem is not new, but the cost of discovering it late is higher.

SDD changes the order of work:

  1. Describe the problem and the desired outcome.
  2. Specify behaviour, constraints and acceptance criteria.
  3. Plan the technical approach.
  4. Break the work into reviewable tasks.
  5. Implement with AI and human collaboration.
  6. Validate the implementation against the specification.
  7. Update the specification so it continues to describe the system accurately.

The order is a discipline, not a claim that the intent is complete before the first line of code exists. What a specification is missing often becomes clear only while the work is under way, which is why the last step is part of the method rather than an afterthought.

The order creates a feedback loop between intent and implementation. Code is no longer the only reliable record of what the system does; the specification becomes a living description of expected behaviour, while code, tests and documentation stay aligned with it. The loop is not automatic. Someone has to notice that the implementation taught something new and carry it back into the specification.

2.4 The cornerstones

SDD frameworks differ in terminology and workflow, but most share a small set of foundational ideas. These are the cornerstones: principles that hold regardless of the tool or the names a team uses. They are not a product feature list. Chapter 1 derived ten needs from the gaps left by direct generation and conversation. The cornerstones are those needs restated as principles that a workflow can be checked against. Three differences are deliberate. Proportionality does not appear as a cornerstone, because it governs how much record to write rather than what the record contains. Living documentation and human control do appear, because chapter 1 stated them as rules of judgment rather than as needs, and a workflow has to carry them.

Cornerstone Meaning How it decays
Explicit intent The purpose, scope, users and expected outcome of a change are written down before implementation. Scope drifts from the work done.
Specification as shared reference The specification describes what the system should do and is the shared reference for intent; code serves it. It is not infallible: it is reviewed, corrected and maintained. Implementation detail goes stale under refactoring.
Current-state knowledge The project describes the capabilities and behaviour it has today, not only the work it plans. Behaviour changes; the description does not.
Change as a first-class unit A modification has its own record: why it is needed, what changes, how it will be built and how the result is checked. Later decisions made in code go unrecorded.
Separation of current and proposed state The team can distinguish what the system does today from what a proposed change adds, modifies or removes. Proposed changes merge into the description before they are built.
Shared project context Conventions, constraints, architectural rules and quality expectations are available to every contributor and every AI session. Conventions are not revisited; agents follow stale rules.
Traceability Requirements connect to the design, tasks, tests and code that realize them. Links go stale when code or tests move.
Reviewability Intent and plan can be reviewed before code is written, not only afterward. Review happens after code; intent is rebuilt from the diff.
Validation Acceptance criteria and tests determine whether the implementation fulfils the specification. Tests check written expectations, not every goal.
Living documentation After a change is completed, the specification is updated so future work starts from an accurate picture. Updates are skipped; the next change plans against stale text.
Human control Humans decide what to build, review trade-offs, approve changes and remain accountable for the result. Approval loses force when the judge produced the work.

These cornerstones are not bureaucratic overhead. They are mechanisms for preserving the context that AI needs and that teams have always needed but often kept in informal conversations. A team that keeps them in place does not add ceremony for its own sake; it reduces the number of things that have to be remembered or guessed.

2.5 Problems SDD solves

SDD is most effective where context is missing, temporary or inconsistent. Chapter 1 showed ambiguity, lost context, drift and weak review in detail. Four further consequences follow from the same gap:

  • Inconsistent AI output. Shared conventions and constraints help agents produce results that fit the project instead of inventing a pattern in every session.
  • Poor onboarding. A new developer or agent can read the current specifications to understand the major capabilities and constraints. Where specifications pass between developers and other roles, that reading pays most; in a team of developers only, it adds a document to read and changes less than the argument suggests.
  • Unclear scope. Explicit requirements and exclusions make trade-offs visible. Chapter 1's CSV export request can quietly grow a filter, a permission rule and a size limit that nobody asked for.
  • Fragmented knowledge. Requirements, rationale, tasks and validation criteria are connected instead of scattered across chats, tickets, wikis and comments.

These are problems of communication and memory, not of coding skill. A team that cannot write a clear requirement will not become able to do so because it adopts a framework; the framework only makes the gap visible sooner.

2.6 Problems SDD does not solve

SDD is not a cure-all. It improves the quality of communication and decision-making, but it cannot replace the responsibilities of software engineering.

  • It does not guarantee correct requirements. A precise specification of the wrong behaviour is still wrong.
  • It does not eliminate testing. Specifications define expected behaviour; tests and verification still prove that the implementation behaves as intended.
  • It does not make a green result independent. Tests are often written by the same agent as the code, from the same reading of the requirement, so a passing run can confirm a shared misunderstanding.
  • It does not remove architectural judgment. Choosing between designs, evaluating trade-offs and understanding long-term consequences remain human work.
  • It does not make bad product decisions good. SDD can clarify a decision; it cannot decide business value, priorities or user needs by itself.
  • It does not remove the need for code review. Generated code still needs inspection for correctness, security, performance, maintainability and fit with the system.
  • It does not make every task worth specifying. Chapter 1 covered how to judge when the cost is worth it; this list is about the limits that remain even then.
  • It does not prevent specification rot automatically. Specifications must be maintained, or they become misleading documentation.

The limits are the limits of any written record, not a defect in the idea.

Decay has a mechanism, and it is the reason the cornerstone asks for what rather than how. Implementation detail helps an agent that lacks context, and it dates the record as soon as the code moves: a named class, function or library version changes under refactoring while the behaviour it produces does not. Detail that is structured well improves what an agent produces, so the answer is not less detail. It is to keep the detail apart from the behaviour it serves, and to expect the detail to be replaced.

A green test is a weak signal on its own. It can pass because the work is right or because the test never looks, and the result looks identical either way. Evidence requires the possibility of failure: only a test that could have gone the other way shows anything about the claim.

A requirement that constrains a state does not say how a transition between two states is carried out. The design records that decision, and the reason it chose one order over another.

2.7 Why developers remain essential

AI changes the daily work of developers, but it does not remove the need for them. Developers translate incomplete human goals into precise, testable intent. They understand the organization around the system, evaluate risk and take responsibility for what is delivered. A model can produce an implementation; it cannot decide what should exist, why it should exist, or whether the result is acceptable.

In an SDD workflow, developers spend more time on activities that require judgment:

  • understanding user and business problems;
  • identifying constraints, risks and non-functional requirements;
  • designing and reviewing architectural options;
  • writing and reviewing specifications;
  • challenging AI-generated plans and implementations;
  • reviewing security, privacy, performance and maintainability;
  • deciding what should be automated and what should remain manual;
  • maintaining a coherent system rather than a collection of isolated generated fragments.

The developer's role shifts from typing every line to directing, reviewing and integrating work. That is a change in emphasis, not a loss of relevance.

Whoever writes a record bears its cost, while its benefit goes to people who arrive later, so a team must settle what earns one.

SDD is best understood as a contract between the people who want a system, the people who build it and the AI tools that help build it. It makes intent explicit, keeps that intent available and connects it to implementation and verification. That is what stops the model from guessing and the team from relying on memory. The cornerstones are the terms of that contract: they name what must be preserved, what must be reviewed and what remains human responsibility. Those terms still have to be carried by something. The next chapter shows one implementation that carries them, and what the conventions cannot carry.

3. How OpenSpec Carries the Cornerstones

Chapter 1 introduced OpenSpec as one example of a spec-driven workflow and named its artifacts in passing. Chapter 2 named the principles those artifacts have to satisfy. This chapter shows how one set of conventions implements those principles, and where the conventions stop.

It is a map, not a manual. One section gives the technical background, for the reader who wants to know what the conventions run on; installation, commands and configuration belong to the tool's own documentation. What matters here is the shape of the record: where intent is written down, how a proposed change is separated from the system as it is, and what keeps the two connected. A different tool could arrange the same material under other names and still serve the same principles. The question to carry through the chapter is not what the tool does, but which principle each convention serves.

3.1 What the tool is made of

OpenSpec is a small program, not a platform. It is an open-source command-line tool, MIT-licensed and maintained by Fission-AI, written in TypeScript and distributed as an npm package or as a standalone binary that runs without Node.js. It is installed once on a machine and used per project; there is no service to sign up for and nothing to host. The project's own development is planned with OpenSpec, so its repository is a working example of the conventions this chapter describes.

All of a project's artifacts are Markdown in the repository. There is no server, no daemon, no database and no API key: nothing the work depends on runs between commands, and what the project plans and specifies lives in Markdown files and nowhere else. The program does keep some state on the machine: the global configuration with its profile, schemas a user shares across projects, skills installed for every project, and stores registered as standalone OpenSpec repositories. It also sends anonymous usage statistics, the command's name and the release and nothing of the project, unless OPENSPEC_TELEMETRY=0 or the configuration turns them off. The openspec/ tree is plain files, versioned and shared by git like any other file. A project that stops using the tool keeps files any editor can read: the format is Markdown, and the tool operates on it rather than containing it.

The work is split between the agent and the program. The agent in the coding tool drafts and edits the artifacts, because that part needs language and judgment. The program does what should not depend on a model: it parses the Markdown structure, checks the conventions, counts task checkboxes to compute progress, and refuses a change that fails validation. The merge of a delta into the main specifications at archive has two paths: the openspec archive command makes it in the program, and the archive workflow has the agent make it, following the rules of the sync workflow, and then validates the main specifications. A later chapter describes both. Reporting commands can emit machine-readable output, so the checks can run wherever checks belong. A model writes, a program verifies, a person approves. A passing validation is a structural fact, not a verdict on the requirements — chapter 2's limits apply unchanged — and structure is exactly the part a program can be trusted with.

Integration with the coding tools is by generated files, not by a protocol. The setup command, openspec init, writes OpenSpec's skills into one shared directory, in whatever file format the tools expect. By default that directory is ~/.agents/skills/, shared by every project on the machine. With --scope project it is the repository's own .agents/skills/, and the line skillsScope: project in the project's configuration records that choice for everyone who clones it. Every skill but one delivers one workflow, which is OpenSpec's word for one action on a change, and a profile chooses which workflows are installed. The exception is openspec, a router that picks the right skill for a request, and every profile installs it alongside the rest. A coding tool reads that directory, directly or through links of its own. The current release writes no slash commands. The release this description was checked against is named in the repository's README. The openspec update command regenerates those files when the program changes, so the instructions an agent sees stay in step with the program that checks its work. No protocol stands between the program and the assistant — not an MCP server, not an API — and no assistant is privileged. What the integration moves is text, and text is the one thing every coding tool already reads.

The shape of a change is data. A schema is a folder of plain files: one YAML file that declares each artifact a change produces — the file it generates, what it requires first, and the instruction the agent receives when creating it — and one Markdown template per artifact. A line in the project's configuration names the schema to use. The default produces the four artifacts this chapter walks through: proposal, delta specifications, design and tasks. A project can fork a schema and edit it — drop an artifact, add one, rewrite the instructions — and the program then enforces the project's schema as if it had shipped that way. The dependencies between artifacts are enablers, not phase gates: they say what becomes possible, not what must happen next. What a change folder contains is fixed by the project, not by the tool, and the tool checks whatever the project declared.

With the tool's nature stated, what remains to describe is what those files hold.

3.2 The shape of the record

The design is easier to hold when it is reduced to two locations in the repository. One set of specifications describes the system as it is today. A separate set of change folders describes work that is proposed or in progress. Both live in a directory called openspec/, next to the code they describe.

Everything else in this chapter follows from that split. If the specifications described only the work in progress, the project would have plans and no memory. If they described only the current system, a change would have no place to say what it intends. Keeping both in one repository is what lets a reader ask two separate questions: what does this system do, and what is about to change?

3.3 The system as it is

The specifications under openspec/specs/ are organized by capability. A capability is a coherent area of behaviour, and each one holds requirements and scenarios. A requirement states what must be true of the system. A scenario gives one concrete case that shows the requirement being met or missed.

This is the cornerstone of current-state knowledge made concrete. A developer or an agent who needs to know how the system behaves can read the capability instead of reconstructing it from code, diagrams or memory. The specification is not a summary of the code and it is not a design document. It states the behaviour the code is supposed to have, which is why it can be used to judge the code rather than merely describe it. That is what the convention asks for, and it is not what most repositories contain: most specifications written this way carry implementation detail, and the detail is there because it helps the agent that reads it. The rule protects the part that has to outlive the code. That is the cornerstone of the specification as shared reference.

3.4 A change as a folder

A proposed modification lives in openspec/changes/<change-name>/. The folder is self-contained: it holds the four artifacts the default schema produces, and the point here is that they sit together.

That grouping is the cornerstone of a change as a first-class unit, and it is the cornerstone of reviewability. A reviewer can read the intent, the expected behaviour and the plan before any code exists, instead of reconstructing them from a diff. It is also what makes a change a unit of work rather than a side effect of version control: it can be reviewed, revised or abandoned without leaving a half-finished branch behind.

Chapter 1 used the request "add CSV export" to show how much a single sentence leaves undecided. The same request shows what a change folder has to hold. As a change it becomes add-csv-export/, and the folder has to answer the questions the sentence left open: which records are exported, which columns, whether the current filter applies, how dates and numbers are formatted, and who is permitted to export what. The illustration is not a change in this repository. Its value is that the request is small enough to hold in mind while the conventions are introduced.

A delta specification does not repeat the whole system specification. It states only what the change does to it, using explicit operations: a requirement can be added, modified, removed or renamed. OpenSpec names the four ADDED, MODIFIED, REMOVED and RENAMED, so the kind of change is part of the record rather than something a reader has to infer. The CSV export change adds a requirement that describes export. It may also modify a requirement about who may see which records, because exporting is one way of seeing them. The rest of the capability is left alone.

The effect is that the behavioural impact of a change is visible in one place. A reviewer sees both the new behaviour and its effect on existing behaviour without holding two versions of the whole specification side by side. This is the cornerstone of separation of current and proposed state, expressed as an operation rather than as advice about where to write things. The same record names what the change leaves alone: an exclusion written down is a decision, not a gap a later reader has to guess at.

3.5 The rules that apply to all work

The repository also holds the rules that apply to every change: how the project is structured, which standards apply, what must not break. They live in the instruction files an agent reads when a session opens — AGENTS.md, which is also the one such file several tools read — and in the project context the tool loads before planning. Because those rules live with the code, the same material is available to a developer, a reviewer and an agent.

That is the cornerstone of shared project context. It does not follow that an agent reads the rules automatically. It follows that the rules have a place where they can be found, and that a session which consults them starts from the project's conventions rather than from a generic default.

3.6 From intent to a merged specification

The artifacts form a path. The proposal says why the work is needed — explicit intent, written down before anything is built. The delta says what behaviour changes. The design says how the work will be approached. The tasks connect the design to implementation steps. Each step can be checked against the one before it, so a disagreement between intent and plan becomes visible before it becomes a disagreement between plan and code.

That path is the cornerstone of traceability, and it is deliberately short. A change does not have to fill every artifact to be traceable. It has to be possible to follow the reasoning from the request to the code without guessing which decision came from where.

A requirement is identified by its own title. The identifier travels with design decisions and tasks, and the specification holds the wording. Everything else points at it: a chapter or an artifact that wants to discuss what the requirement says uses the name and leaves the sentence where it is. Carrying the wording along is how a second copy of a rule appears in a document edited on a different schedule, and two copies of one rule can disagree.

Validation is the check at the end of the path. That check is the cornerstone of validation. Acceptance criteria and tests decide whether the implementation satisfies the specification, and the specification is the reference for that decision rather than the implementation being its own judge. This is what keeps a written record from becoming a description written after the fact. If the code decides what counts as correct, the specification records the outcome of the work. If the specification decides, the work can fail to meet it, and the failure is visible.

Completion is what keeps the record alive. When the work is finished, the delta is merged into the capability specification, so the description of the system matches the system again. The change folder then moves into a dated archive, where it keeps the record of what changed and the design that went with it.

That is the cornerstone of living documentation, and it is the difference between a specification written before coding and one that is maintained. The current specification is updated because the work changed, not because someone remembered to update it. The archive is not a backup; it is the record of how the current description reached its form. A decision that was settled in a conversation and never written into the change is not in it, and nothing later can recover it.

3.7 What the conventions leave to people

None of this decides what to build. The conventions give intent a place, a shape and a check; they do not supply the intent. A change folder can hold a proposal that argues for the wrong feature, a delta that specifies the wrong behaviour and tasks that implement it carefully. The record does not prevent that. It makes the decision visible, which is what allows it to be challenged before it is built.

That is the last cornerstone, human control, and it is the one the conventions cannot carry. A tool can hold a decision. It cannot make one.

Validation happens at the end of the change, and nothing checks afterwards whether the specification and the code still agree. A later change can satisfy its own requirement, pass its own tests and quietly break a constraint from an earlier one; no tool in the sample was shown to look for that, and the practitioners who wanted it had to build checks of their own. A check would show a disagreement, not which of the two is wrong.

Most people who work this way read a specification in part rather than in full, or hand the review to another agent. Partial reading is partly what the record is for: the problem, the decisions and the acceptance criteria carry the intent, and the rest is context for whoever implements. Delegating the review is the risk, because it removes the one point at which a person decides what the system should do. The record does not help there either: it shows the path that was taken, and a rejected alternative survives only if someone wrote it down.

The conventions are worth reading as answers to the cornerstones rather than as a directory layout. Ten of the eleven cornerstones have a convention in this chapter that carries them; human control is the limit named above. The split between what the system is and what is about to change carries most of the principles; the rest are carried by where the material lives, by the path from proposal to tasks, and by the fact that the specification rather than the code is what the work is checked against. The next chapter takes one requirement through this path, from a sentence that looks complete to the constraint that settles it.

4. One Change from Request to Archive

A customer pays 100 cents for a product that costs 70 cents, and the machine owes 30 cents back. Written as a request, that sentence sounds complete. It does not say which coins the machine should use, what happens when it has none left, or whether the product is handed over before the change is counted. Those questions have to become artifacts before anyone writes code. This chapter follows one change through the path from its request to its archive, on a small example: a vending machine that gives change. The example is kept in its own repository, with its own OpenSpec root, and it contains no code. What the reader sees here is what the tool produces at each stage.

4.1 A change is a folder

In OpenSpec a change is a folder under openspec/changes/, named after the change. The path from a request to an archived change has four stages, shown in the first table. The folder holds the artifacts the path produces, and the second table lists them with the other files of a change.

Stage What happens
Request The starting statement of what the change should do, as in the opening paragraph.
Create the artifacts The propose workflow creates the four artifacts listed in the second table. It creates them in the order the schema declares. The specification and the design each need only the proposal, and the tasks need both of them. That order decides what can be made next. It is not a set of gates that must be passed in turn; chapter 3 explains this.
Validation The validate command checks the change's delta specifications, and it looks in the main specifications for the capabilities the change says it will modify.
Archive Archiving merges the change's specification into the main specification and moves the change folder into the archive.

The artifacts come from the default schema of the tool, spec-driven.

Item File What it says Discussed in
Change openspec/changes/<change>/ The folder of one change. Chapter 4
Proposal proposal.md Why the change exists and what it changes. Chapters 4 and 5
Capability specs/<capability>/ The folder for one area of behaviour, such as purchase. Chapters 4 and 6
Specification specs/<capability>/spec.md What one change adds, modifies or removes. Chapters 4 and 6
Main specification openspec/specs/<capability>/spec.md The system as it stands. Chapters 4 and 6
Design design.md How the work is done. Chapters 4 and 7
Tasks tasks.md The checks that turn the design into work. Chapters 4 and 8
Schema marker .openspec.yaml The schema the change follows, and skip_specs when it has no deltas. Chapter 4

The two tables answer different questions, and a reader who keeps them apart will see that the tool's stages are not documents, and that the documents are not a checklist of stages. Validation and archive are the only stages that do not add a file to the change.

The example change is give-exact-change. It lives in ../vending-machine, a separate repository with its own OpenSpec root, and it adds a capability called purchase. Its first requirement is the one this chapter follows to the end: the machine gives change in coins from its stock. A second change, refuse-without-exact-change, revises that requirement. Both changes are archived in the example repository, and the quotations below are taken from them as they were written.

4.2 The proposal

The proposal is the first artifact. It says why the change exists and what it changes. It does not say how the work is done; that belongs to the design. The default template has four parts: Why, What Changes, Capabilities and Impact.

Proposal Description
Why The problem or opportunity in one or two sentences: why the change is needed. The first change gives two sentences.
What Changes A list of what is added, modified or removed. The first change adds the capability purchase with two requirements.
Capabilities The capabilities the change creates or modifies, each with the spec file it needs. The first change creates purchase.
Impact The files, specifications or systems the change touches. The first change names the spec file that archiving will create.

The proposal of the change give-exact-change, proposal.md, is shown in full as archived:

## Why

A customer who pays more than the price of a product expects the difference back.
The machine holds coins, so it has to decide which coins make up the difference.

## What Changes

- Add a capability `purchase` with two requirements: the coins the machine holds,
  and the change it returns for a purchase.

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities

- `purchase`: the coins the machine holds, and the change it returns for a purchase.

## Impact

- `openspec/specs/purchase/spec.md` — created when this change is archived.

4.3 The specification

The specification, which is the delta in the change's folder, states what the system must do. Each requirement is a statement with SHALL, and each has scenarios. A change does not rewrite the whole main specification, which holds the requirements of the system as they now stand, at openspec/specs/<capability>/spec.md. A delta says what the change adds, modifies or removes, and the archive merges the delta later. The delta is written to specs/<capability>/spec.md in the change folder.

Specification Description
Purpose For a new capability: one or two sentences on what the capability is for. Archiving copies it into the main specification. The first delta has one.
ADDED / MODIFIED Requirements The operation the delta performs on the requirements of the main specification.
Requirement One statement of what the system must do, written with SHALL.
Scenario One case under a requirement, written as WHEN, the condition that can be set up, and THEN, the outcome that can be decided.

The first change uses ADDED, because the capability did not yet exist. Its delta, specs/purchase/spec.md in the change give-exact-change, is shown in full as archived. It opens with a Purpose section, and it holds two requirements, each with its scenarios:

## Purpose

Defines the coins the vending machine holds and the change it returns for a purchase, so that a customer who pays more than the price receives the difference in coins from the machine's stock.

## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: The machine holds coins of four denominations

The machine SHALL hold coins of 10, 20, 50 and 100 cents only. Amounts are stated in
cents.

#### Scenario: Stock holds only the four denominations

- **WHEN** the machine is stocked
- **THEN** every coin in its stock is a coin of 10, 20, 50 or 100 cents

### Requirement: The machine gives change in coins from its stock

The machine SHALL return to the customer the difference between the amount inserted
and the price of the product, in coins from its stock.

#### Scenario: Change is given from stock

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents, 100 cents is inserted, and the stock holds at least
  one coin of 10 cents and at least one coin of 20 cents
- **THEN** the machine returns 30 cents as one coin of 20 cents and one coin of 10
  cents

#### Scenario: Exact payment gives no change

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents and 70 cents is inserted
- **THEN** the machine returns no change

This scenario can be set up with a stock of coins, and it says exactly which coins come back. The requirement alone does not say that; the scenario does. The second change adds a third scenario of the same kind, which the first version did not have. It appears in section 4.8.

4.4 The design

The design is the third artifact. It records the decisions the requirement leaves open, and the reason for each. The requirement says what the machine returns. The design says in which order the machine works and how it finds the coins.

Design Description
Context The current state and the constraints that shape the approach. It does not restate the motivation, which is in the proposal. The first design's Context restates the requirement and says what the design covers.
Goals / Non-Goals What the design aims for and what it leaves out at design level. The first design states one goal and two non-goals. One of its non-goals is the case that section 4.7 shows the design failing.
Decisions Each decision, with the reason for it and, where one was rejected, the alternative. The default template asks for "rationale and alternatives considered".
Risks / Trade-offs Each risk, followed by its mitigation. The first design names one risk: the stock of coins runs down, and refilling is left outside the change.

The layout of each decision, as a decision, a reason and, where one was rejected, an alternative, is this project's own. The tool's template asks for decisions with rationale and alternatives, and does not prescribe a layout. The design of give-exact-change, design.md, is shown in full as archived. It reads:

## Context

The purchase capability requires the machine to return the difference in coins from
its stock. This design says how the machine works out those coins and in what order
it does its steps.

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**

- Return the difference between the amount inserted and the price, in coins from the
  stock.

**Non-Goals:**

- Deciding what happens when the stock cannot make the change. This design does not
  say.
- Choosing the coins so that the stock stays balanced, or so that the fewest coins are
  returned.

## Decisions

**Decision**: release the product first, then work out the change from the coins in
stock.

**Why**: the customer should not wait at the machine after the payment is complete.

**Decision**: work out the change greedily. Take the largest coin that does not
exceed the amount still owed, for as long as the stock of that coin lasts. Repeat
until nothing is owed.

**Why**: the method is short to state and easy to trace by hand.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- The stock of coins shrinks with each purchase, and nothing in this design refills it.
  → Refilling is outside this change; the design assumes a stocked machine.

## Findings

Each scenario is traced through the design by hand.

- **Scenario "Change is given from stock"**: 100 inserted, 70 price, 30 owed. The
  largest coin that does not exceed 30 is 20; one is returned, 10 is owed. The
  largest coin that does not exceed 10 is 10; one is returned, nothing is owed.
  Result: 20 and 10. Matches the scenario.
- **Scenario "Exact payment gives no change"**: 70 inserted, 70 price, nothing owed.
  No coin is returned. Result: none. Matches the scenario.

The first design records no rejected alternative. Its two decisions are the ones the rest of the chapter depends on.

The file does not end with its risks. It closes with a Findings section, and the template's design has no such part: its parts are Context, Goals / Non-Goals, Decisions and Risks / Trade-offs. The example keeps the section as a stated exception. The walkthroughs have to be written down somewhere, and beside the decisions they test they are read by anyone who reads the decisions. The price of the exception is that the chapter has to keep the section true, because no part of the tool checks it.

4.5 The tasks

The tasks are the last artifact. They turn the design into checks, one for each part of the design that must be verified. Each task is a checkbox, and the tool counts the checkboxes to show progress.

Tasks Description
Group heading A numbered heading that groups related tasks. The first change has one group, "Check the first version".
Task A checkbox with a number and a description of the check. [ ] is open and [x] is done.
Verified by A clause after the task that names the evidence the check passed. The example's own rules fix the clause's wording, the default instruction asks each task to state how it is verified, and the template has no part for it.

The tasks of give-exact-change, tasks.md, are shown in full as archived:

## 1. Check the first version

- [x] 1.1 Trace the scenario "Change is given from stock" through the design by hand. **Verified by** the trace in the design's Findings, which matches the scenario.
- [x] 1.2 Trace the scenario "Exact payment gives no change" through the design by hand. **Verified by** the trace in the design's Findings, which matches the scenario.
- [x] 1.3 Run `openspec validate --strict`. **Verified by** the command passing.

The first two tasks send the reader to the Findings section of the design quoted in section 4.4, and the trace each one names is there. The third task records validation. Validation passed the first version. The validate command reads the change's delta specifications, and the main specifications only to see what the delta modifies; it does not read the proposal, the design or the tasks of a change that has not been archived. It does not check whether the design agrees with the scenarios, and chapter 3 names that limit. Here it has a concrete consequence. The first change was complete by every check the tool runs, and the design still did not satisfy a case that had not yet been written down.

A task list is easy to read as a plan of work. The tasks in this example are checks, and ticking one records that the check was made, not only that someone intended to make it. That difference matters later, when the box is the only record of what was done.

4.6 Archiving the first change

Archiving closes a change. It is done in one run, but it decides what the next change is checked against, so it is shown here on its own.

The first change is ready for archiving when two things hold: its tasks are checked, and its design's Findings walk through both of its scenarios, so the design and the scenarios agree on the cases that existed when the change was written.

For a new capability, archiving does four things. It creates the main specification for the capability, openspec/specs/purchase/spec.md. It copies the delta's Purpose into that file, which is why the delta begins with a Purpose section: without one, the new file carries a placeholder that someone has to replace by hand. It writes the delta's requirements into the file. And it moves the change folder into the archive, under its date, so the folder is kept as a record but is no longer work in progress, and the behaviour it describes is part of the main specification. The first lines of openspec/specs/purchase/spec.md, as give-exact-change left them when it was archived, read:

# purchase Specification

## Purpose
Defines the coins the vending machine holds and the change it returns for a purchase, so that a customer who pays more than the price receives the difference in coins from the machine's stock.

## Requirements

### Requirement: The machine holds coins of four denominations

The machine SHALL hold coins of 10, 20, 50 and 100 cents only. Amounts are stated in
cents.

The example was archived with an earlier release; current releases also leave a blank line after the ## Purpose heading, and otherwise the file reads the same. The file has a title, a Purpose and the requirements of the first change, and nothing else. It does not name the change that wrote it. That record is the archived folder, which holds the proposal, the design, the tasks and the delta. The main specification says what the system is; the archive says how it came to be.

Archiving does not decide whether the change is right. That was decided earlier, by the tasks and the walkthrough of the scenarios. Archiving records a decision that has already been made, and it does so only when the change is closed. This is why the first change is archived before the second one begins: the second change modifies a requirement that exists in the main specification only after the archive.

4.7 The case nobody had written

The second change, refuse-without-exact-change, starts from the main specification that section 4.6 created. Its archive is in section 4.14. The case it starts from is one the first version lacked. The requirement says the machine returns the difference in coins from its stock, so the question is what happens when the stock cannot make that difference. The stock in the case holds one coin of 10 cents and no coin of 20 or 50 cents. Walked through the first design, the case fails. The design had named this case as a non-goal, so it never decided it. The walkthrough is recorded in the Findings of design.md in the change refuse-without-exact-change, labelled Trace A. It reads:

**Trace A: the first design, scenario "Stock cannot make the change".** The price is
70, 100 is inserted, so 30 is owed. The stock holds one coin of 10 and none of 20.
The first design releases the product first. The largest coin that does not exceed 30
is 10, so one is returned and 20 is still owed. No coin can be returned for 20. The
customer leaves with the product and 10 of the 30 owed, and nothing says so.

The walkthrough shows two symptoms. The product is released before the change is worked out, and the change returned is less than the amount owed without any sign of it.

4.8 The correction

This section describes the second change, refuse-without-exact-change. It is a separate change, with its own folder and its own artifacts, and it does not edit the first change: the first change's design was not reopened. The second change starts where section 4.7 ends.

The second change does three things, and each one is in a different artifact:

  • Its proposal changes the requirement. The machine must return the exact amount, and if it cannot, it refuses the purchase, releases no product and returns the amount inserted.
  • Its specification adds a scenario for a stock that cannot make the change.
  • Its design works out the change before the product is released.

Each of the four files of the second change has its own section below, in the order the schema declares them: the proposal, the specification, the design and the tasks. Each section follows the pattern of the matching section for the first change, so that the two can be read side by side.

4.9 The proposal of the second change

The proposal of the second change answers a different question from the first. The first proposal says why a customer should receive change at all. This one says why a rule that the first change wrote has to be changed, and its reason is a walkthrough rather than a situation. The four parts are the same, and each is filled from that reason.

Second change: proposal What this change puts there
Why The failure the walkthrough found: two symptoms, and the fact that validation passed the first version anyway.
What Changes Three changes: the requirement requires exact change, a scenario is added for a stock that cannot make the change, and the design works out the change before release.
Capabilities One modified capability, purchase, and the requirement it changes. No capability is created.
Impact The main specification that the first change created. This change modifies that file when it is archived.

refuse-without-exact-change, proposal.md

## Why

While writing the scenario for a stock that cannot make the change, the first version
has no answer. Tracing the scenario through the design of `give-exact-change` shows two
symptoms:

1. The product is released before the change is worked out. A customer who is short
   of change keeps the product.
2. With short stock the change is less than the amount owed, and nothing says so.

`openspec validate` passed the first version. It checks the structure of the
artifacts, not whether a design agrees with a scenario.

## What Changes

- The requirement "The machine gives change in coins from its stock" requires exact
  change. If the exact change cannot be made, the purchase is refused and the amount
  inserted is returned. No product is released.
- A scenario is added for a stock that cannot make the change.
- The design works out the change before the product is released.

## Capabilities

### Modified Capabilities

- `purchase`: the requirement "The machine gives change in coins from its stock" changes to require exact change.

## Impact

- `openspec/specs/purchase/spec.md` — the change requirement is modified when this
  change is archived.

The Why section differs most from the first proposal's Why. The first contains no reference to any file. The second cites one: the design of give-exact-change, the artifact that the walkthrough tested. A reader can therefore check the reason by following the trace in section 4.7. The first proposal could not have been written in this form, because the failure was not known until the walkthrough had been made.

The Capabilities section uses the Modified heading. The template asks for the exact path of an existing specification under that heading, so the delta has to match a file that is already there. The first change created its capability and used the New heading, which carried no such constraint.

Impact names the main specification and no new file. The first change's Impact named the file that archiving would create. This one names the file that archiving will change. Neither proposal has a Non-goals part, because the example removed it: the default template does not have one.

4.10 The specification of the second change

A delta for a modified capability has one job: it replaces a requirement in a specification that already exists. It therefore carries the requirement as a whole, and it carries no Purpose, because the specification it changes already has one. The tool ignores a Purpose in such a delta. The first delta began with a Purpose because it created a capability; this one begins with the requirement.

Second change: specification What this change puts there
MODIFIED Requirements One requirement, under a MODIFIED heading. The delta replaces the existing requirement of that name.
Requirement "The machine gives change in coins from its stock", written out in full. It gains the word "exactly" and a second sentence about refusal.
Scenario Three scenarios. The first two keep the text they had in the first change, and the third is added here.
Purpose Not present. The main specification keeps the Purpose it already has.

refuse-without-exact-change, specs/purchase/spec.md

## MODIFIED Requirements

### Requirement: The machine gives change in coins from its stock

The machine SHALL return to the customer the difference between the amount inserted
and the price of the product, exactly, in coins from its stock. If it cannot return
that exact amount, it SHALL refuse the purchase, release no product, and return the
amount inserted.

#### Scenario: Change is given from stock

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents, 100 cents is inserted, and the stock holds at least
  one coin of 10 cents and at least one coin of 20 cents
- **THEN** the machine returns 30 cents as one coin of 20 cents and one coin of 10
  cents

#### Scenario: Exact payment gives no change

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents and 70 cents is inserted
- **THEN** the machine returns no change

#### Scenario: Stock cannot make the change

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents, 100 cents is inserted, and the stock holds one coin
  of 10 cents and no coin of 20 or 50 cents
- **THEN** the machine refuses the purchase, releases no product, and returns the 100
  cents inserted

Set the first sentence of the requirement beside the first change's version. One word has been inserted, "exactly". The sentence after it is new. It states the outcome that the first requirement left open, and the scenario is the only place where that outcome can be decided as a case.

The two earlier scenarios keep their text, so the requirement is now checked against those two cases and the new one. The new scenario uses the same price and the same coin inserted as the first scenario, but a different stock. The first scenario needs at least one coin of 20 cents; the new one needs no coin of 20 or 50 cents. The two cases divide the stock by the 20-cent coin, although they do not cover every stock.

The schema warns that a MODIFIED delta with partial content loses detail when it is archived. The requirement is therefore quoted whole, as the replacement that archiving writes into the main specification.

4.11 The design of the second change

The design of the second change explains the requirement's new outcome, not only the order of steps. It is the file that replaces the first design's order, records the alternatives that were rejected, and records the walkthrough that shows the new order works for the case that failed.

Second change: design What this change puts there
Context Names the first design by its change and says that this design replaces its order of steps.
Goals / Non-Goals One goal: exact change, or refusal with the amount inserted returned. Two non-goals: the coin denominations and any message to the customer.
Decisions Two decisions, each with a reason, and two rejected alternatives.
Risks / Trade-offs One risk: refusals become more likely as the stock runs down. The design leaves the mitigation outside the change.
Findings Traces B, C and D for the revised design, and Trace A for the first. Not a template part; the example keeps it as a stated exception, explained in section 4.4.

refuse-without-exact-change, design.md

## Context

The design of `give-exact-change` released the product first and then worked out the
change greedily from the stock. Its findings traced the first two scenarios correctly.
The scenario "Stock cannot make the change" was not traced then, because it did not
exist. This design replaces the order of steps and records the trace that shows why.

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**

- Return the exact difference in coins from the stock, or refuse the purchase and return
  the amount inserted.

**Non-Goals:**

- Changing the coin denominations.
- Telling the customer why a purchase was refused.

## Decisions

**Decision**: work out the change before the product is released.

**Why**: the requirement says the change is exact. A product that is released before
the change is known cannot be taken back, so the exactness of the change must be
decided first.

**Decision**: if the greedy method does not reach the exact amount, refuse the
purchase, release no product, and return the amount inserted.

**Why**: the requirement gives no near-miss outcome. Refusing is the only outcome the
requirement allows when the exact change cannot be made.

**Alternative rejected**: release the product and return the change that can be made.
Rejected because it returns less than the requirement allows, and the customer keeps a
product for money not paid back.

**Alternative rejected**: release the product and refund the rest later. Rejected
because the product is already gone when the refund is decided.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- The stock of coins shrinks with each purchase, so refusals become more likely as the
  stock runs down. → Refilling the stock is outside this change; the design does not
  mitigate it.

## Findings

[Trace A, quoted in section 4.7.]

This trace shows both symptoms. The product is released before the change is worked
out (symptom 1), and the change returned is less than owed without a signal (symptom
2). The scenario is not satisfied by the first design.

**Trace B: the revised design, scenario "Stock cannot make the change".** The same
inputs. 30 is owed; 10 is returned, 20 still owed; no coin can return 20. The change is
not exact, so the purchase is refused, no product is released, and the 100 inserted
is returned. The scenario is satisfied.

**Trace C: the revised design, scenario "Change is given from stock".** 30 is owed. The
largest coin that does not exceed 30 is 20; 10 is owed. The largest coin that does
not exceed 10 is 10; nothing is owed. The change is exact, so the product is released
and 20 and 10 are returned. The scenario is satisfied.

**Trace D: the revised design, scenario "Exact payment gives no change".** Nothing is
owed. The change is exact, so the product is released and no coin is returned. The
scenario is satisfied.

The first design's non-goals set aside the case that this design decides. That is the central difference in this file. This design takes the case into its decisions, and keeps only the coin denominations and the customer message out of scope.

The two rejected alternatives show what this design gave up. The first, releasing the product and returning what can be made, keeps the first design's behaviour in a form the new requirement forbids. The second, releasing the product and refunding the rest later, moves the failure to a later time without removing it, because the product is already gone when the refund is decided. Both alternatives keep the release-first order, which is why the order is the decision that changes.

The risk has the same subject as the first design's risk, but a different result. In the first design a stock that runs down produced a change that fell short without a signal. Here it produces refusals. The design accepts that consequence and leaves refilling outside the change.

Trace B takes the case from section 4.7 through the revised order: 30 is owed, the change is not exact, and the purchase is refused. Traces C and D repeat the first change's two cases, so the revised design is checked against all three scenarios, not only the one that failed.

4.12 The tasks of the second change

The tasks of the second change form two groups, and the groups follow the work. The first group reproduces the failure in the artifacts, and the second group changes the design and checks it again. Each group depends on the one before it, so the order of the groups is part of the record.

Second change: tasks What this change puts there
Group heading Two groups: "Trace the first version", then "Revise and trace again".
Task Five checks. Two in the first group: writing the scenario, and walking it through the first design. Three in the second: revising the design, walking all three scenarios through it, and running validation.
Verified by Each task names its evidence: the scenario in the delta, Trace A, the decisions, Traces B to D, or the passing command.

refuse-without-exact-change, tasks.md

## 1. Trace the first version

- [x] 1.1 Write the scenario "Stock cannot make the change" from the requirement's word "exact". **Verified by** the scenario in the spec delta.
- [x] 1.2 Trace the scenario through the first design of `give-exact-change`. **Verified by** Trace A in the design's Findings, which records both symptoms.

## 2. Revise and trace again

- [x] 2.1 Revise the design so that the change is worked out before release, and a change that is not exact is refused. **Verified by** the decisions in the design.
- [x] 2.2 Trace all three scenarios through the revised design. **Verified by** Traces B, C and D in the design's Findings.
- [x] 2.3 Run `openspec validate --strict`. **Verified by** the command passing.

The task is quoted as written. The word "exact" is in the revised requirement and in the change's name, and the scenario it writes is for a case the first requirement did not mention. The first change's tasks traced scenarios that already existed. This task creates one.

Task 2.1 is verified by the decisions in the design, not by a walkthrough. That is a weaker check than the others, and it is shown here as it is written. The revision is accepted on the strength of its own text until task 2.2 tests the revised design against all three scenarios. The walkthrough, not the revision, is what closes this part of the change.
