Task 2.3 runs validation again, and it passes. As in the first change, the pass says nothing about the case; the traces in task 2.2 carry that evidence.

4.13 How the second change differs from the first

The two changes use the same four artifacts, but they do different work on the main specification. The first creates a file, and the second changes a requirement in it. Each difference that sections 4.9 to 4.12 point out between the two comes from that job, not from the format.

4.14 The archive of the second change

When the second change is archived, its delta is merged into the main specification that the first change created. The delta modifies one requirement, so it replaces that requirement, adds no file and leaves the Purpose as it was. From then on the specification is the record of the requirement. The requirement as the change refuse-without-exact-change left it in openspec/specs/purchase/spec.md begins:

The machine SHALL return to the customer the difference between the amount inserted
and the price of the product, exactly, in coins from its stock. If it cannot return
that exact amount, it SHALL refuse the purchase, release no product, and return the
amount inserted.

The archive keeps the change folder with its design and its findings, so the path from the first version to the corrected one can still be read, and the two commits in the history of the example repository show what was written first and what replaced it. The main specification is different: a wrong requirement that reaches it is paid for by every later change that relies on it. Archiving is therefore the point at which a change stops being a proposal and starts being the system's description.

The path from request to archive has four artifacts, taken in the order of section 4.1, and each answers a question the one before it left open. The proposal says why, the specification says what must hold, the design says how the machine gets there, and the tasks say what has to be checked for each part of the design. The example also showed that a passing validation is not the same as a design that agrees with its scenarios. The first version passed validation and every task, and it still failed a case that had not yet been written. The failure was found by writing that case down, and it was fixed in the artifacts. The next chapters take each artifact in turn; this one has shown what each looks like and where they meet.

5. The Proposal and the Scope It Sets

Chapter 4 followed one requirement through two changes, and in both of them the proposal came first. It showed what a proposal contains and quoted two of them in full. This chapter stays with that first artifact and asks the questions the overview could not: who actually writes the file, which of its parts a reader has to get right, how a reviewer decides that it is finished, and what happens when the review finds something wrong. The example is the same vending machine and the same two changes. Nothing new is decided about the machine here.

The table shows the files of a change and the paths of its specifications. The rows this chapter discusses are in bold.

Item File What it says Discussed in
Change openspec/changes/<change>/ The folder of one change. Chapter 4
Proposal proposal.md Why the change exists and what it changes. Chapters 4 and 5
Capability specs/<capability>/ The folder for one area of behaviour, such as purchase. Chapters 4 and 6
Specification specs/<capability>/spec.md What one change adds, modifies or removes. Chapters 4 and 6
Main specification openspec/specs/<capability>/spec.md The system as it stands. Chapters 4 and 6
Design design.md How the work is done. Chapters 4 and 7
Tasks tasks.md The checks that turn the design into work. Chapters 4 and 8
Schema marker .openspec.yaml The schema the change follows, and skip_specs when it has no deltas. Chapter 4

5.1 Who writes the proposal

A coding agent drafts the first version of the file. In an OpenSpec project the agent reads the change's schema — the template for the artifact and the instruction attached to it — together with the specifications the repository already has and the request as the developer phrased it, and it drafts proposal.md. The developer does not begin from a blank file. What the agent supplies is form and the state of the repository: the parts the project's schema asks for, and which capabilities already exist. What it cannot supply is intent. Whether the problem is the right problem, whether the change is the smallest one that answers it, and whether two requests are really one change are decisions about the work, and the agent has nothing to decide them from.

So the developer's part is not to proofread generated text. It is to say what the change is for, to refuse the version that has restated a solution, and to accept responsibility for the scope the file sets. Chapter 2 called human control the cornerstone that no convention carries, and chapter 3 described the division of work as a model that writes, a program that verifies and a person who approves. The proposal is the earliest artifact at which that division becomes visible, because nothing written after it can be checked until the problem is settled. A draft that reads well is therefore the weakest signal available: the agent produces text that satisfies the schema and the sentences of the request, which is exactly what it was asked to produce, and that is not the same thing as a proposal that is right.

5.2 The parts of a proposal

Both example proposals answer four questions, and the default template asks for exactly those four parts.

Part What the tool checks The question it answers
Why Nothing at validation. At archive, a warning if it is under 50 or over 1,000 characters. Why is this change needed, and why now?
What Changes Nothing at validation. At archive, a warning if it is empty. What will the system do, or say about itself, that it does not today?
Capabilities Nothing. Which specification does the change create or modify?
Impact Nothing. What else is expected to be touched?

openspec validate reads the delta specifications, and opens the main ones only to check the capabilities a delta modifies or removes. It never opens proposal.md. openspec archive opens the file and prints the two warnings the table names, calling them non-blocking, and archives the change anyway. Two of the four parts are therefore checked by no program, and the other two by a warning a developer can ignore. Everything else in the proposal is judged by the person reviewing it, which is the reason section 5.8 exists.

The four parts are the whole of the template, and it is worth saying so plainly, because proposals are not always written from it. An exclusion goes into the design instead, and section 5.7 says where. A project that wants a part the template does not have adds it to the schema it forked, which chapter 3 described as a folder of files rather than a fixed format. The names in the table are the template's names, and a forked schema may rename them. What a part has to do is answer a question a reviewer needs answered, and the file is only finished when each question has an answer that can be checked. The rest of the chapter quotes each of the four parts from both example proposals where it discusses them, so the artifact can be followed here without turning back to chapter 4.

5.3 A problem, not a solution

The first proposal argues from a situation. The file is proposal.md in the change give-exact-change, and its Why reads as archived:

## Why

A customer who pays more than the price of a product expects the difference back.
The machine holds coins, so it has to decide which coins make up the difference.

Two sentences, both about a customer and a machine. Neither names a denomination, an order of steps, a method for choosing coins, or anything about a stock that is too short for the difference owed. Each of those is decided later, in the specification and in the design, and section 4.2 shows the file in one piece.

A Why that names the method has already made the design's decision. Suppose the first proposal had said that the machine should work out the change by taking the largest coin that fits and repeating until nothing is owed. The problem would no longer be that a customer is owed money. It would be that the machine should use a particular method, and a reviewer who doubted the method would be arguing about the solution instead of about whether the machine should give change at all. The first Why leaves that argument open. The difference could be paid in any combination of coins from stock, returned before or after the product is released, chosen to keep the stock balanced or to use as few coins as possible. The design decided among those options, and section 4.4 shows which decision it made and why. Because the Why had not chosen first, the design had something to decide and the reviewer had something to challenge.

5.4 A reason can be evidence

The second proposal argues from a different place. Its Why does not begin with a customer; it begins with a finding. The file is proposal.md in the change refuse-without-exact-change, and its Why reads as archived:

## Why

While writing the scenario for a stock that cannot make the change, the first version
has no answer. Tracing the scenario through the design of `give-exact-change` shows two
symptoms:

1. The product is released before the change is worked out. A customer who is short
   of change keeps the product.
2. With short stock the change is less than the amount owed, and nothing says so.

`openspec validate` passed the first version. It checks the structure of the
artifacts, not whether a design agrees with a scenario.

The claims the second Why makes about the first version can be checked against a walkthrough that is in the archive. Section 4.7 shows the trace that makes the second symptom visible, and section 4.9 shows the file in one piece.

Both reasons are legitimate, and they are doing different jobs. A proposal written before anything has been built has no findings to cite; it can only argue from the use the change is meant to serve, which is what the first one does. A proposal written after a failed attempt can cite what the attempt showed, and it is stronger for it, but only because the evidence exists. Evidence is therefore not a mark of a better proposal. And a proposal that claims evidence without saying where it can be read is a wish written in the past tense. The useful question is not whether a Why cites something, but whether a reader can check the reason it gives.

5.5 What changes, and which capability

What Changes describes the difference the change makes to the system, not the work that produces it. The file is proposal.md in the change give-exact-change, and its What Changes and Capabilities read as archived:

## What Changes

- Add a capability `purchase` with two requirements: the coins the machine holds,
  and the change it returns for a purchase.

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities

- `purchase`: the coins the machine holds, and the change it returns for a purchase.

One bullet, and a capability that says the same thing again, which is the split the template asks for: What Changes says what is added, and Capabilities says where it will be written down. Neither says that a delta will be written, then a design, then a task list. That order is the schema's, and chapter 3 is where it belongs. A What Changes that lists the artifacts, or the files to be edited, has recorded a plan.

The test is short: after reading the part, can a reader say what the system will do that it does not do now? If the answer describes activity rather than behaviour, the part has been written for the wrong artifact. The template puts two conditions on What Changes that neither example needs: a removal is stated as a removal, and a change that breaks existing behaviour is marked BREAKING, which is the schema instruction's own marker. Neither proposal removes anything, so neither has to say so.

Naming the capability is the part that binds the change to a file. The second proposal changes the same capability, so it names it under a different heading. The file is proposal.md in the change refuse-without-exact-change, and its What Changes and Capabilities read as archived:

## What Changes

- The requirement "The machine gives change in coins from its stock" requires exact
  change. If the exact change cannot be made, the purchase is refused and the amount
  inserted is returned. No product is released.
- A scenario is added for a stock that cannot make the change.
- The design works out the change before the product is released.

## Capabilities

### Modified Capabilities

- `purchase`: the requirement "The machine gives change in coins from its stock" changes to require exact change.

The second proposal's What Changes is less clean than the first, and it is worth reading closely. The first bullet carries the change: the requirement now demands exact change and says what happens when it cannot be made. The second names a scenario, which is the specification's artifact rather than behaviour. The third states the order in which the design works, and chapter 4's section 4.4 gives that order to the design. Both of them read as a plan, and the part survives because the first bullet is doing the work: a reader can still answer what the system will do.

A capability is an area of behaviour, and its specification lives at that name. The template asks for a path, so a capability can sit inside an area rather than directly under the root, and every segment the change introduces is written in kebab-case.

The name is a boundary decision with a cost on both sides. One capability too coarse puts unrelated requirements into a single file, so every later change to either of them modifies the same document and a reader cannot tell which requirements belong together. One capability too fine fragments a behaviour across files, so a change that touches one behaviour has to open three. There is a case for putting the coins and the change in one capability, since neither is meaningful alone: a stock of coins exists in order to make change, and change is made from a stock. Impact is where the consequence is stated, because the capability's name is the path of the file the change will write.

5.6 Impact is a forecast

Impact is a forecast of what the change will touch, and it is the part easiest to write as an inventory. The file is proposal.md in the change give-exact-change, and its Impact reads as archived:

## Impact

- `openspec/specs/purchase/spec.md` — created when this change is archived.

The second proposal names the same file and one thing that changes about it. The file is proposal.md in the change refuse-without-exact-change, and its Impact reads as archived:

## Impact

- `openspec/specs/purchase/spec.md` — the change requirement is modified when this
  change is archived.

One line each, naming one file and saying whether it will appear or change. Neither lists the change's own design or task list, because every change has those and naming them says nothing about this one.

What the part is for is the reader who wants the size of the change before reading the delta: which capability is affected, whether an existing description changes or a new one appears, and whether anything else moves — code, an interface, a dependency or a system outside the repository. That reader is better served by an honest guess than by a complete-looking list, because the design does not exist yet and the files it will touch cannot be known. An Impact that is wrong costs a sentence to correct. An Impact that is missing hides the cost of the change until it has been paid.

5.7 What the template does not carry

The template has no part for what the change will not do. Exclusions are worth writing down, because they stop the scope growing and tell a reviewer which absences are decisions rather than oversights, but the default schema records them somewhere else: the design has a Goals / Non-Goals part, and it sits beside the decisions those goals and non-goals constrain. That is the design's artifact, not the proposal's, and chapter 7 takes it up there. An unknown that can wait does not belong here either: the schema's instruction gives the design an Open Questions part for those, and the proposal has none. A question that cannot wait is settled before the proposal is written, or it stays a conversation until it can be.

5.8 Reviewing a proposal

Reviewing a proposal is a single reading of one file, done at the only moment when it is still cheap: after the draft exists and before anything is generated from it. The reading has three passes:

  1. Intent: does the draft answer the request as the developer meant it, or an assumption the agent made while drafting?
  2. Size: is it one change? The split is far easier here than after the specification exists.
  3. Claims: is each capability the file names as Modified a file that already exists under openspec/specs/, and is each one it names as new absent from there?

The first two passes come first, because nothing written after the proposal can find what they find. A draft that answers the wrong problem is answered faithfully by every later artifact, and a draft that holds two changes produces a specification that serves neither of them.

Waiting until the delta and the design exist does not make this reading unnecessary. It makes it a reading of three files that were written from one wrong premise, which is the most expensive reading there is.

Each part fails in ways a drafting agent produces readily, and the table below puts those failures beside the check that catches them. It is ordered the way the file is read: the request as a whole first, then each part in the template's order, then what follows the proposal.

Check The proposal passes when How a draft can fail
The request is answered as meant A reviewer can say which request the draft answers, and nothing in it answers an assumption the agent made instead The draft serves a request nobody made, because the agent took a solution named in the request as the problem, and every part after the Why follows it
The change is one change A reviewer can name the single problem it answers, and no part of the request would survive on its own Two unrelated requests sit in one folder, and the delta modifies two capabilities for no reason they share
Why: the problem is stated without its solution The Why names a situation or a finding, and no method, data structure or requirement wording has been carried into it The Why names a method, a data structure, a library or a requirement's wording, or it describes the change rather than the problem and reads as a summary of What Changes
Why: the reason can be checked The claims in the Why can be confirmed from the request, an artifact or the running system The Why cites evidence a reader cannot follow to a file, or names a failure without saying where it was found
What Changes: behaviour, not a plan The part says what the system will do or say that it does not today, and lists no artifact, file or step The part lists artifacts to write, files to edit or steps to take, and three effects on three capabilities read like one change
What Changes: removals and breaking changes are visible Anything the change takes away, or breaks for an existing user of the system, is stated as such, and a breaking change is marked BREAKING A removal is written as an addition, or a breaking change is not marked, so the reader does not see what the change takes away
Capabilities: the boundary is deliberate Each name is either an area of behaviour already under openspec/specs/, or genuinely new, and the heading matches which one it is The agent invents a capability name, or files a new one under Modified; validation does not read the part (section 5.2), and archive refuses a Modified entry for a capability that is not there
Impact: the forecast is honest The expected blast radius is named, files that may be created are marked as such, and nothing is claimed that the design will have to contradict The part is an inventory of files that do not exist yet, or it is empty
The scope stays open downstream Any case the proposal deliberately leaves to the specification is visible to the next artifact rather than lost between them The boundary is drawn where the specification or the design cannot honour it, and the disagreement is found after all three exist

The table is a memory aid rather than a gate: no part of the tool reads it, so a row that passes records a person's judgment and not a machine's check. The last row is the only one that is not about the file on its own. A proposal is finished when its boundary can be honoured by what follows, not when its parts have been filled.

5.9 Changing a proposal after review

When the review finds something, two decisions follow: what has to change, and who changes it. The first depends on how much of the change exists:

What exists What the revision covers
Only the proposal The part, and the parts coupled to it: Capabilities and Impact are written from What Changes, so a change to one can move the other two. A review that found two changes in one ends with two folders rather than with a longer sentence. The file should be right rather than faithful to its first draft, and version control already holds the history worth keeping.
The delta, the design or the tasks Those artifacts too, because they were written from the part that changed. A proposal that says one thing while the delta says another is worse than either alone, and the disagreement will be found later by somebody who has to guess which of the two was meant.
An archived change Nothing in the archive. The archive is the record of what was decided when it was decided, and editing it afterwards destroys the only account of how the current specification reached its form. A gap that appears later is argued in a new change whose Why cites the change that missed it.

The example shows the bottom row and not the middle one. Its second change was written after the first was archived, from the failure that section 4.7 shows, and its artifacts were written together, so the archive holds no proposal that was revised while its delta, design or tasks existed. The bottom row is what refuse-without-exact-change does to give-exact-change: it argues the gap in a new change rather than revising the one that is closed.

The second decision is about the means, and there are two of them. The developer can open proposal.md and write the replacement, or the developer can ask the agent to revise the part. The choice turns on one question: is the corrected text already known? A developer who can say the sentence before opening the file should write it, because the file open in an editor costs a minute and leaves a diff that shows only what moved. A developer who knows only that something is wrong has to have the right text worked out, and working it out means reading openspec/specs/, the request or the artifacts already written. That is the agent's part of the work, and it is the division section 5.1 described. The two means differ in when they are right, in what they cost, and in how they go wrong:

The developer edits the file The agent is asked to revise it
Right when The replacement is already known, and the fault sits in one part The correct text has to be worked out from the repository, or from a request the developer can describe but not yet phrase
What it costs A minute with the file open, and a diff that shows one sentence A request that has to be specific, a whole file to read back, and a diff that may show more than was asked for
How it goes wrong The named part is fixed and the parts coupled to it are not, so the file contradicts itself further down A request that names a symptom — asking for the Why to be clearer — returns a rewrite whose scope has moved, and the size of the diff hides it
What to check afterwards The coupled parts listed in the earlier table The whole file, including the parts that were not meant to move

The first case is small. Suppose the first draft's What Changes had listed the specification among the things to write, as section 5.5 warns against. The review finds a task in a part that describes behaviour, and the replacement is a sentence the developer can write without help: that the machine holds coins, and that it returns the difference between what was inserted and the price. Nothing else needs to move. Capabilities already names purchase, Impact already names the file that will carry the requirement, and the Why never mentioned the specification at all. One sentence is wrong, its replacement is known, and the diff should show nothing but that sentence.

The second case is where the answer is not in the developer's head. Suppose the draft had filed the change under a new capability called change-giving, while openspec/specs/purchase/spec.md already holds the requirement that changes. The name in the file has to be the name the repository uses, and correcting it moves three places at once: the heading that says whether the capability is new or modified, the bullet beneath it, and the Impact line that names the file. A request for that revision works when it says three things:

  1. which part to revise;
  2. what is wrong with it, namely that change-giving is not a capability under openspec/specs/, and that the capability already there is purchase;
  3. what must not move, which here is the Why and the What Changes, because the review has already passed them.

A request that leaves out the third part invites a rewrite of the file, and an agent has no reason to keep what it was not told to keep.

Both means end in the same reading, and the reading is what decides whether the proposal is approved. An edit is checked by its diff: the diff shows what moved, and anything outside the coupled parts is a mistake to revert. A revision made by asking is a rewrite rather than an edit, so the whole file is read as a new draft, and the parts nobody asked about are where a moved boundary hides. The passes from section 5.8 are what that reading consists of, and the file is ready again only when each of them holds for the text that is now in it.

5.10 What the proposal hands on

The proposal does not make every decision the change needs, and the sections above named the artifact that takes each one it leaves. The cases a requirement must satisfy go to the specification, which the next chapter takes: the proposal says what the system will do, and the specification says it as a requirement with scenarios that decide it case by case.

What the proposal keeps is the problem and the scope that answers it. Each of its four parts is checked against an artifact that comes later, and the proposal is the cheapest place to correct any of them.

The proposal leaves this chapter at the point where its promise becomes testable. Everything so far has been about the argument: why the change exists, what it changes, and whether the boundary it draws is honest. The next artifact is not an argument. It is a requirement the system must satisfy and a set of scenarios by which that requirement can be decided, and the case the example's first requirement left open is found at that step, when a scenario is written for a stock the first requirement did not mention.

A proposal is drafted by an agent and owned by a person, and that ownership is what the review exists for. The file asks four questions, and the tool checks almost none of the answers. The parts that are easy to get wrong are the ones that describe a solution, a plan or a complete inventory, because those are what a drafting agent produces most fluently. The review is one reading, written out as a checklist in the file's own order, and the two checks that come first are the ones nothing later can repair. When the review finds something, the question is how much of the change already exists, and then whether the replacement is known: an edit is cheaper when it is, and a request to the agent is the way when it is not. The proposal is the statement made first and revised most cheaply. What a reader should carry away is therefore not a template but a habit. Treat the proposal as the first place a boundary is stated, review it before anything is built from it, and expect the artifacts that follow to hold it to what it opened.

6. The Specification and the Cases That Decide It

Chapter 5 ended with the proposal's scope handed to the next artifact, which that chapter called the specification. This chapter takes that artifact up and asks the same four questions of it: who writes it, which of its parts must be right, how a reviewer decides that it is finished, and what happens when the review finds something wrong. The example is the same vending machine and the same two changes.

Before the questions, two files have to be kept apart, because OpenSpec calls both of them specifications. The delta is the spec.md inside a change's folder, at openspec/changes/<change>/specs/<capability>/spec.md, and it says what that one change adds, modifies or removes. The main specification is the spec.md at openspec/specs/<capability>/spec.md, which holds the system's description as it now stands, and which archiving writes. Chapter 3 introduced the two files and chapter 4 showed both in full, so this chapter defines them and does not explain them again. From here, "the delta" is the artifact, and "the main specification" is the file it is merged into.

The table shows the files of a change and the paths of its specifications. The rows this chapter discusses are in bold.

Item File What it says Discussed in
Change openspec/changes/<change>/ The folder of one change. Chapter 4
Proposal proposal.md Why the change exists and what it changes. Chapters 4 and 5
Capability specs/<capability>/ The folder for one area of behaviour, such as purchase. Chapters 4 and 6
Specification specs/<capability>/spec.md What one change adds, modifies or removes. Chapters 4 and 6
Main specification openspec/specs/<capability>/spec.md The system as it stands. Chapters 4 and 6
Design design.md How the work is done. Chapters 4 and 7
Tasks tasks.md The checks that turn the design into work. Chapters 4 and 8
Schema marker .openspec.yaml The schema the change follows, and skip_specs when it has no deltas. Chapter 4

Both files are organized by capability, the area of behaviour that a folder name stands for, and a capability is not a file, a feature or a screen. The coins a machine holds and the change it returns are one capability in the example, and chapter 5 explains why that boundary was drawn. The name is the one thing that the proposal, the delta and the main specification must agree on. A change that modifies an existing capability writes its delta to the path the main specification already has, and archive refuses a MODIFIED delta whose capability does not exist. Every later question in this chapter is about the contents of such a file, and the path is where those contents are kept.

6.1 Who writes the delta

The agent writes one delta for each capability that the proposal lists in its Capabilities part, as a file at specs/<capability>/spec.md in the change folder. To do that it reads the proposal, the main specifications under openspec/specs/, and the developer's request. Section 5.1 described the same division for the proposal, and chapter 2 gave the reason human control stays with the developer.

The agent supplies the form that the template asks for: the headings, the SHALL sentence of each requirement, and the WHEN and THEN lines of each scenario. It cannot supply which behaviour the machine ought to have, which cases matter, or whether two requirements are really one. Those decisions belong to the developer, and a delta that follows the template exactly can still describe the wrong behaviour. That is why the review in section 6.7 reads for meaning as well as for form.

openspec validate reads the delta and reports the form problems it finds, and openspec archive merges the delta into the main specification.

6.2 The parts of a delta

A delta has four parts in the default template, and the table shows what the tool checks of each one.

Part What the tool checks The question it answers
Purpose Only in a delta for a new capability. The tool does not check its length in a delta; the main specification warns when its Purpose is under 50 characters. In a delta for an existing capability the Purpose is ignored. What is this capability for?
Operation: ADDED, MODIFIED, REMOVED or RENAMED validate reports an error for a MODIFIED that drops a scenario the main specification has, and for a change with no delta unless it declares skip_specs. A MODIFIED for a capability that does not exist passes validate with a note, and archive refuses it. What does the delta do to the main specification?
Requirement Without SHALL or MUST, a warning that --strict fails. Without a scenario, an error. Over 500 characters, a warning that --strict fails, for an ADDED requirement and for a MODIFIED one that grows past the limit. What must the system do?
Scenario A scenario header with three hashtags is ignored, so its requirement has none and validate reports an error. Without a WHEN or GIVEN step, or without a THEN step, a warning that --strict fails. In what case, and with what outcome, is the requirement tested?

The four parts are the whole of the default delta, and the tool reads them for form only. A part that a project adds lives in a schema the project has forked, as chapter 3 described, and the default template has no such part. The quotations below show each part as the example's archive holds it.

6.3 A purpose, and the requirement it introduces

The file is specs/purchase/spec.md in the change give-exact-change, and its Purpose reads as archived:

## Purpose

Defines the coins the vending machine holds and the change it returns for a purchase, so that a customer who pays more than the price receives the difference in coins from the machine's stock.

A Purpose says what a capability is for, in one or two sentences. Section 4.6 shows where archive puts it. The second delta has none, since the capability already has a Purpose in the main specification, and a Purpose written into such a delta is ignored.

The file is specs/purchase/spec.md in the change give-exact-change, and its operation and first requirement read as archived:

## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: The machine holds coins of four denominations

The machine SHALL hold coins of 10, 20, 50 and 100 cents only. Amounts are stated in
cents.

#### Scenario: Stock holds only the four denominations

- **WHEN** the machine is stocked
- **THEN** every coin in its stock is a coin of 10, 20, 50 or 100 cents

The heading says what the delta does to the main specification. ADDED is the operation for a capability with no main specification yet, and its requirements are appended. The requirement is one statement with SHALL, carrying one behaviour, that the stock holds four denominations, and one convention, that amounts are stated in cents. Its name is what the tool matches on: an ADDED requirement must not already exist, and a MODIFIED or REMOVED entry must name one that does. The other two operations exist as well. REMOVED takes a requirement out of the main specification, and RENAMED changes a requirement's name. The example uses neither, so this chapter does not show them.

6.4 Scenarios, and the case nobody wrote

The file is specs/purchase/spec.md in the change give-exact-change, and its second requirement reads as archived:

### Requirement: The machine gives change in coins from its stock

The machine SHALL return to the customer the difference between the amount inserted
and the price of the product, in coins from its stock.

#### Scenario: Change is given from stock

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents, 100 cents is inserted, and the stock holds at least
  one coin of 10 cents and at least one coin of 20 cents
- **THEN** the machine returns 30 cents as one coin of 20 cents and one coin of 10
  cents

#### Scenario: Exact payment gives no change

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents and 70 cents is inserted
- **THEN** the machine returns no change

A scenario is one case, written so that a tester can set it up and read the result. WHEN names a condition the developer can produce, and THEN names an outcome that can be judged yes or no. The scenario with a price of 70 cents and 100 cents inserted says which coins come back, which the requirement's sentence does not. A reviewer uses a scenario as a developer uses a test: set up the condition, read the outcome, and ask whether it is the one the requirement promises.

The two scenarios cover a stock that holds the coins needed, and an exact payment. The requirement says the machine SHALL return the difference in coins from its stock, and says nothing about a stock that cannot make that difference. Both scenarios pass, validation passes, and nothing in the delta asks what happens for that stock. The case is found by varying what the requirement depends on, the price, the amount inserted and the stock, and asking what each variation should do. Section 4.7 shows the walkthrough that found it. The first delta is not defective: it decides the cases it lists, and it lists two.

6.5 A revision of one requirement

The file is specs/purchase/spec.md in the change refuse-without-exact-change, and it is shown in full as archived:

## MODIFIED Requirements

### Requirement: The machine gives change in coins from its stock

The machine SHALL return to the customer the difference between the amount inserted
and the price of the product, exactly, in coins from its stock. If it cannot return
that exact amount, it SHALL refuse the purchase, release no product, and return the
amount inserted.

#### Scenario: Change is given from stock

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents, 100 cents is inserted, and the stock holds at least
  one coin of 10 cents and at least one coin of 20 cents
- **THEN** the machine returns 30 cents as one coin of 20 cents and one coin of 10
  cents

#### Scenario: Exact payment gives no change

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents and 70 cents is inserted
- **THEN** the machine returns no change

#### Scenario: Stock cannot make the change

- **WHEN** the price is 70 cents, 100 cents is inserted, and the stock holds one coin
  of 10 cents and no coin of 20 or 50 cents
- **THEN** the machine refuses the purchase, releases no product, and returns the 100
  cents inserted

The second delta is written out whole, because a MODIFIED requirement replaces the whole requirement in the main specification. Set against the first delta's requirement, the revision is small: a word, a sentence and a scenario. The earlier scenarios stand as they were. The tool reports a MODIFIED that drops a scenario the main specification has, as an error, and it compares scenario names and not their text. A scenario whose wording changes under the same name is therefore not noticed.

The new scenario is the case from the previous section, written down so that it can be decided. With the scenario in place the requirement can be judged for that stock. Chapter 7 takes up the design's answer.

6.6 What the delta leaves to the design

The delta says what the system must do, and it leaves how to the design. The schema's instruction for specifications gives a quick test: "if the implementation can change without changing externally visible behavior, it likely does not belong in the spec." Neither requirement in the example fixes an order of steps or a method for finding coins; section 4.4 shows the first design deciding both. A decision written into a requirement would make the requirement change every time the method does.

6.7 Reviewing a delta

A delta is reviewed after the proposal is approved and before the design is written from it, because a scenario that is wrong is cheapest to fix before anything is traced against it. The review has four passes. Intent asks whether this is the behaviour the developer meant. Decidability asks whether each scenario can be set up and its outcome judged. Coverage asks which price, payment and stock have no scenario. Fit asks whether there is one delta for each capability the proposal lists, at a path that matches, with an operation that matches New or Modified. Decidability and coverage matter most, because the tool cannot see either of them, and every later artifact is checked against the scenarios.

The table is one checklist, in the order the file is read, and the column names use the artifact's name, the specification, which here means the delta. Like the review table in chapter 5, it is a memory aid, and no part of the tool reads it.

Check The specification passes when How a draft can fail
The request is answered as meant The delta states the behaviour the developer meant The agent wrote the behaviour it thought the request implied, and the scenarios test that instead
One file per capability Each capability has one spec.md, at the path the Capabilities part names Two capabilities share one file, or a path is spelled differently from the proposal
Operation matches the proposal ADDED for a capability that does not exist, MODIFIED for one that does A new capability is filed under MODIFIED, or an existing requirement under ADDED, which archive refuses when the name is the same and adds beside the old one when the name differs
Purpose A new capability has one or two sentences of Purpose, and an existing one has none The Purpose is missing for a new capability, or it is written for an existing one
Requirement Each requirement states one behaviour with SHALL or MUST A requirement says "should" or "may", which validation only warns about, or it holds several behaviours in one block
Scenario Each requirement has at least one scenario at four hashtags, with a WHEN and a THEN A scenario is written at three hashtags and is ignored, which leaves its requirement with none, or it restates the requirement and names no case
Coverage Each price, payment and stock the requirement depends on has a scenario, or the gap is named The requirement depends on the stock, and no scenario varies it
Modified requirement The MODIFIED block carries the whole requirement, every scenario the main specification has, and the new ones A partial MODIFIED drops a scenario, or it changes a scenario's text under its old name
Downstream The design can be traced against every scenario A scenario is written that the design cannot be traced against, or the design sets aside a case that a scenario tests, and the disagreement is found only later

6.8 Changing a delta after review

Once a review has found a fault, two questions follow: what the revision covers, and who makes it. The table answers the first.

What exists What the revision covers
Only the delta The part, and the parts coupled to it: a new scenario can change the wording of its requirement.
The delta, with the design and the tasks written from it Those too. They were traced against the old text, and a trace that was true of the old text says nothing about the new.
An archived change Nothing in the archive. A later gap goes into a new change.

Of the three rows, the example shows only the bottom one, and chapter 5 gives the reason the archive has no case of the middle row.

The second decision is which means to use, and there are two. The developer can edit the delta, or ask the agent to revise it. The choice turns on whether the corrected text is already known, and the table compares the two on four points.

The developer edits the file The agent is asked to revise it
Right when The replacement is known, and the fault sits in one scenario or one sentence The text must be worked out from the main specification or the other scenarios
What it costs A minute with the file open, and a diff that shows one change A request with three parts, a whole file to read back, and a diff whose size hides what actually changed
How it goes wrong An edit to one scenario leaves the requirement's wording, or the other scenarios, out of step with it A request for a clearer scenario returns a rewrite that changes more than was asked, and a MODIFIED block can lose a scenario
What to check afterwards The requirement and every scenario it has The whole file, including the scenarios nobody meant to change

Suppose the first delta's Change scenario had said that the machine returns "an appropriate set of coins", and the developer knows the sentence the archive holds: 30 cents as one coin of 20 cents and one coin of 10 cents. The edit is right because the replacement was known before the file was opened. One sentence changes, nothing else moves, and the diff shows nothing else.

Suppose instead that the developer sees that no scenario covers a stock without a 10-cent coin, but cannot yet say what the machine should do in that case. A request to the agent has three parts:

  1. which part to revise: the one requirement and its scenarios;
  2. what is wrong with it: no scenario covers a stock with no coin of 10 cents;
  3. what must not move: the requirement's text, its header and the scenarios that already exist.

The request asks the agent to propose the outcome from the main specification and the other scenarios, and the developer reviews that proposal before it is accepted. Without the third part, the agent may rewrite the whole block.

The two means meet at the same reading. An edit is judged by its diff, and a change outside the scenario is an error. A revision made by asking rewrites the file, so the reader checks the whole delta again, using the passes of section 6.7, and reads the text of every scenario, which section 6.5 says the tool does not compare.

6.9 What the delta hands on

The delta hands the design a set of cases that the design must satisfy, and each scenario is a case the design will be traced against. Chapter 7 takes up what a design should do with a case it has set aside. The delta hands the tasks nothing directly, because the tasks are written from the design, as section 4.5 shows.

The next artifact answers how: in what order the machine works, by what method and with which coins. The delta leaves those open by design.

A delta is a requirement and the cases that decide it. An agent writes it and supplies the form, and a person reviews it and owns what the behaviour should be. A program checks the form, and it cannot check whether the cases are enough, so a delta can pass every check and still leave a case undecided. The cases nobody wrote are found by writing them, by varying what the requirement depends on and asking what each variation should do. The design is then traced against those cases, and it decides how the behaviour is produced.

7. The Design and the Decisions That Can Be Traced

Chapter 6 ended with the cases that a requirement must satisfy handed to the next artifact, which it said answers how: in what order the machine works, by what method and with which coins. This chapter takes that artifact up and asks the same four questions of it: who writes it, which of its parts must be right, how a reviewer decides that it is finished, and what happens when the review finds something wrong. The example is the same vending machine and the same two changes.

The table shows the files of a change and the paths of its specifications. The row this chapter discusses is in bold.

Item File What it says Discussed in
Change openspec/changes/<change>/ The folder of one change. Chapter 4
Proposal proposal.md Why the change exists and what it changes. Chapters 4 and 5
Capability specs/<capability>/ The folder for one area of behaviour, such as purchase. Chapters 4 and 6
Specification specs/<capability>/spec.md What one change adds, modifies or removes. Chapters 4 and 6
Main specification openspec/specs/<capability>/spec.md The system as it stands. Chapters 4 and 6
Design design.md How the work is done. Chapters 4 and 7
Tasks tasks.md The checks that turn the design into work. Chapters 4 and 8
Schema marker .openspec.yaml The schema the change follows, and skip_specs when it has no deltas. Chapter 4

7.1 Who writes the design

The agent drafts the first version of design.md from the schema's instruction for the design and from the proposal. It supplies the four parts of the template, in the form the instruction asks for, and it supplies a reason for each decision that reads as sound. The instruction also says when a design is needed: a change that crosses several modules or brings a new architectural pattern, a new external dependency or a significant change to the data model, a concern about security, performance or migration, or an ambiguity that technical decisions would settle before coding. The developer decides whether one of those conditions applies, and the agent cannot decide it for them.

What the agent cannot supply is what the developer knows about the work. It cannot say which alternatives were really open, which constraints the code or the team imposes, or which cases the design may leave out. The example has no code, so its Context has no state of a codebase to describe; a design in a project with code begins there. The developer's part is to challenge the reasons, not to proofread the form. Section 5.1 describes the same division for the proposal, and chapter 2 gives the reason human control stays with the developer.

In the spec-driven schema the design requires only the proposal, while the tasks require both the specification and the design. The tool therefore does not wait for the delta before it offers the design. The order this book follows, in which the delta is reviewed before the design is written from it, has a reason: the design is traced against the scenarios, and a scenario that changes after the design is written means the traces have to be done again. Chapter 3 says that the dependencies between artifacts are enablers, not phase gates. This is the case where the tool shows it, because it does not enforce the order the book recommends.

7.2 The parts of a design

The table says what the tool checks of each part of the design. For this artifact the answer is the same in every row.

Part What the tool checks The question it answers
Context Nothing. What does a reader need in order to follow the decisions?
Goals / Non-Goals Nothing. What does the design achieve, and what does it leave out at design level?
Decisions Nothing. What was chosen, for what reason, and what was given up?
Risks / Trade-offs Nothing. What can go wrong, and what is done about it?

The tool reads nothing of the design. validate reads the delta and never opens design.md, and archive does not open it either. status counts the file as done if it exists, whatever it contains: a design of one character and an empty design both show as done. A change with no design validates and archives. That is the finding of this section, and it does not mean the design matters less than the other artifacts. It means that every check on it is a person's. The instruction asks for a design only when one of its four conditions applies, and the schema makes the tasks wait for the file; those are two rules, and the tool enforces only the second. The four parts are the whole of the default template, and a part that a project adds belongs in a forked schema, as chapter 3 described. The two parts that the instruction names beyond the template are named in section 7.7.

7.3 A context that points back

The file is design.md in the change give-exact-change, and its Context reads as archived:

## Context

The purchase capability requires the machine to return the difference in coins from
its stock. This design says how the machine works out those coins and in what order
it does its steps.

A Context says what a reader needs in order to follow the decisions, and it points at the proposal and the delta for the rest. The instruction asks for the current state and the constraints, and it asks the design to refer to the proposal and the specifications rather than restate them. The first Context names the requirement it serves in one sentence, and then says what the design covers. A reviewer can keep that sentence or cut it. It restates the requirement, which the delta already holds, but a reader who has not opened the delta needs to know which requirement is meant.

The file is design.md in the change refuse-without-exact-change, and its Context reads as archived:

## Context

The design of `give-exact-change` released the product first and then worked out the
change greedily from the stock. Its findings traced the first two scenarios correctly.
The scenario "Stock cannot make the change" was not traced then, because it did not
exist. This design replaces the order of steps and records the trace that shows why.

This Context ties the design to the one before it, so a reader of this file alone can find the thing it replaces. The full account of the first design is in section 4.11, and this chapter does not repeat it.

7.4 Goals and non-goals

The file is design.md in the change give-exact-change, and its Goals / Non-Goals reads as archived:

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**

- Return the difference between the amount inserted and the price, in coins from the
  stock.

**Non-Goals:**

- Deciding what happens when the stock cannot make the change. This design does not
  say.
- Choosing the coins so that the stock stays balanced, or so that the fewest coins are
  returned.

The goal states what the design achieves, in the behaviour the delta already states. The two non-goals say what the design leaves out at design level, and they are the part of the template that turns an absence into a statement. The first non-goal is the case that section 4.7 shows the design failing: a stock that cannot make the change. The file says that the design does not decide it, so a reader who meets that scenario later can see that the case was set aside on purpose and was not missed. The instruction asks a design to add only design-level boundaries and not to restate the proposal's scope. Both non-goals meet that test: one concerns a case, and the other a method for choosing coins.

The file is design.md in the change refuse-without-exact-change, and its Goals / Non-Goals reads as archived:

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**

- Return the exact difference in coins from the stock, or refuse the purchase and return
  the amount inserted.

**Non-Goals:**

- Changing the coin denominations.
- Telling the customer why a purchase was refused.

The goal restates the delta's outcome in the design's own words, so a reviewer can set it beside the requirement and compare them. None of the three scenarios of the requirement that this change modifies tests either of them. A non-goal that no scenario tests costs little to state, and a reviewer can confirm from the delta that it is safe to state.

A non-goal makes a case visible, but it does not decide the case, because what the system must do belongs to the delta (section 6.6). When a reviewer reads the non-goals, the question is the same for each one: does a scenario test this case? If one does, the design cannot list it as a non-goal, because the scenario says what the system must do and the design has to produce it. If none does, the reviewer asks whether the requirement's wording covers the case. If the wording covers it, the case belongs in a scenario, and the delta is where chapter 6 found the stock case, by varying what the requirement depends on (section 6.4). If the wording does not cover it, the non-goal stands. That is the answer to the question chapter 6 left open: a design records the case it sets aside, and the reviewer decides, with the delta open, whether the case was the design's to set aside.

7.5 Decisions and their reasons

The file is design.md in the change give-exact-change, and its Decisions reads as archived:

## Decisions

**Decision**: release the product first, then work out the change from the coins in
stock.

**Why**: the customer should not wait at the machine after the payment is complete.

**Decision**: work out the change greedily. Take the largest coin that does not
exceed the amount still owed, for as long as the stock of that coin lasts. Repeat
until nothing is owed.

**Why**: the method is short to state and easy to trace by hand.

A decision is a choice with a reason, and the reason is the part a reviewer can check. The first design has two decisions, and each has a Why. The first Why says that the customer should not wait at the machine after payment, which is a preference that no scenario tests. The second says that the method is short to state and easy to trace by hand, which concerns the design's own convenience. Neither reason is wrong. A reviewer asks which kind of reason each one is, and what would contradict it. The layout, a decision followed by its reason, is the example's own. The template asks for decisions with rationale and alternatives and does not prescribe a layout, as section 4.4 says.

The file is design.md in the change refuse-without-exact-change, and its Decisions reads as archived:

## Decisions

**Decision**: work out the change before the product is released.

**Why**: the requirement says the change is exact. A product that is released before
the change is known cannot be taken back, so the exactness of the change must be
decided first.

**Decision**: if the greedy method does not reach the exact amount, refuse the
purchase, release no product, and return the amount inserted.

**Why**: the requirement gives no near-miss outcome. Refusing is the only outcome the
requirement allows when the exact change cannot be made.

**Alternative rejected**: release the product and return the change that can be made.
Rejected because it returns less than the requirement allows, and the customer keeps a
product for money not paid back.

**Alternative rejected**: release the product and refund the rest later. Rejected
because the product is already gone when the refund is decided.

Both reasons of the second design cite the requirement: "the requirement says the change is exact" and "the requirement gives no near-miss outcome". A reviewer can set each reason beside the delta and decide whether it holds. The decision that changes between the two designs is the order of steps. The first design released the product first, and this design works out the change before the release, so the reasons support the decision that moved.

The instruction asks for alternatives that were considered for each decision. The first design records none. The second records two, both under its second decision, and none under its first. A file with no alternative does not say whether one was open, so a reviewer cannot tell a decision from a default. The reviewer's question is which alternative someone would actually have chosen. The two in the second design are the two that keep the first design's order, and those are the ones that matter. What each rejected alternative gave up is set out in section 4.11.

7.6 Risks and what they cost

The file is design.md in the change give-exact-change, and its Risks / Trade-offs reads as archived:

## Risks / Trade-offs

- The stock of coins shrinks with each purchase, and nothing in this design refills it.
  → Refilling is outside this change; the design assumes a stocked machine.

A risk names what could go wrong and what is done about it. The instruction gives that as an arrow from the risk to its mitigation, and the first design follows the form. The risk names its cause, but it does not name what the machine does once the stock has run down, which is the case the first design set aside in its Goals / Non-Goals. A reviewer reads the arrow for whether the mitigation is a decision or a deferral, and here it is a deferral that the design states.

The file is design.md in the change refuse-without-exact-change, and its Risks / Trade-offs reads as archived:

## Risks / Trade-offs

- The stock of coins shrinks with each purchase, so refusals become more likely as the
  stock runs down. → Refilling the stock is outside this change; the design does not
  mitigate it.

The second design has the same cause and names a consequence, and it says that it does not mitigate the risk. A risk left unmitigated is a decision once it is stated, and a reviewer can judge whether the consequence is acceptable. Section 4.11 says what changed between the two risks.

7.7 What the template leaves out

The instruction for the design asks for two parts that the template does not have. Migration Plan asks for the steps to deploy and the rollback strategy, if one applies. Open Questions asks for unknowns that can be answered later without changing the specifications, the approach or the task breakdown, and it says that a question which would change any of them is resolved now. The instruction for the tasks adds a step: the agent reads the design's Open Questions and resolves with the user any that would change what gets built. Neither example design has either part, so this chapter names them and shows neither. The Findings section that the example adds to its designs is not in the template either, and section 4.4 explains why the example keeps it. Section 5.7 already says where an unknown that can wait is recorded, and this chapter does not repeat it.

7.8 Reviewing a design

A design is reviewed after the delta is reviewed and before the tasks are written from it. The tasks are written from the design, so a decision that nobody traced becomes a task that nobody can check. The review has four passes. Intent asks whether the design serves the behaviour the delta states. Reasons asks whether each decision's reason can be checked, and, where the delta leaves a choice open, whether an alternative was recorded. Trace asks whether each scenario can be walked through the decisions to the outcome it states, as section 4.7 walks one. Boundaries asks whether each non-goal is a case that no scenario tests, and whether each risk says what happens when it occurs. Trace and boundaries matter most, because the tool cannot see either of them, and chapter 6 handed the design the cases it must meet.

A trace tests the design against the cases that exist, and it cannot supply a case. A trace walks one scenario through the decisions by hand: the WHEN gives the inputs, the decisions are applied in order, and the result is compared with the THEN. The example's designs record their traces, and its tasks cite them, in sections 4.5 and 4.12. The second design traces all three of its scenarios, including the two that the first design had passed, as section 4.11 shows.

The table is one checklist, in the order the file is read. The column names use the artifact's name, which here is the design.

Check The design passes when How a draft can fail
The request is answered as meant The design serves the behaviour the delta states, and nothing in it answers an assumption the agent made instead The design decides a behaviour the delta does not state, and the tasks are written from it
Context It says what a reader needs to follow the decisions, and points at the proposal and the delta for the rest It restates the proposal or the requirement at length, or it describes what the design will do rather than the state it starts from
Goals Each goal is a behaviour the delta states, in the design's words A goal restates the proposal's scope, or it states a method the delta leaves open as if the delta required it
Non-Goals Each non-goal is a case that no scenario tests, or the scenario that tests it is named and the non-goal is removed A non-goal is a case that a scenario tests, or a case the requirement's wording covers, and no one has decided it
Decisions: reason Each reason can be checked against the delta, a constraint or a stated preference A reason is only the design's convenience, and nothing could contradict it
Decisions: alternative Where the delta leaves a choice open, the rejected alternatives are recorded, and each is one someone would choose No alternative is recorded for a decision that could have gone another way, so a reviewer cannot tell a decision from a default
Risks / Trade-offs Each risk names its cause, its consequence and what is done about it A risk names a cause and no consequence, or its mitigation is one the design cannot keep
Trace Each scenario of the delta can be walked through the decisions to the outcome it states A trace covers only the scenarios that existed when the design was written, and a scenario added later is never traced
Downstream The tasks can be written from the design, and each decision has a check that can mark it done A decision is one that no task can check, or a task asks for something the design does not decide

The table is a memory aid, and no part of the tool reads it. A row that passes records a person's judgment, not a machine's check. The last two rows are the only ones that are not about the file on its own. A design is finished when it can be traced, not when its parts are filled, and a design that passes every other row but leaves a scenario untraced is not finished.

7.9 Changing a design after review

When the review finds a fault, two decisions follow: what the revision covers, and who makes it. The first depends on how much of the change exists.

What exists What the revision covers
Only the design The part and the parts coupled to it. A changed decision can move the goal it served, the risk it created and the traces, so every scenario is walked again, not only the one that prompted the change.
The design, with the tasks written from it Those too, because the tasks were written from the decisions that changed.
An archived change Nothing in the archive. A later gap goes into a new change, whose design names the design it replaces in its Context.

The archive keeps the decisions as they were made, as section 5.9 says of the proposal, and the same reason applies here. The example shows the bottom row and not the middle one. The second change's design is a new design in a new change, as section 4.11 shows, and the first design is not touched. The middle row, a design revised while its tasks exist, has no case in the archive, for the reason chapter 5 gives: the second change was written after the first was archived, from a finding.

A revision is made by editing the file or by asking the agent to change it, and the choice turns on whether the replacement is known. The table compares the two means on four points.

The developer edits the file The agent is asked to revise it
Right when The replacement is known, and the fault sits in one decision or one reason The decision has to be worked out from the delta, the other decisions or the traces
What it costs A minute with the file open, and a diff that shows one change A request with three parts, a whole file to read back, and a diff whose size hides what changed
How it goes wrong An edit to one decision leaves its goal, its risk or its trace out of step with it A request for a clearer decision returns a rewrite that changes what was decided
What to check afterwards The goals, risks and traces that the decision touches The whole file, including the decisions nobody meant to change

Suppose the second reason of the first design had said that the method is the usual one, and the developer knows the sentence the archive holds: that it is short to state and easy to trace by hand. One sentence changes, and nothing else needs to move, because a reason's wording is not an input to any trace. The diff shows that sentence and nothing else.

Suppose a design, not one of the example's, records one decision with no alternative, and the developer cannot yet say what was open. The request to the agent names that decision, says that no alternative is recorded for it, and says that the decision's text, its reason, the other decisions and the traces must not move. The agent proposes alternatives from the delta and the design's other decisions, and the developer decides which of them anyone would have chosen. Without the third part, the agent may rewrite the whole Decisions part, and the rewrite may change decisions that nobody asked about.

Both means end in the same reading. An edit is checked by its diff, and a revision made by asking is a rewrite, so the whole design is read again as a new draft, with the four passes of section 7.8. Chapter 6 said that the tool catches a scenario dropped from a MODIFIED block and does not catch one whose text moved. A design has no such check. A decision can be dropped, or its reason changed, and validate still passes. The trace is what notices, and it notices only for the scenarios that exist.

7.10 What the design hands on

The design hands the tasks the decisions to check and the traces that have been done. Section 4.5 shows the first two tasks of the example, which are traces of its two scenarios. The design also hands over any open question, which the instruction for the tasks asks to be resolved before the tasks are written. What the delta handed to the design, the design now holds as decisions, each with its reason and, where one was open, its alternative.

The tasks do not say what the system must do, and they do not decide how it works. They say how each decision is checked, and they turn those checks into items that can be marked done. A command and a workflow that are not files, validate and archive, close the change. Chapter 8 takes up the tasks and outlines what follows them, and chapters 11 and 12 describe them in full.

A design is the decisions that meet the cases. An agent drafts it, a program reads none of it, and a person judges it by tracing the cases through it. The agent supplies the four parts and the form the instruction asks for, and the developer decides whether a design is needed and whether each reason holds. A reason that can be set beside a requirement can be checked, and a reason that is only convenience cannot. A non-goal is a statement that the review reads against the scenarios, and a trace is the pass that finds a decision in conflict with a case. The reader should carry away that a design is judged by whether its scenarios can be traced through it and whether what it leaves out is honest. A design that the tool accepts can still leave a scenario untraced, and finding that scenario is the reviewer's work.

8. The Tasks and the Evidence That a Check Was Made

Chapter 7 ended with the decisions and the traces handed to the next artifact, which it said says how each decision is checked. This chapter takes that artifact up and asks the same four questions of it: who writes it, which of its parts must be right, how a reviewer decides that it is finished, and what happens when the review finds something wrong. The example is the same vending machine and the same two changes. What comes after the tasks, the apply and archive workflows and the validate command, is given an outline at the end of this chapter, and chapters 11 and 12 describe them in full.

The table shows the files of a change and the paths of its specifications. The row this chapter discusses is in bold.

Item File What it says Discussed in
Change openspec/changes/<change>/ The folder of one change. Chapter 4
Proposal proposal.md Why the change exists and what it changes. Chapters 4 and 5
Capability specs/<capability>/ The folder for one area of behaviour, such as purchase. Chapters 4 and 6
Specification specs/<capability>/spec.md What one change adds, modifies or removes. Chapters 4 and 6
Main specification openspec/specs/<capability>/spec.md The system as it stands. Chapters 4 and 6
Design design.md How the work is done. Chapters 4 and 7
Tasks tasks.md The checks that turn the design into work. Chapters 4 and 8
Schema marker .openspec.yaml The schema the change follows, and skip_specs when it has no deltas. Chapter 4

8.1 Who writes the tasks

The agent drafts the first version of tasks.md from the delta and the design. Before it writes, the instruction tells it to read the design's Open Questions and to resolve with the user any that would change what gets built, so that no unstated assumption is built into the list. It supplies the form of the template, a task for each decision that reads as sound, and a way of verifying each one. What it cannot supply is what the team can really verify, which evidence could fail, or what size of check fits one session. The developer's part is to ask of each task what would show that it had failed. Section 5.1 describes the same division for the proposal, and sections 6.1 and 7.1 describe it for the delta and the design. Chapter 2 gives the reason human control stays with the developer.

In the spec-driven schema the tasks require both the delta and the design, so openspec status shows them as blocked until both exist, and the apply workflow requires the tasks. The instruction of the apply workflow tells the agent to work through the pending tasks and to mark each one complete as it goes. In the default schema the agent therefore writes the check and ticks it, and nothing records which of the two made it. A person is the only party who can tell the check from the tick, and the rest of this chapter is about how.

8.2 The parts of the tasks

The table says what the tool checks of each part of the tasks. For this artifact the answer is a count.

Part What the tool checks The question it answers
Group heading Nothing. Which checks belong together, and in what order?
Task list, instructions apply and archive count the checkbox lines. A box holding only x or X is done. What has to be checked, and has it been?

The tasks are the one artifact whose content the tool counts, and it counts nothing but checkboxes. validate never opens the tasks.md of a change that has not been archived. Only the form --archived opens a tasks.md: it reads the tasks of archived changes and reports an open box as an error, as chapter 11 shows. status counts the file as done if it exists, whatever it contains: a file of one character, a file of prose and an empty file all show as done. list shows a file with no checkbox as "No tasks", instructions apply calls that change blocked, and archive goes ahead, because there is nothing to count. A box holding x, X or x is done. The markers [~], [-] and [] read as unfinished and are still counted, and a line with no checkbox is not counted. The "1.1" in a task is text: instructions apply numbers the tasks by their position in the file, and a group heading appears nowhere in its output. The two parts are the whole of the default template, and a part that a project adds belongs in a forked schema, as chapter 3 described. The tool therefore reads a number, and the number says how many boxes are ticked. It does not say whether any check was made, and that is the finding of this section.

8.3 Groups and tasks

The file is tasks.md in the change give-exact-change, and it is shown in full as archived:

## 1. Check the first version

- [x] 1.1 Trace the scenario "Change is given from stock" through the design by hand. **Verified by** the trace in the design's Findings, which matches the scenario.
- [x] 1.2 Trace the scenario "Exact payment gives no change" through the design by hand. **Verified by** the trace in the design's Findings, which matches the scenario.
- [x] 1.3 Run `openspec validate --strict`. **Verified by** the command passing.

Its single group, "Check the first version", holds three tasks: two traces and a validation run. Each is one check. The numbers 1.1 to 1.3 are the author's, as the previous section said.

The file is tasks.md in the change refuse-without-exact-change, and it is shown in full as archived:

## 1. Trace the first version

- [x] 1.1 Write the scenario "Stock cannot make the change" from the requirement's word "exact". **Verified by** the scenario in the spec delta.
- [x] 1.2 Trace the scenario through the first design of `give-exact-change`. **Verified by** Trace A in the design's Findings, which records both symptoms.

## 2. Revise and trace again

- [x] 2.1 Revise the design so that the change is worked out before release, and a change that is not exact is refused. **Verified by** the decisions in the design.
- [x] 2.2 Trace all three scenarios through the revised design. **Verified by** Traces B, C and D in the design's Findings.
- [x] 2.3 Run `openspec validate --strict`. **Verified by** the command passing.

The second change has five tasks in two groups. In the first the failure is written down and traced, and in the second the design is revised and checked again, so the second group cannot begin before the first has given an answer. The instruction asks for the tasks to be ordered by dependency and to be small enough to finish in one session, and both files meet that: each task is one check. Section 4.12 says what the groups do.

Every box in both files is ticked, and the archive keeps them. A tick does not hold its evidence. Each task points at the delta, at a trace in the design's Findings, at the decisions, or at a command, so the box is a pointer, and the file it names holds what it points at. A reader of the tasks alone learns that someone ticked, and has to open the file the task names to learn why. Section 4.5 says what a tick records. This chapter asks what a reader can do with one.

8.4 What the template leaves out

The instruction for the tasks asks for two things that the template does not have. The first is a statement in each task of how it is verified. The instruction says that each task must state how to verify completion, with a test, a command, an observable behaviour or a delivered artifact, and that the statement goes in the task's own description. The template has two checkbox placeholders and no part for it. The example fixes the wording through a rule in its project configuration, and Verified by is the example's wording of what the instruction already asks.

The file is tasks.md in the change give-exact-change, and its task 1.1 reads as archived:

- [x] 1.1 Trace the scenario "Change is given from stock" through the design by hand. **Verified by** the trace in the design's Findings, which matches the scenario.

A reviewer opens the design, reads the trace and compares it with the scenario. The trace could have disagreed with the scenario, and the reviewer can see whether it did. Section 4.7 shows a trace of this kind.

The file is tasks.md in the change refuse-without-exact-change, and its task 2.1 reads as archived:

- [x] 2.1 Revise the design so that the change is worked out before release, and a change that is not exact is refused. **Verified by** the decisions in the design.

Here the decision is both what was done and the proof that it was done, so this evidence cannot show a failure of its own. The question a reviewer asks of any task is whether its evidence could have come out the other way. Task 2.2 of the same file, which traces all three scenarios through the revised design, is the task whose evidence can fail. The example shows both kinds side by side, as written.

The example has three kinds of evidence. A reading, such as a trace in the design or a scenario in the delta, can be opened by someone who was not there. The work itself, such as the decisions of task 2.1, is the claim again. A command's result, as in the last task of each file, which runs openspec validate --strict and names the command passing, is recorded by the box and by the clause, and nowhere else unless the task says where. Section 8.2 says what validate reads, so those two tasks are evidence about the delta and no more. Section 4.5 says what followed for the first change.

The instruction's second addition is for steps that need the archive.
