It asks that the tracked tasks be work that can be completed before the archive, and that any step which waits for the archive be a plain bullet under an optional ## Workflow follow-up section, where the tool does not count it. The reason shows in what archive does with an open box: it asks whether to continue. A box for the archive itself could not be ticked before the archive ran, so it would be an open box at the moment the archive counts. The instruction names the section for use when it applies, and neither example file has one.

8.5 Reviewing the tasks

The tasks are reviewed twice. The first review is made after the design is reviewed and before apply begins, and it asks whether the checks are the right ones. The second is made when the boxes are ticked, and it reads each ticked box against the evidence its task names. The tool shows the count at both moments and checks neither review. The review has four passes. Intent asks whether the tasks check this change and not another. Coverage asks whether each decision of the design, and each trace it hands on, has a task that checks it, and whether each task checks something the design holds. Evidence asks whether each task's evidence could have come out the other way, and whether someone who was not there can open it. Order asks whether the tasks are small, ordered by dependency and grouped so that each group lands its own tests and documentation. Coverage and evidence matter most, because the tool counts boxes and sees neither.

When every box is ticked, instructions apply reports the change as all done, and it tells the agent to review or verify the change as appropriate before archiving. The tool leaves the verification to a person, and the second review is the one the count cannot do: it finds the box whose evidence is absent.

The table is one checklist, in the order the file is read. The column names use the artifact's name, which here is the tasks.

Check The tasks pass when How a draft can fail
The request is answered as meant The tasks check the change that the design describes, and nothing in them answers an assumption the agent made The list checks another change, or adds work that the design does not hold
Group heading Each group names one stretch of work, and the groups follow the order that the work depends on A group collects unlike checks, or a final group holds tests or documentation that an earlier group owed
Task: size Each task is one check that can be finished in one session One task holds several checks under one box, so one tick stands for several claims
Task: coverage Each decision of the design, and each trace it hands on, has a task that checks it, and each task checks something the design holds A decision has no task, so nothing checks it, or a task checks something that no decision states
Verification: statement Each task says how it is verified, in the form the instruction asks for A task names no evidence, or names only the work itself as evidence
Verification: evidence The evidence could have come out the other way, and someone who was not there can open it The evidence is the claim itself, or it sits where no one can find it
Box Each ticked box has its evidence in the place the task names, and each open box has none yet A box is ticked and its evidence is absent, or the task was reworded after the tick
Workflow follow-up A step that waits for the archive is a plain bullet and not a box An archive step is written as a box, so the list cannot be finished before the archive it waits for
Downstream The count is complete because each task is ticked with its evidence, and the change can go to archive The list reads complete because an open task was removed or reworded, or an open box is left for the archive to ask about

The table is a memory aid, and no part of the tool reads it. A row that passes records a person's judgment, not a machine's check. The rows on evidence, on the box and on what is downstream look beyond the file to the files its tasks name, and they are the ones that cannot be read from the tasks alone. A task list is finished when each tick can be traced to its evidence, not when the count is complete.

8.6 Changing the tasks after review

When the review finds a fault, two decisions follow: what the revision covers, and who makes it. The first depends on how many boxes are ticked and whether the change is archived.

What exists What the revision covers
Only the tasks, and no box ticked The task, its order and the tasks that depend on it.
The tasks, with boxes ticked Those too. A tick belongs to the task as it was, so a task whose wording changes is reopened until its check is made again.
An archived change Nothing in the archive. A later gap goes into a new change, whose tasks name the change they check.

The archive keeps the tasks as they were, as section 5.9 says of the proposal, and the same reason applies here. The example shows the bottom row and not the middle one. The second change's tasks are a new list in a new change. Its task 1.2 traces the design of the first change, and the first change's list is untouched, with every box still ticked. The middle row, a list revised while boxes are ticked, has no case in the archive, for the reason chapter 5 gives: the second change was written after the first was archived, from a finding.

A revision is made by editing the file or by asking the agent to change it, and the choice turns on whether the replacement is known. The table compares the two means on four points.

The developer edits the file The agent is asked to revise it
Right when The replacement is known, and the fault sits in one task The check has to be worked out from the design, or several tasks have to move together
What it costs A minute with the file open, and a diff that shows one line A request with three parts, a whole file to read back, and a diff whose size hides what changed
How it goes wrong An edit changes what a task checks while its box stays ticked A request for a clearer list returns a renumbered one, in which boxes have turned over and the count has changed
What to check afterwards The task's box against its new wording, and the tasks that depend on it Each box against its evidence, and the whole list with its count

Suppose the first change's task 1.2 had named the first scenario, "Change is given from stock", and the developer knows the name the archive holds: "Exact payment gives no change". One name changes. The box was ticked against the trace of the first scenario, so the developer reads the trace the task now names before the box stays ticked. The diff shows one name, and the tick is the part the diff does not show.

Suppose a task list, not one of the example's, holds a task whose evidence is "the design", and the developer cannot yet say what would fail. The request to the agent has three parts:

  1. which task to revise: the one whose evidence is the design;
  2. what is wrong with it: the evidence cannot fail, because it is the work itself;
  3. what must not move: the other tasks, their order and the boxes already ticked.

The agent proposes evidence from the delta's scenarios and the design's traces, and the developer decides which of them would catch a wrong design. Without the third part, the agent may renumber the list and turn boxes over.

Both means end in the same reading. An edit is checked by its diff, which includes the state of each box. A revision made by asking is a rewrite, so the whole list is read again as a new draft, with the passes of section 8.5 and each box against its evidence. Chapter 6 said that the tool reports a scenario dropped from a MODIFIED block, and chapter 7 said that it notices nothing of a design. The tasks fall between. The count moves, and a box turned over and an open task removed both make the list read complete, in the same words. The tool is not wrong to count. It counts what it can see.

8.7 What the tasks hand on

The tasks are the one artifact that the next workflow reads, and the schema names them as the file that apply tracks. Three things follow them: the apply workflow, the validate command and the archive workflow. This section gives each one a paragraph, saying what it does with the tasks and one fact that a reader would not guess.

Apply is the workflow in which the boxes change. instructions apply reports one of three states: blocked when there is no task to work on, ready when some are open, and all done when none is. The developer's part is the second review of section 8.5: to read the evidence and not the ticks.

The example's tasks run the validate command as a check. openspec validate --strict fails on a warning, such as a requirement that says should where SHALL or MUST belongs, and archive does not: it blocks on errors, and a warning passes it without being shown. The main specification then fails the strict check for the same warning. A task that names "the command passing" is therefore evidence about whichever form the task names.

The archive command reads the tasks to count them. It prints the count, and when some boxes are open it asks whether to continue. The default answer is no, and a run with no one to answer is refused unless it is told to continue. The archive workflow reads the same count from list and asks the user to confirm before it goes on. A change with no tasks.md, or with no checkbox in it, raises no question about the tasks. The archive command refuses a delta it cannot merge and changes no file, and when it succeeds it moves the change into the archive under the date; the workflow stops before it moves the change if its merge fails. Sections 4.6 and 4.14 describe what that leaves in the main specification.

The tasks said how each decision is checked, and what is described above uses them. Chapters 9 to 12 describe what the tool does in each, who decides, and what to review. The frame of this chapter fits a file with parts, and it bends for a workflow: those chapters give each workflow a card, and a table of its stages or forms, in place of a file's parts.

The tasks are the checks of the design. An agent drafts them, a program counts them without being able to read them, and a person judges them by opening the evidence behind each box. The agent supplies the form of the template, and the developer decides what counts as evidence and whether each task could have failed. The tool reads a number, so a tick is a claim, and a claim whose evidence is the work itself, or cannot be found, is one that no one can check. A reading that someone who was not there can open is evidence, and so is a result that could have come out the other way. The review is made twice, before the work and when the boxes are ticked, because the tasks are the one artifact that changes after it is reviewed, and the update paths turn on whether a box is already ticked. The workflows and the command that follow count and move what the tasks record, and none of them verifies it. The reader should carry away that a list of ticked boxes shows that someone ticked, and that a task is done when its evidence can be opened and could have failed.

9. The Workflows and Who Does the Work

Chapters 4 to 8 followed one change from its first artifact to the archive and took the four artifacts apart. Along the way they met apply, validation and archive, which are not files, and gave each of them an outline. OpenSpec defines twelve workflows. The core profile installs six of them, and this book examines continue as a seventh. This chapter names those seven, the one command that belongs to no workflow and the one skill that is not a workflow, and chapter 15 takes the other five. It asks four questions: what a workflow is, who does the work in it, which workflows a project has, and what the three chapters that follow rest on.

9.1 The workflows and the order they are met in

The table lists the seven workflows and the validate command, in the order a change first meets them, with the entry point of each and a short description.

Workflow Entry point What it does
Explore the skill openspec-explore Think about a problem or idea with the agent before there is a change. It writes nothing unless the user confirms.
Propose the skill openspec-propose Create a change and all of its planning artifacts in one run.
Continue the skill openspec-continue-change Create the next missing artifact, one per run. Not in the core profile.
Update the skill openspec-update-change Revise the artifacts a change has and make them agree.
Apply the skill openspec-apply-change Work through the tasks and tick each box when its work is done.
Validate the command openspec validate Check the delta and the main specifications against the format rules. A command, not a workflow.
Sync the skill openspec-sync-specs Merge a change's delta into the main specifications without archiving it.
Archive the skill openspec-archive-change and the command openspec archive Merge the delta unless told not to, count the tasks, and move the change into the archive.

The order of the table is a reading order, and the tool enforces none of it. Continue is another way of doing what propose does: propose creates every planning artifact in one run, and continue creates one artifact in each. Update and validate can be run again whenever the artifacts exist. Sync is optional, because archive can make the same merge. The skill openspec-apply-change, as OpenSpec installs it, tells the agent that apply can be invoked at any time, including before every artifact is done, as long as tasks exist. OpenSpec's documentation names its model "actions, not phases", and chapter 3 said the same of the artifacts when it described their dependencies as enablers and not gates.

9.2 What a workflow is made of, and who acts in it

A workflow is delivered as a skill, and a skill is a text that the agent reads. Its heart is a Markdown file, SKILL.md, in an .agents/skills/ folder, the project's or the machine's as chapter 3 describes. Each skill has a folder of its own, and that folder may also hold a references/ folder of further instructions, which the agent opens only when a task calls for them. SKILL.md begins with front matter and goes on with instructions to the agent. In the seven workflow skills of this chapter and in the router, the front matter gives the skill's name, a description of what it is for and which words invoke it, and the one program the skill may run in a shell, openspec. It also carries a licence, an author and a version of the skill's own, and the router's adds references, a short hash of its reference files. Skills of earlier releases also named the release that generated them; the current ones do not. The coding tool the book was checked with shows the model each skill's name and description each time it calls the model, and loads the body of a skill only when the model asks for it by name or the developer mentions it. The program does not run a skill. The agent reads it and does what it says.

What the program contributes is facts and checks. The skills tell the agent to ask a command and not to assume. The skill openspec-propose tells it to run openspec context --json to find the project's root and openspec new change to create a change. The skills tell it to run openspec status for the state of a change's artifacts, openspec instructions for the template and the instruction of an artifact, and openspec instructions apply for the tasks and the count of those done. The skill openspec-archive-change tells it to run openspec list --json for a change's task counts, and the skill openspec-sync-specs tells it to run openspec validate --specs after a merge. The skills also tell it not to assume names that the program knows: the skill openspec-continue-change says to use the schema's artifact sequence and not to assume artifact names, and the skill openspec-apply-change says to use the files that the command returns and not to assume file names. The skill gives the order of the work, and the program gives the state that the work starts from.

The table says what each of the three parties does and what it leaves to the others.

Party Does Leaves to others
The agent Follows the skill: reads the files, calls the commands and writes the files, and in the archive workflow can make the merge of a delta itself. The facts about the state of a change, which the program reports, and every decision, which the developer makes.
The program Reports the state and the counts, checks the format, and, as the commands validate and archive, checks a delta, can merge it and moves a change into the archive. The reading of the project and the writing of its files, which the agent does, and what is wanted, which the developer says.
The developer Decides what is wanted, confirms what a skill asks to have confirmed, and reviews the result. The writing of the files, which the agent does, and the checks of format, which the program does.

The same division holds in every workflow; it is chapter 3's pattern, and each workflow weighs its three parties differently. In explore the agent writes nothing until the developer confirms that it may, so the developer decides what is written, if anything. In propose the agent writes every planning artifact. In validate there is no skill, and the program does the work. In archive the work can be the program's or the agent's. The chapters that follow ask, for each workflow, who does what.

9.3 Which workflows are installed, and what they are called

OpenSpec installs the workflows that a setting called the profile asks for, so no project has all twelve unless its profile names them. The core profile installs six:

  • propose: for when the developer can already say what is wanted.
  • explore: for when something has to be thought through, before a change or during one.
  • apply: for when the plan is ready and the work starts, or has to be picked up again.
  • update: for when the plan has changed, or an artifact was edited by hand and the others no longer agree with it.
  • sync: for when the main specifications should show a change before it is archived.
  • archive: for when the work is finished and the change is to be closed.

Continue is not one of them; a profile that names it installs it. The profile is a setting of the machine, not of one project. The command openspec update rewrites the installed skills so that they match it. Every profile also installs one skill that is not a workflow: openspec, the router. openspec config list does not show it, because no profile chooses it. A workflow whose skill is not installed cannot be called by its name.

The router changes who picks the workflow. Its description tells the agent to reach for it when the developer asks for OpenSpec work without naming a skill, and its text then leaves the agent three moves: answer a question, hand the request to one skill, or run several skills in order. A table in the skill maps requests to the twelve workflow skills. When a request fits more than one row, the agent asks which is meant; when it runs several skills, it finishes each before starting the next, and every skill's own stops still hold. The agent picks the workflow from the table, and the program checks nothing about that choice. The developer can still name a skill directly; the router is written for the request that names none. Its table also covers the workflows whose skill is not installed. For those, the router tells the agent to say so, to point to openspec config profile and openspec update, and then to follow a shorter path from one of its reference files, which chapter 15 describes.

Some of the names are easy to mix up:

  1. openspec update is a command that rewrites the installed skills. It is not the update workflow, which revises a change's artifacts.
  2. Archive is both a command and a workflow. The command is archive, and the workflow is archive. The table lists both as its entry points.
  3. Explore, apply and sync have no command of their own name. openspec apply, openspec sync and openspec explore each give an error, "unknown command".

A workflow is therefore written in plain text, and a command or a skill in code font.

9.4 What comes next

What the next chapters say about a skill comes from reading it, and what they say about a command comes from running it. Each time the book moved to a newer release, every run was repeated, and the results stayed the same except for the number of skills a profile installs, for the reason section 9.3 gives: the router. A skill is a text, and one agent can follow the same text differently from another, so the developer's review covers that difference.

The next three chapters take the workflows in the order of the table, in three groups: those that write the plan, those that do the work and check it, and those that bring the project's record up to date. Each asks the same four questions of every workflow:

  1. Who does the work?
  2. What does it read and write, and what can stop it?
  3. How does a reviewer judge what it did?
  4. What happens when its result is wrong?

Each workflow gets a card with the same five rows, so that one can be compared with another.

Item What it says
Entry point The skill or the command that starts the workflow, and the words that call it.
Who acts Which of the agent, the program and the developer does each part of the work.
Writes The files that the workflow creates or changes, or that it changes none.
What can stop it The check, the missing input or the question to the developer that halts it before it is done.
The developer's part What the developer decides, confirms or reviews, and what the workflow leaves to them.

The workflows that write the plan come first, because the reader already knows them by their results.

A workflow is a skill that the agent reads and the commands that skill calls, and the order of the table is not an order that the tool enforces. The question to carry into the next chapters is who does the work in a workflow, because the answer differs: the agent writes in propose, the program checks in validate, and in archive the work can be the program's or the agent's.

10. The Planning Workflows and What Each Leaves Behind

The previous chapter said who does the work in general: the agent writes, the commands report facts and check, and the developer decides and reviews. This chapter takes the four workflows that write or revise a change's plan, which are explore, propose, continue and update. For each it asks what the developer does, what the workflow writes, how a reviewer judges what it did, and what happens when its result is wrong. The chapters on the four artifacts showed what the files contain. This chapter shows what creates them and what the developer does while they are made.

10.1 Explore: thinking before there is a change

The skill openspec-explore, as OpenSpec installs it, calls itself "a stance, not a workflow". In explore the agent thinks with the developer, reads the project before asking what it can find out itself, asks one question at a time, and never writes code. Writes are allowed only within a scope the developer has confirmed. Before the first write, the agent names the files and asks a yes or no in a separate message. An answer to a design question is never consent.

The card sets out the five rows that every workflow's card has.

Item Explore
Entry point The skill openspec-explore, called by naming it or by the words "openspec explore" or "opsx explore".
Who acts The agent reads, asks and draws. The developer, as the last row says.
Writes Nothing, except what the next table allows.
What can stop it A project with no OpenSpec root, where the agent sets nothing up, and the lack of a yes before a write.
The developer's part To steer the thinking, to decide when it is enough, and to say yes or no to a write.

Explore has no stages to list, so the table says what it may do and what allows each thing.

What explore may do What allows it What is checked
Read files and run read-only commands Nothing is needed; a read needs no confirmation list, list --specs and show change no file.
Scaffold a change The developer's request to capture the exploration, or a yes to an offer that named the change new change refuses a name already in use.
Write the artifacts the request names The same request or yes, for those artifacts only Nothing at the write. status later counts a file as done if it exists.
Write anything else Nothing allows it Nothing.

The commands explore runs give read-only facts: the changes in flight with their task counts, the capabilities, and the text of one specification. None of them changes a file. Nothing checks that explore stays read-only. In a directory with no root, the commands answer no_openspec_root and create nothing.

Explore leaves nothing unless something is captured. It ends when the developer asks for the exploration to be captured as a change. That request needs no separate yes: the agent creates that change and writes the artifacts the request names, and nothing else. Explore ends in a proposal, in updated artifacts, or in clarity and nothing more.

10.2 Propose: the whole plan in one run

Propose creates a change and writes every artifact the change needs in one run. The agent asks the developer only about an ambiguity that would change the scope, the observable behaviour, the compatibility or the acceptance criteria. It makes a reasonable assumption for a minor detail and records it in the artifacts. The request authorizes planning only. The agent stops once the artifacts exist and does not implement what the request asked to build. Sections 5.1, 6.1, 7.1 and 8.1 say who writes each artifact and what the developer's part is in it, and this chapter does not repeat them.

Item Propose
Entry point The skill openspec-propose, called by naming it or by the words "openspec propose" or "opsx propose".
Who acts The agent writes, and runs the commands of the stages below.
Writes The change's folder and its .openspec.yaml, and every artifact in the required set, except one whose own instruction makes it conditional and that the agent reports as skipped.
What can stop it A question the agent asks about an ambiguity, the answer no_openspec_root at stage 2, and the refusal of a name at stage 4.
The developer's part The request, the answers to the questions, the assumptions in the drafts, and the review of each draft.

The table sets out the seven stages of the skill.

Stage What happens
1. Understand the request and clarify material ambiguity The agent derives a name for the change from the request. It asks the developer about an ambiguity that would change the scope, the observable behaviour, the compatibility or the acceptance criteria, and assumes a minor detail and records the assumption.
2. Load project context context --json returns the project's root, and the agent reads its openspec/config.yaml. Where there is no root, the command answers no_openspec_root, and the agent stops and changes no file.
3. Determine the workflow schema The project's default schema is used. Only when the developer names another or asks which schemas exist does the agent run schemas --json, which lists each schema and its artifacts.
4. Create the change directory new change creates the folder with its .openspec.yaml under the name from stage 1, and refuses a name already in use. In a directory with no root it creates a root as well, which is why stage 2 checks for one.
5. Get the artifact build order status --json returns each artifact's status, the artifacts it requires, and applyRequires, the artifacts apply needs. From it the agent works out which artifacts the change needs and which can be written now.
6. Create every artifact in the required set For each artifact that is ready, instructions <artifact> --json returns the template and the instruction, and the agent reads the files it depends on from disk, inspects the project, and writes the file from the template. status then reports which artifacts are ready now, counting a file as done if the file exists, until every artifact in the required set exists.
7. Show final status status reports each artifact and whether planning is complete, and the agent shows its output to the developer.

For each artifact, instructions returns the template, the schema's instruction, the artifacts it depends on and the path of its file. When openspec/config.yaml has a context or rules, the command returns them too. They are constraints for the agent and are not to be copied into the file, and nothing checks that they were not.

What propose leaves is a folder of files. In a scratch project, a new change holds .openspec.yaml alone, and the proposal is the only ready artifact. After the proposal, the specification and the design are ready. A specification is done as soon as one file matches its path, however many the proposal named. A file of one character also counts as done. A change that declares skip_specs shows the specification as skipped from the start. Chapter 4 shows the four files of each of the example's two changes in full.

For the developer, propose is one session of reading. The four drafts arrive together, so the review covers all of them at once. The minor assumptions are the part to check, because a reader who does not look for them will miss them. In the output of status, an artifact shown as skipped was skipped on the agent's reading of its own instruction. In the default schema the design is the artifact whose instruction makes it conditional, so decide whether you agree with the skip.

10.3 Continue: one artifact at a time

Continue writes one artifact per run and then stops. Which artifact comes next is not the agent's choice: it is the first one that status reports as ready. If an earlier run stopped part way through a specification, finishing it counts as the run's one artifact. If planning is already complete, the agent says so and writes nothing.

Item Continue
Entry point The skill openspec-continue-change, called by naming it or by the words "openspec continue" or "opsx continue". It is installed only in a profile that adds it.
Who acts The agent writes the artifact that status reports as ready next.
Writes One artifact per run: the first that is ready, or the missing files of a specification that is partly written.
What can stop it Planning that is already complete, and no artifact that is ready.
The developer's part To choose the change when several are in flight, to read each draft before asking for the next, and to decide the pace.

The skill has four stages.

Stage What happens
1. Select the change The agent uses the change the developer names, infers it from the conversation, or takes the only change in flight. Otherwise list --json returns the changes in flight, the latest modified first, and the developer chooses.
2. Check current status status --json returns each artifact as done, ready, blocked or skipped, and whether planning is complete, and the agent reads from it what is next.
3. Act based on status A specification that an earlier run left partly written is finished first. If planning is complete, the agent says so and stops. Otherwise it takes the first ready artifact, runs instructions for it as at stage 6 of propose, reads the files it depends on from disk, writes the file, and stops after that one artifact.
4. After creating an artifact, show progress status shows the artifact just written as done and the artifacts that are ready now, and the agent shows the developer what the new file unlocked.

The order in which artifacts become ready is the one section 10.2 found: the tasks wait for the specification and the design, and a skipped artifact never becomes ready. The order of writing therefore follows the schema, and not the agent.

For the developer, continue gives a review point after each artifact, at the price of one run for each. Read each draft before you ask for the next, because the next artifact is written from it. There is one thing status cannot show. A run that was interrupted after one of three specification files leaves the specification looking finished, so count the files against the capabilities the proposal lists, one spec.md for each, as chapter 6 said.

10.4 Update: revising what exists

Update revises the artifacts that exist and keeps them coherent. The agent drafts every revision in the conversation first, writes a file only after the developer confirms its revision, one artifact at a time, and never edits code. When the request changes the intent of the change rather than its detail, the agent recommends a new change under a new name.

Item Update
Entry point The skill openspec-update-change, called by naming it or by the words "openspec update change" or "opsx update". It is not the command openspec update.
Who acts The agent drafts and reconciles. The developer, as the last row says.
Writes The artifact files that exist, and never code. After a confirmation, a missing file under a specification that already has one.
What can stop it A revision the developer rejects, and a request that changes the intent.
The developer's part The revision, the confirmation of each write, and the call on whether the intent has changed.

The skill has six stages.

Stage What happens
1. Select the change As at stage 1 of continue.
2. Get the change's artifacts status --json returns each artifact's status and the files that exist, and the agent takes the files to revise from its output and not from assumed names.
3. Understand the request The agent decides whether the developer asked for a specific revision or only for the artifacts to be made to agree.
4. Read and reconcile The agent reads the artifacts, drafts the requested edit in the conversation and not in a file, and checks every other existing artifact against it, in either direction. It notes what is now inconsistent or missing.
5. Confirm and apply, one artifact at a time The agent shows each proposed revision with its reason, writes it only after the developer confirms, and leaves a rejected one unwritten. Before a substantial rewrite it runs instructions, which returns the template and the rules. Nothing checks the confirmation.
6. Point to what comes next The agent names the workflow that follows and does not start it. If tasks are already ticked, it tells the developer which may need revisiting.

The decisions in update are the agent's reading and the developer's confirmation, and nothing checks either.

In a scratch change whose tasks exist, an edit to the design changes no status, because every file still exists and every artifact is still done.

For the developer, update is where the reading happens, and no tool does it for you. Name the file and say what must not move. Chapter 5 shows what happens when a request leaves that out. Read every proposed revision, including those to files you did not name, because a revision to one of them may be one you did not ask for. Reject any revision that goes beyond the request. If your request changes what the change is for, do not push it through update. Take the recommendation of a new change, so that the archive keeps the old change as it was.

10.5 What the planning workflows leave out

No planning workflow decides that the plan is right. What is reported is that files exist. status reads no artifact for its content, and validate reads the delta and the main specifications and never the other three artifacts of a change in flight, as chapter 5 showed. The agent asks about an ambiguity and, in explore and update, asks for a write to be confirmed. That is the agent asking, not a check. Chapter 8 said that the tool counts the boxes in the tasks and nothing more. The review of the content is the developer's.

Continue is not in the core profile, so a project on that profile has propose and update and no continue. The choice between propose and continue is a choice about review points, which sections 10.2 and 10.3 set out. Neither is better in itself. The difference is where the developer reads.

10.6 Reviewing what a planning workflow did

This review asks whether the workflow did what its skill describes. It does not ask whether the file is right, which the checklists of the four artifact chapters do. It has four passes. Authority asks whether each write was asked for or confirmed. Coverage asks whether every artifact the plan needs exists and whether each was written from the one it depends on. Record asks whether every decision made in the conversation reached a file. Order asks whether each artifact was written after the ones it depends on. Record and Authority matter most, because no check sees who asked for a write or a decision that stayed in the conversation, and a decision that stays there is not in the archive.

The table is one checklist, ordered the way a change is made.

Check The workflow has done its job when How a run can fail
The request is answered as meant A reviewer can say which request the run answers, and nothing in the files answers an assumption made instead The run serves an assumption the developer did not make, and every artifact after it follows the assumption
Explore kept to what it may write Every file explore wrote is one that the table in section 10.1 allows A file was written on the strength of an answer to a design question, or beyond what the confirmation named
Propose wrote what its card names Nothing is missing that the card names, and nothing outside the change's folder was edited An artifact is missing though no skip was reported, or code was edited because the request asked for something to be built
Continue wrote what its card names The run wrote what the card names and nothing more Two artifacts were written in one run, or one was written before the ones it depends on
Update wrote what was confirmed Each changed file is one whose revision the developer confirmed A file changed that was not shown, or a rejected revision was written anyway
No context or rules text was copied into an artifact The artifacts say what the change is and do not repeat the project's constraints A constraint from the configuration was copied into a file as if it were content
A decision made in the conversation is in a file Each decision the developer remembers making is written in the artifact that owns it The decision was settled in the conversation and no file records it, so the archive will not hold it
Downstream The artifacts are ready for the reviews of the four artifact chapters Every file exists, and the plan has still not been reviewed

The table is a memory aid, and no part of the tool reads it.

Across the four workflows the developer can follow one routine:

  1. Commit the repository before a run, so that the run's changes show as one diff.
  2. Say in one sentence what the run is for.
  3. After the run, read status and the list of changed files. A changed file outside the change's folder, or any change under code, is a reason to stop and ask.
  4. Read the drafts in dependency order: the proposal first, then the artifacts written from it.
  5. Confirm, or revise. Revise by hand when the fix is one phrase. Ask for a revision when several files have to agree.
  6. Commit again once the drafts are read, so that the next run starts from a state that has been reviewed.

10.7 Changing the result

When the review finds that a planning workflow went wrong, two decisions follow: what the revision covers, and who makes it. The first depends on what already exists.

What exists What the revision covers
Only an exploration, with nothing written Nothing to revise. The conversation continues, or propose writes the plan. This is a new run and not an edit.
Drafts written and not yet reviewed An edit to the draft at its own part, by the paths of the chapter on that artifact.
Drafts reviewed, and later artifacts written from them An update that reconciles forwards: the artifacts written from the changed one are revised too, by the paths of the chapters on those artifacts.
Tasks ticked, and apply begun The update, and then a check of what apply has done. The skill says that the code may no longer match the revised plan.
The change archived Nothing in the archive. The correction is a new change.

The example's archive holds no revision of a draft, so of these rows it shows only the last: section 4.8 of chapter 4 says that the correction of the first change was made in a second change, because the first had been archived.

The second decision is about the means. The developer can revise the artifact by hand, or can ask the agent to run the workflow again. They differ in cost and in how they go wrong.

The developer revises by hand The agent is asked to run the workflow again
Right when The edit is one phrase that the developer can write without help Several artifacts have to agree, or the right text has to be worked out from the others
What it costs The developer's reading of every artifact that depends on the one changed A confirmation for each write, and a request that says what is not to move
How it goes wrong A dependent artifact is left as it was, so the files disagree The agent's reconciling misses a file, or a confirmation is given without reading what it confirms
What to check afterwards The diff, and each artifact written from the one that changed Each confirmed diff, and the artifacts that were not named

Suppose the developer changes one decision in the design of a vending machine change, so that the machine works out the change before it releases the product, and edits nothing else. By hand, the tasks are left as they were. status still shows every artifact done, and the tasks still check the order the design had before. The diff of the design shows the new decision and does not show the task that checks the old one.

Suppose the developer, instead, asks the update workflow to make the tasks agree with the changed decision. The tasks that checked the old decision are among the revisions the agent proposes, and the developer decides which to confirm. They are reopened or rewritten, and a ticked box is the part that the diff shows least.

Both means are checked in the same way: by the diff, and by reading what depends on the file that changed, because the diff shows words and not whether the artifacts agree. A revision is read as a new draft, with the passes of the review above.

10.8 What the planning workflows hand on

The planning workflows hand the plan to apply. The artifacts are its input, and apply requires the tasks. What it reads is the proposal, the specification, the design and the tasks. A plan that the developer has not reviewed is passed on as it is.

The next chapter takes the workflow that does the work and the command that checks the plan: apply and validate.

The planning workflows write a plan, and what is checked is only which files of it exist, so the plan is the developer's to judge. A change whose artifacts all exist is not a change whose plan is right.

11. Apply and Validate, and What a Tick and a Pass Show

The previous chapter took the four workflows that write or revise a plan, and it ended with the plan handed on to the workflow that carries it out. This chapter takes the next two entries of the table in section 9.1: apply, the workflow that does the work and ticks the boxes, and validate, the command that checks the form of the delta and the main specifications. They share a chapter because each leaves a result that a reader can take for more than it is, a count of ticks and a pass. For each it asks what the developer does, what it reads and writes and what can stop it, how a reviewer judges what it did, and what happens when its result is wrong. The examples are the tasks files of the vending machine's two changes, which hold ticks and no code, and a scratch project in which the commands were run.

11.1 Apply: working through the tasks

Apply carries out the plan one task at a time and keeps each change minimal. The agent stops and asks when a task is unclear, when an error occurs and when the developer interrupts, and in the two cases of scope and design set out below. Section 8.1 says who ticks the boxes and what that means for the evidence, and this chapter does not repeat it.

Item Apply
Entry point The skill openspec-apply-change, called by naming it or by the words "openspec apply", "opsx apply" or "openspec implement". The command openspec instructions apply serves it.
Who acts The agent works and ticks the boxes. The developer, as the last row says.
Writes The work that the tasks name, and a tick in the box of each finished task.
What can stop it A blocked state, a pause that the skill names, an error, and an interruption.
The developer's part To decide at each pause, and to judge each tick against its evidence.

The table sets out the seven stages of the skill.

Stage What happens
1. Select the change The agent uses the change the developer names, infers it from the conversation, or takes the only change in flight. Otherwise list --json returns the changes in flight, and the developer chooses.
2. Check the status to understand the schema status --json returns the schema's name and the artifacts, and from it the agent finds out which schema is in use and which artifact holds the tasks.
3. Get the apply instructions instructions apply --json returns the state, the context files, the progress, and each task with its file and line. When the state is blocked, the agent shows why and pauses. When it is all done, the agent says so and suggests a review. Otherwise it goes on.
4. Read the context files The agent reads every file the instructions list: for spec-driven, the proposal, the specification, the design and the tasks.
5. Show the current progress The agent shows the developer the schema, the count that stage 3 returned, and the tasks that remain.
6. Implement the tasks, in a loop For each pending task the agent does the work and keeps it minimal, checks that the box at the returned line still matches the task, ticks it, and runs instructions apply again to confirm that the count changed. The count is read from the box and not from the work. The agent pauses where the skill's rules for a pause apply.
7. Show the status on completion or pause The agent shows what this run did and the overall count, and the state is all done when no box is open. If the work paused, the agent says why and waits.

instructions apply reports a state and a count, and it checks that a tick registers and not that the work is done. In a scratch project, ticking one of two boxes moved the count from one complete to two and the state from ready to all done, and each returned line was the line of its box. A paragraph added above the tasks moved both returned lines by two, which is why the agent uses the line that is returned and not one it remembers. The instructions also return the project's context when the configuration has one. The skill says that neither that context nor the optional operationGuidance is evidence that a task is done. Section 8.7 describes the three states, and this chapter does not repeat them.

Apply has two kinds of rule, and nothing checks either. The first is the rule for a tick, whose guardrail in the skill reads "Only mark a task - [x] when its specified behavior is fully implemented, not when it is partially done or deferred". The second is the rules for pausing. When a task needs work beyond what the specification and the tasks describe, or the agent is tempted to drop, narrow, defer or accept an exception to specified behaviour to make the work fit, the agent surfaces the added scope and asks, and does not absorb it. When the work runs into a design issue, the agent suggests updating the artifacts.

Apply is defined by the schema, and it is not a gate. The schema's apply block says what apply requires, which file it tracks and what instruction it gives. The spec-driven schema requires the tasks and tracks tasks.md, and its instruction is two sentences that tell the agent to take the pending tasks in turn, to mark each complete, and to pause on a blocker or a need for clarification. A forked schema can rewrite that instruction, as chapter 3 described, so a fork can change the instruction that the agent is given. The skill says that apply can be invoked at any time, including before every artifact is done, as long as tasks exist, and that it can be interleaved with updates. In a scratch change that held only a tasks file, instructions apply reported the state ready, listed the proposal, the specification and the design as missing prerequisites, and warned that the change had no delta specification. Apply needs the tasks and not a complete plan.

Both archived tasks files of the vending machine have every box ticked: the first change's file has three tasks and the second change's has five. What the archive holds of the work is the ticks and the evidence each task names. Sections 4.5 and 4.12 show the two files in full, and chapter 8 takes them apart.

For the developer, apply is where a plan turns into work, and the review of what it did is the second review of section 8.5. When the agent pauses, the pause is a question for you, and the answers that matter are about scope: a task that needs more than the plan describes is a decision for the developer, and a design issue is a reason to revise the artifacts before the work goes on. In the diff, a box that is ticked with no change is a question to ask, and so is a change that no task names. The state all done means that no box is open, and the review the agent suggests at that point is yours.

11.2 Validate: checking the form of the delta

validate is a command, and OpenSpec has no skill for it. The command does the work, and something else runs it. The developer runs it, a task can name it, and the sync workflow runs openspec validate --specs after a merge. An agent runs it only when a task or a workflow says so. What the developer needs to know is which form was run, because the forms check different things.

Item Validate
Entry point The command openspec validate, with a name or an option. It has no skill.
Who acts The command checks. A developer, a task or another workflow runs it.
Writes Nothing. In a scratch project, runs of the plain, strict, bulk and archived forms left every file as it was.
What can stop it A failing result, which the paragraph after the next table explains. A run with no name and no option, and no one to ask, prints what to try and fails.
The developer's part To read the result, and to know what the form that was run covers.

A command has no stages, so the table sets out its forms, what each checks, and the question each answers.

Form What it checks The question it answers
openspec validate <change> The change's delta against the form rules of chapter 6, and the main specification that a MODIFIED requirement names. A MODIFIED requirement that the main specification lacks passes, with a note that the archive would refuse the delta. Is this delta well formed?
openspec validate <specification> One main specification against the same rules. Is this specification well formed?
--changes Every change in flight, with one result for each. Archived changes are not read. Are all the deltas well formed?
--specs Every main specification. Are all the specifications well formed?
--all The changes in flight and the main specifications. Is everything well formed?
--strict Added to any form: a warning fails as an error does. Is it free of warnings too?
--json Added to any form: the same checks, with the result as data. Each item has its type, whether it is valid and its issues, each with a level, a path and a message, and the totals follow. Can a script read the result?
--archived The archived changes only: that the tasks.md of each has no open box. It reads no delta. Was every task of each archived change ticked?

The options --type, --report, --concurrency, --no-interactive and --store are in the command's help and are not used here.

validate reads the delta and the main specifications, and the forms above do not open proposal.md, design.md or tasks.md of a change in flight. In a scratch change with no proposal, no design and an empty tasks.md, the command reported the change valid. The one form that opens a tasks.md is --archived, and it opens only archived ones. Chapters 4, 6 and 8 say what each file leaves to a person, and section 6.2 says what the delta is checked for, so chapter 11 adds nothing to them. An error and a warning differ in what they stop. An error fails the run in every form. A warning passes the plain form and fails the strict one. A note changes neither.

A pass is about the form of the delta, and the example's first change shows what that leaves out. Both tasks files of the example end with a task that names openspec validate --strict passing, and that is evidence about the delta and about nothing else. The first change passed validation and every task, and a case that no one had written still defeated its design. Section 4.5 says so, and section 4.7 walks through the case.

validate can be a gate. The command's help describes --archived as a check for pre-commit linting, and --json lets a script read the result as data and not as text. Running a form before archiving makes that form a precondition of the archive. The gate checks form. Run against the example, --archived passed both archived changes, because both files have all their boxes ticked.

For the developer, validate is a quick check with a narrow answer. Read the whole result and not the last line, because an error, a warning and a note mean different things, and the note is the only place the command says that the archive would refuse a delta. Run it again after any change to a delta, because a pass before the change says nothing about the delta after it.

11.3 What apply and validate leave out

Neither apply nor validate checks that the work is right. Apply's result is ticks. The work is the agent's, and the ticks are counted and reported. validate is structural, and it depends on neither the design nor the tasks of the change. No workflow in this chapter runs a project's tests or turns a scenario into one. A specification defines the expected behaviour, and tests and verification still have to check it, which chapter 2 says. A pass of validation is no verdict on the requirements, which chapter 3 says. A project that has code has its own tests, and the example has none.

11.4 Reviewing what apply and validate did

This review asks whether apply and validate did what their rules say. It does not ask whether the work is right, which is for the project's own tests and the second review of section 8.5. It has four passes. Evidence asks whether each tick is backed by evidence that could have failed, as section 8.5 describes. Scope asks whether anything was done that the plan does not name, or dropped that it does. Form asks whether validate was run, in which form and on what. Return asks whether a design issue found in the work went back to the artifacts. Evidence and Scope matter most, because what is checked is the count of ticks and the form, and neither shows them.

The table is one checklist, ordered the way the work is done.

Check The workflow has done its job when How a run can fail
The request is answered as meant A reviewer can say which change and which tasks the run answers, and the work follows the plan and not an assumption The run serves the tasks of another change, or an assumption the developer did not make
Apply read the context files and worked task by task Each task has its own change in the diff, in the order of the list One change stands for several tasks, or boxes were ticked together after the work
Each tick matches its task and its evidence Each tick has its evidence where its task says to look, and the evidence could have failed The evidence its task names is absent from a ticked box, or the evidence is the work itself
No behaviour was narrowed or deferred Each behaviour the delta names is in the work, and any added scope was put to the developer A behaviour was dropped, narrowed or deferred under a ticked box, or work that no task names was done
A pause was resolved by the developer Each question the work raised has an answer from the developer, in the conversation or in an artifact A question was settled without the developer, or the answer stayed in the conversation and no file holds it
A design issue went back to the artifacts The artifacts say what the work now does, and the boxes that rested on the old plan were reopened The work went round the issue and the design still states the old decision
validate was run in the form the project uses The form is the one the project names, run on the files as they now stand A form that does not read the changed files was run, or the result predates the last change to the delta
The result is read as being about form The pass is reported as covering the delta and the main specifications A pass is read as showing that the design, the tasks or the work are right
Downstream Every box is ticked with its evidence and the delta is valid, so the change is ready for archive The count is complete and the delta is valid, and neither says that the work is right

The table is a memory aid, and no part of the tool reads it. A result is accepted when a person has read what stands behind it.

Across the two, the developer can follow one routine:

  1. Commit the repository before apply runs, so that the run's changes show as one diff.
  2. Name the change the run is for, and read its tasks first, so that you know what each tick should be backed by.
  3. Answer each pause as a decision.
  4. After the run, read the diff beside the ticks, task by task, and open the evidence each task names.
  5. Run validate in the form the project uses.
  6. Commit once the result is read, so that the next run starts from a state that has been reviewed.

11.5 Changing the result

When the review finds that apply or validate went wrong, two decisions follow: what the revision covers, and who makes it. The first depends on how far the work has gone.

What exists What the revision covers
No box ticked An edit of the plan, by the paths of the chapter on that artifact, and then apply from the start.
Some boxes ticked The same edit, and the ticked tasks that rest on it are reopened, as section 8.6 says.
Every box ticked The same, and apply is run again. In a scratch change, one reopened box turned the state from all done back to ready.
A failing validation A fix in the delta, by the path of chapter 6, and validation run again.
The change archived Nothing in the archive. The correction is a new change.

The example shows the last row and none of the others. Section 4.8 says that the first change was corrected in a second change because the first had been archived, and section 8.6 says that the first change's list was left untouched, all its boxes still ticked. Section 8.6 gives the reason for its own middle row, and a failing validation writes no file for an archive to keep.

The second decision is about the means. The developer can revise the files by hand, or can ask the agent to run the workflow again. They differ in cost and in how they go wrong.

The developer revises by hand The agent is asked to run the workflow again
Right when One box or one word is wrong and the developer knows the replacement A task has to be done again, or several tasks and the work have to move together
What it costs The developer's reading of each task that depends on the one changed A run, and a request that says which tasks to redo and what must not move
How it goes wrong A dependent box is left ticked on evidence that no longer fits The box is ticked again over the same evidence, or the run does more than the request named
What to check afterwards The diff, and each box that depends on the one changed Each reopened box against its new evidence, and the files outside the tasks the run named

Suppose the developer revises the design of a vending machine change so that the machine checks the coins it holds before it accepts the payment, and finds that the ticked task that traces a scenario through the design no longer fits. By hand, the developer reopens the box and rewrites the task so that it names the revised design. The diff shows the box and the words. It does not show that a later box was ticked on the strength of the trace that has changed.

Suppose apply stops over a design issue, as the rule for a pause allows. The developer revises the plan with the update workflow, as the previous chapter described, and then asks for apply again. The boxes that were ticked against the old plan are the ones to reopen before the work goes on.

Both means are checked in the same way: by the diff, and by running validate again for the delta. A revision to a tick is read as a new draft, with the passes of the review above.

11.6 What apply and validate hand on

Apply and validate hand archive a ticked list and a delta that is well formed. A reviewer who takes the two results as the whole hands archive a change that has not been checked.

The next chapter takes the workflows that merge the delta and close the change: sync and archive.

Apply is an agent working to rules while the boxes are counted, and validate checks the form of the delta and the main specifications, and neither reads whether the work is right. A change whose boxes are all ticked and whose delta passes has a count and a pass, and the evidence and the scope behind them are the developer's to review.

12. Sync and Archive, and the Record They Leave

The previous chapter ended with a ticked list and a delta that is well formed, handed on to the workflows that make the record current. This chapter takes the last two entries of the table in section 9.1: sync, the workflow that merges a delta into the main specifications and leaves the change open, and archive, which merges unless told not to and moves the change into the archive. They share a chapter because they leave the same thing, the main specifications that every later change is checked against, and because archive has two answers to the first question, who does the work. For each it asks what the developer does, what it reads and writes and what can stop it, how a reviewer judges what it did, and what happens when its result is wrong. The examples are the vending machine's main specification and archived changes, and a scratch project in which the commands were run.

12.1 Sync: merging without closing the change

Sync merges each delta of a change into its main specification, applies the four operations as a merge and not as a copy, and keeps everything the delta does not mention. The skill calls the operation agent-driven, so that a delta can add one scenario to a requirement without the whole requirement being copied. The same skill's closing principle says the opposite of the last point for a modified requirement: a MODIFIED block carries the whole requirement, and validate and archive both reject a block that drops a scenario the main specification still has. The agent stops when the change has no delta, when the lookup of the rules fails, and when a capability is blocked. Chapter 6 says what the operations of a delta are, and this chapter does not repeat it.

Item Sync
Entry point The skill openspec-sync-specs, called by naming it or by the words "openspec sync" or "opsx sync". No command has that name.
Who acts The agent merges. The developer, as the last row says.
Writes The main specifications that the delta names, and nothing else. The change folder is not touched.
What can stop it A change with no delta, a failed lookup of the rules, a capability that is blocked, and a failed validation.
The developer's part To decide whether to merge before the change is archived, and to read the merge.

The skill has six stages.

Stage What happens
1. Select the change The agent uses the change the developer names, infers it from the conversation, or takes the only change in flight. Otherwise list --json returns the changes in flight, and the agent offers those that have a delta.
2. Resolve the change context status --json returns the root under which the main specifications live, and the agent uses it for every path to a main specification.
3. Find the delta specifications The paths of the deltas are taken from the output of status at stage 2, and from nowhere else. If there are none, the agent says so and stops.
4. Apply each delta Before the first write the agent runs instructions specs --json once, which returns the rules that the project configured for specifications, and stops if it fails. Then it reads each delta and its main specification and merges them by the rules of the next table.
5. Validate the main specifications validate --specs checks the form of every main specification. If it fails, the agent reports the problems and does not claim that the sync succeeded.
6. Show the summary The agent tells the developer which capabilities changed, what changed in each, and which new main specification still has a placeholder Purpose.

The merge itself is read by nothing. The check at stage 5 is about the form of the main specifications and not about whether the merge says what the delta says. In a scratch project, status reported the root and the one delta path that existed, instructions specs returned a rules list only after the project's configuration named a rule, and openspec sync was an unknown command, so the skill is the only definition of sync.

The skill gives a rule for each operation, and the rules say what the main specification should hold afterwards and when the merge stops. The table sets them out.

Operation What the agent does When the agent stops
ADDED Adds the requirement. If one of that name exists, it updates it to match. Not by itself.
MODIFIED Finds the requirement and applies the change, whether a new scenario, a changed scenario or a changed description, and keeps the text the delta does not mention. The skill expects the block to carry every scenario the main specification has: validate and archive reject a block that drops one, in a scratch project the first at validation and the second by stopping with no file changed. When the capability has no main specification. For a capability that has one, the skill says to find the requirement and says nothing of one that is missing; the archive command refuses that delta.
REMOVED Removes the whole requirement block. It removes the capability's spec.md only when six conditions hold: among them that no requirement is left, that the rest of the file is well formed, and that the change's .openspec.yaml declares retire_capabilities: true. When the capability has no main specification, where it skips the operation and warns. When removing would leave no requirement and a condition fails, it changes nothing for that capability and names the condition. It never leaves an empty ## Requirements section.
RENAMED Finds the requirement under its old name and gives it the new one. When the capability has no main specification.
Purpose For a new capability, copies the delta's Purpose verbatim, and writes a placeholder only when the delta has none. For an existing one, leaves the main specification's Purpose alone. Never.

A capability with no main specification can be created by ADDED requirements and by nothing else. MODIFIED and RENAMED have no requirement to act on there, and the agent stops for that capability and never invents the missing requirement. REMOVED has nothing to remove, and the agent skips it and warns. The agent creates the file with a title, the delta's Purpose and the requirements. Section 4.6 shows the first lines of the file as the first change left them. The skill says that the merge it describes matches what openspec archive does for a new capability and for the Purpose, and it claims no more than that.

Sync leaves the change open and the main specification ahead of it. After a sync, the main specification holds the new requirement and the change folder is where it was, with its tasks as they were. That is why sync is optional: archive can make the same merge, and in its workflow the agent offers to. It also means that between a sync and the archive, the main specification can be read by the next person before the change is done.

For the developer, sync is a decision to make the record current before the change is closed. Name the change, and when it has several deltas, say which are to be merged. Write a modified requirement whole, as chapter 6 teaches, and do not rely on the merge to keep a scenario the block left out. Read a modified requirement whole in the main specification, because a diff shows only the words that moved. Read the summary for a Purpose that was left as a placeholder, because no later step asks anyone to write it.

12.2 Archive: merging and moving the change

Two parties can archive a change, and they are not the same. The command openspec archive does everything itself. In the workflow of the skill openspec-archive-change, the agent reads the status and the task count, asks the user to confirm what is open, compares each delta with its main specification and offers a sync, runs the sync workflow inline, checks the result against the delta, and moves the folder. The first answer to the question of who does the work is the command, and the second is the agent. The developer decides which to use, answers what is asked, and reads the main specification afterwards.

The card for archive gives an answer for each path where they differ.

Item Archive
Entry point The command openspec archive, and the skill openspec-archive-change.
Who acts The command: it merges and moves on its own. The workflow: the agent. The developer, as the last row says.
Writes The main specifications that the delta names, and the change folder, which is moved into archive under its date.
What can stop it A refusal, or an answer of no, at any of the points that the table of the two paths below sets out.
The developer's part To choose the path, to answer what it asks, and to read the record.

The skill openspec-archive-change has six stages.

Stage What happens
1. Select the change, and read the archive inputs The agent uses the change the developer names, infers it from the conversation, or takes the only change in flight. Otherwise list --json returns the changes in flight, and the developer chooses among them. Then instructions archive --json runs. It is advisory: the agent uses what it adds and goes on without it if it fails. In the scratch project it returned the change's name and the root, and it carries project context or guidance only when the project adds them.
2. Check the artifact status status --json lists each artifact as done, skipped or neither. If an artifact is neither, the agent warns the developer and goes on only if the developer confirms.
3. Check the task count list --json returns this change's total and completed count; only x and X count as complete. If a box is open, the agent warns and goes on only on confirmation. If the lookup fails, it stops.
4. Assess the delta, and sync if chosen The agent checks that the archive target is free, compares each delta with its main specification, and offers to sync, to archive without syncing, or to cancel. For a sync, it runs instructions specs once, runs the sync workflow inline, in which validate --specs checks the form of the main specifications, and waits for it. It then compares each main specification with its delta again, and stops on any difference.
5. Perform the archive The agent checks once more that the target is free, and moves the change folder into the archive under its date with the shell command mv.
6. Display the summary The agent tells the developer the change, the schema, where it was archived, whether the specifications were synced, and every warning.

The sync inside stage 4 is the sync workflow of the previous section and not a command. The agent runs it inline and waits, because moving the folder while a sync is still reading it would leave the change archived and the main specifications never updated. After the sync the agent checks the structure of each main specification, confirms that no delta heading remains, and compares every capability with its delta again. If anything differs, the agent stops, and nothing has moved.

The two paths differ in who merges, in what is checked and in what stops them. The table sets them side by side. The column for the command is what was run in a scratch project; the column for the workflow is what the skill describes, and no agent was run.

What The archive command The archive workflow
Who merges The command. The agent, following the sync workflow inline, or, where that skill is not installed, merging itself under the same safeguards and then running validate --specs.
Whether the change is passed through validate Yes, first, when there is a delta. An error stops it before the task line is printed. The skill names no validate run on the change. The agent runs validate --specs on the main specifications, inside the sync.
Where the task count comes from The command reads the tasks file and prints a line, for example "Task status: 1/2 tasks". list --json, as at stage 3. The agent stops if the lookup fails or the counts are invalid.
Whether artifact completion is checked No. In the scratch project, a change with one of four artifacts complete was archived on --yes, and the command printed no warning about the missing artifacts. Yes, at stage 2.
What asks the user, and the default "Continue?" for open tasks, with the default no, and "Proceed with spec updates?", with the default yes. With no one to answer, it fails and names --yes. The same two matters, as confirmations, and a choice of "Sync now", "Archive without syncing" or "Cancel", or "Archive now", "Sync anyway" or "Cancel" when the delta is already merged. The agent asks again on any other answer.
A delta that cannot be merged It refuses, prints "Aborted. No files were changed.", and the change stays. A capability that cannot be merged is marked blocked, and only "Archive without syncing" and "Cancel" are offered. If the sync reports a stop, the archive stops with nothing moved.
What is checked after the merge Before it writes, the command validates the rebuilt main specification, and writes nothing if that fails. After the merge is written, the agent checks the structure, confirms that no delta heading remains, and compares each capability with its delta again.
How the folder is moved and named By the command, under the date. It fails with "Archive ... already exists" when the name is taken, and the change stays. The agent moves it with the shell command mv, after making the archive directory, under the date, never stacking a second date. The target is checked at stages 4 and 5, and the change stays in place if it is taken.
The options that skip a check --yes, --skip-specs and --no-validate. The answer "Archive without syncing", and the answers to each confirmation.

Both paths can skip a check, and which one is the developer's decision. The command's help describes --yes as skipping the confirmation prompts, --skip-specs as skipping the spec update operations, and --no-validate as skipping validation, which it calls not recommended and says requires confirmation. In the scratch project, --skip-specs moved a change whose delta was never merged, and --no-validate merged a requirement that had no scenario. The main specification then failed validate --specs, and the next archive of a change that touched it was refused until the requirement was removed. The command reports what it was told to skip and does not say whether skipping was right.

For the developer, archive is where the change stops being work and the record changes, and the review is of what the merge left. Choose the path before the run and know what each checks: the command validates the delta and the rebuilt specification before it writes anything, and in the workflow the agent compares the result with the delta after writing it. The question that defaults to yes, the merge, is read as carefully as the one that defaults to no, the open tasks.

The example shows what an archive leaves and nothing of the path. After the first change, the main specification purchase holds the first change's requirements and nothing about the change that wrote it, and the folder with the proposal, the delta, the design and the tasks sits in the archive under its date. Section 4.6 shows both. After the second change the modified requirement is replaced and the file has no new section, as section 4.14 says. The archived folders hold the artifacts and a metadata file that records the schema and the date the change was created. None of the files says which path made the record, or whether a check was skipped.

An archive is a record, and nothing in it is edited. A change that has been moved into the archive is not changed again, and an archived design that was wrong stays as it was, with a new change to correct it. Chapter 5 says so for the proposal, and section 4.8 shows it: the first change's requirement was found wanting, and the correction was a second change. The one form of validate that reads the archive is --archived, and it checks that each archived tasks.md has no open box.

12.3 What sync and archive leave out

Neither path reads whether the record is right. What is checked is the form of the delta and of the main specifications, and in the workflow the agent compares its own merge with the delta. Section 4.14 says why that matters: every later change relies on what the record holds, so an error in it is carried forward. The two paths need not give the same result, either, because nothing checks the skill's claim, set out in section 12.1, that its merge matches the command.

12.4 Reviewing the record

This review asks whether sync and archive did what their rules say. It does not ask whether the requirement is right, which is for the review of the delta in chapter 6. It has four passes. Merge asks whether the main specification says what the delta says and no more, with everything else kept. Form asks whether no delta heading remains, the Purpose is not a placeholder, the file has the format of a main specification and validate passes. Folder asks whether the change is in the archive under its date with all its artifacts. Path asks which path was used and which checks were skipped. Merge and Path matter most, because what is checked is the form and not the content, and a skipped check leaves no record in the archive.

The table is one checklist, ordered the way the record is read.

Check The workflow has done its job when How a run can fail
The request is answered as meant A reviewer can say which change and which deltas the run answers, and the record follows them The run merges the delta of another change, or only some of the deltas the change holds
The delta merged is the delta of the change The main specification changed only where the change's delta names a requirement A requirement outside the delta changed, or one the delta names did not
Each operation did what the merge rules say Added requirements are present, a modified one carries the change and every scenario it had before, removed ones are gone, and a renamed one has the new name only A modified requirement lost a scenario, a removed one is still there, or a rename left both names
Nothing the delta did not mention changed The rest of the main specification is as it was, in its order A requirement was reworded or moved in passing
No delta heading remains The main specification has one ## Requirements section and no ## ADDED or other delta heading The delta file was copied in as it stood
