The Purpose is not a placeholder A new capability carries the delta's own Purpose, and an existing one is untouched A new specification carries the placeholder, or an existing Purpose was rewritten
validate passes on the main specifications The form run is the one the project uses, run on the files as they now stand The result predates the merge, or a form that does not read the main specifications was run
The folder is in the archive under its date with every artifact The folder, with the proposal, the delta, the design and the tasks, sits under archive The change was archived without its merge, or the folder lacks an artifact
The path and the skips are known Someone can say which path was used and what it skipped The record was made by a path nobody wrote down, with a check skipped
Downstream The next change starts from a record that a person has read The folder moved and no one read the main specification

The table is a memory aid, and no part of the tool reads it. A change in the archive is a change that was moved, and the main specification is what the next change relies on, so the record is accepted when the main specification has been read and not when the folder has moved.

Across the two, the developer can follow one routine:

  1. Commit the repository before the run, so that the merge and the move show as one diff.
  2. Read the delta first and say which requirements it changes, and decide the path and whether to sync before the archive.
  3. Answer each question the path asks as a decision, and note each check that was skipped.
  4. After the run, read the diff of openspec/specs/ beside the delta, operation by operation.
  5. Run validate in the form the project uses, and read the whole result.
  6. Commit once the record is read, and name the path and the skipped checks in the message.

12.5 Changing the result

When the review finds that the record is wrong, two decisions follow: what the revision covers, and who makes it. The first depends on whether the merge has happened.

What exists What the revision covers
The delta only, nothing merged An edit of the delta, by the paths of chapter 6, and then either path.
The sync run and the change open The same edit, and the sync again. The skill says that the operation should be idempotent, so that a second run gives the result of one.
The change archived with a wrong requirement Nothing in the archive. The correction is a new change.

The example shows the last row and none of the others, as section 12.2 says, and section 4.14 shows the main specification after the correction, with the first change's folder as it was. The example holds no other case: it runs no sync, so no change reached the main specification before it was archived, and none is left in flight.

The second decision is about the means. The developer can revise the main specification by hand, or can ask the agent to run the workflow again. They differ in cost and in how they go wrong.

The developer revises by hand The agent is asked to run the workflow again
Right when One word or one block of the main specification is wrong and the developer knows the replacement, such as a Purpose, which a delta cannot change for an existing capability The delta changed, or several requirements have to move together
What it costs The change records nothing of the edit, and a delta that modifies the block does not know of it Another merge, and a request that names the change and the deltas
How it goes wrong A later MODIFIED copies the old block and the correction is gone An operation is not idempotent, or the run changes a requirement the delta does not name
What to check afterwards The diff of the main specification, and the delta of any open change that names the block The diff of the main specification against the new delta, and validate --specs

Suppose the developer corrects a word in the requirement of purchase by hand, in the main specification, and a change that was drafted before the correction modifies that requirement by copying the block from its own earlier draft. The merge replaces the block with the delta's, and the correction is gone. The diff shows the old word coming back, and nothing says that it was ever corrected.

Suppose a delta is edited after a sync and the sync is run again. No run was observed, so that the second run gives the result of one rests on the skill's instruction, and the check that the main specification says what the new delta says is the developer's.

Both means are checked by reading the main specification and not only the diff. A revision is read as a new draft, with the passes of the review above.

12.6 What sync and archive hand on

Sync and archive hand the next change a record. The main specification is the living description that chapter 3 spoke of, and section 4.14 says that archiving turns a change from a proposal into part of that description. The workflows of the last four chapters end here: the plan is written, carried out, checked and made current, and the next change starts from the record, and its requirements are read against what the record holds.

Sync merges a delta without moving the change, and has no command of its own. Archive merges and moves, either as the archive command or as a workflow in which the agent does it. The two paths differ in who merges and what is checked, and both can skip a check. The merge rules say what the main specification should hold, and the review is of the main specification the merge left and not of the folder that moved. Where the skill says two things about one operation, a delta can rely on the stricter one, which validate and archive check, and a modified requirement is written whole. The archive is a record, and a mistake in it is corrected by a new change. The question to ask of any archive is which path made the record and what it checked.

13. Customizing the Harness, and What the Tool Checks

The previous four chapters took the workflows of OpenSpec and what each leaves behind. All of them rested on the default: the core profile or one workflow added to it, the schema spec-driven, and a configuration file with a few lines of context. This chapter is about changing that default. It names four kinds of customization, sets the possibilities that OpenSpec offers in one table, and asks of each kind where it is made, what it changes, what the tool checks, and how it is changed later. The example is the vending machine, given a schema of its own, which the next chapter builds file by file.

13.1 Four kinds of customization, and the possibilities in one table

A project can change four things, and they differ in how far a change reaches. The profile decides which workflows are installed, and it belongs to the machine. The project configuration holds the default schema, text that is added to what the agent is told, and advice for apply and archive, and it belongs to one project. The schema defines the artifacts of a change, what each requires and what the agent is told when it writes each, and it belongs to one project and can be shared between projects. The instruction file, AGENTS.md, holds rules the agent reads when a session opens. It sits beside OpenSpec and is not part of it.

The first three are OpenSpec's own, and each is a file that the machine or the project controls. The fourth is named here because it is the fourth place in which a rule can be written, and section 13.7 says why it is not set in the table below.

The question to ask of a need is which kind it belongs at. A rule about one artifact's wording belongs in the configuration. A new file that every change must have belongs in the schema. Which workflows a person can call by name belongs in the profile. A rule for every task in the project, OpenSpec or not, belongs in the instruction file. The tool will accept the same text in more than one of them, and it will not say which was the right place.

The table has one row for each file in which OpenSpec can be customized, so that a possibility is found in the row of the file it is written in. Its columns say which kind the file belongs to, how the file is made, what it holds, and what the tool checks. A cell that says "Nothing" means that no command reads or reports on it. The fields of schema.yaml are those of the schema reference on openspec.dev, which lists every field, the artifact's description and the apply block's instruction among them.

File Kind Made with What it holds What the tool checks
The global configuration Profile openspec config profile The profile and its workflow list openspec config list reports it, and openspec update writes the skills to match
openspec/config.yaml Config openspec init, then by hand schema; context; rules by artifact id; operations.apply.guidance; operations.archive.guidance; an opt-in for a hosted coding agent; store and references, for stores; skillsScope Read when instructions are fetched, and nothing about what the text says
schema.yaml Schema openspec schema fork or init, or by copying a folder The name, version and description; for each artifact its id, generates, description, template, instruction and requires, and their order; the apply block with requires, tracks and instruction openspec schema validate reports a syntax error, a missing template, a duplicate id and a cycle; openspec status shows a blocked artifact; nothing about the instruction texts, the order or apply.instruction
A file in templates/ Schema By hand, or copied with the schema The headings and comments the agent starts from openspec schema validate reports a missing file, and nothing about its content
.openspec.yaml of a change Schema openspec new change; --schema sets it The schema that change uses openspec status reports it

A schema has one more place than the project's openspec/schemas/<name>/ folder: the user's data directory, where every project on the machine finds it. The file is the same, and section 13.4 says how openspec schema which tells the two places apart. A schema written by someone else, such as one of the seven community schemas the customization page lists, is copied into either place, and is then checked like any other.

13.2 The profile: which workflows exist

The profile is the customization that reaches furthest and is checked least. It decides which workflows are installed as skills, and so which ones a person can ask for. Chapter 9 defines the profile and names the six workflows of the core profile. What is added here is that the profile is not a setting of the project. It is set with openspec config profile, and openspec config has only the global scope, so a person who sets it changes it for every project on the machine. The program reminds the person to run openspec update in each project, because the skills are only rewritten then.

A project that wants a profile of its own has no setting for it. The way to get one is to keep a separate configuration directory and start the session with that directory named, so that the program reads the profile from there and from nowhere else. The profile has one retired field, delivery, which the program still reads and ignores. Where the skills are installed is a second choice of the same reach: by default openspec init puts them in the machine's ~/.agents/skills/ unless it is given --scope project, and a project that keeps its own records that in its configuration.

What the tool does is report the result in openspec config list. It does not say whether the workflows that were installed suit the project, and a person who is in the wrong directory gets the global profile without a warning.

13.3 The project configuration: text that is added, and none of it enforced

The project configuration is a file, openspec/config.yaml, and openspec init creates it with commented examples of context, rules and operations. It does four things.

It names the default schema, so that a new change needs no flag. It holds context, which is added to the instruction of every artifact. It holds rules, which are added to the instruction of the artifact whose id matches, so that a rule about the design is read when the design is written and at no other time. And it holds advice for apply and archive, in operations, which is kept apart from the rules because it describes how the work is done and not what an artifact contains.

When the agent asks for an artifact's instruction, the program returns the schema's instruction with the context, the rules and the template, each in its own field. The agent asks for the apply and archive instructions in the same way, and gets context and operationGuidance as fields of their own. The command that returns the archive instruction only reads: in the scratch project it wrote no file, and its answer held the change's name, the root, the context and the guidance. The customization page says that context is a required input to the prompt and that guidance is additive. The same page says that neither is enforceable: a workflow follows the entries that apply, reports a conflict, and copies none of the text into a file unless the person asks.

One key of the file is about files and not about the prompt. It is the opt-in for the files that let one hosted coding agent run OpenSpec, a workflow file and an agent file. When it is true, openspec update writes them and keeps them current. When it is false, openspec update removes the ones it generated. When it is absent, the choice is undecided and update writes nothing. A second key is about files too: skillsScope: project says that the project keeps OpenSpec's skills in the repository, so openspec update refreshes them there and does not ask where to keep them.

The archive and sync workflows read one more thing, the specs rules, before they write a merge into a main specification, and they stop if the lookup fails. That is the one place where the configuration is read for something that is not a prompt.

What the tool checks of all this is the file, which it reads. It checks nothing about what a rule says or whether an agent kept it. A context that is wrong is injected as willingly as one that is right.

13.4 Which schema a change uses

Four places decide which schema a change uses, and the tool reads them in order. The --schema flag on the command that creates the change comes first. After it comes the schema the change itself recorded, in the .openspec.yaml of its folder. Then comes the default named in the configuration, and last the default of the program, spec-driven.

A new change writes its own schema into its .openspec.yaml when it is created. In the scratch project, a change created under a fork reported spec-driven as its schema after its .openspec.yaml was edited by hand, though the configuration still named the fork.

When a schema is not the one a person expects, openspec schema which says where it comes from. It reports the schema's name, its Source and its Path, and with --all it lists the project schemas, the user schemas and the schemas of the package. A project schema outranks a user schema of the same name. The customization page recommends project schemas, because they are kept with the code.

13.5 Building a schema

A schema is a folder, openspec/schemas/<name>/, that holds one file, schema.yaml, and a templates/ folder. There are two ways in. A fork copies an existing schema whole, so that the project starts from spec-driven and removes or adds. A new schema starts from nothing but the artifacts that are named: in the scratch project, a schema of two artifacts was written with the proposal and the tasks, neither requiring anything, and an apply block that requires and tracks the tasks. The command openspec schema init with no option writes four artifacts, the proposal, the specs, the design and the tasks, each with a template, and the same kind of apply block. An option names a different list of artifacts, and another makes the new schema the project's default.

The file's top-level keys, and the fields of each artifact, are those that the table of section 13.1 lists.

The fields differ in what they decide. requires decides what is possible: an artifact whose requirements do not exist is blocked, and openspec status says by which. An artifact counts as done when its generated file exists, and in the scratch project a change whose design file was empty was reported as complete. The order of the list decides only which artifact comes first when several are ready. A template is Markdown that is injected into the prompt, and it may hold headings, comments with guidance and a sample. generates may be a pattern, which is how the default schema writes one file for each capability. The apply block says which artifact must exist before apply and which file's boxes are counted. Its instruction is what openspec instructions apply returns while the change is ready. When the change is blocked or every task is done the program writes its own text, and the schema's instruction does not appear.

openspec schema validate checks that the file is well formed. In the scratch project it reported a template file that was missing, an artifact id that was used twice, and a cycle of requirements, which it named. The customization page lists the same four checks: the syntax, the templates, the cycles and the ids.

A schema is shared by copying its folder into one of the two places that section 13.1 names. A schema copied from elsewhere is a fork of it, and a fork does not receive what is later changed in the schema it was copied from; the project keeps it up to date by hand or not at all.

13.6 Placing the needs of an example

The next chapter walks one example from the first command to the archive, and this section only places its needs. Chapter 4 told how the vending machine's first version passed validation and every task and still left a case undecided. The design had named the case as a non-goal, and chapter 7 said that a design that sets a case aside has not decided it. The review that finds this is a habit of the reviewer, and nothing in the tool knows whether it was done. The example turns the habit into a file: a fork of spec-driven, named with-trace, whose trace names for every scenario the decision in the design that satisfies it.

The example needs four things, and each belongs at a different place. The table says where and why.

The need Where it is made Why there
A file that every change has to have before its tasks The schema: the trace artifact, and requires on the tasks It is a new artifact with its own place in the order, and only the schema can add one.
A design states a non-goal only when no scenario tests the case The configuration: a line in rules for the design It is about the wording of one artifact, and not about a file.
The agent checks the trace before each task The schema: a line in apply.instruction It belongs with the trace and travels with the schema, so another project that copies the schema gets it.
The archive summary says whether the trace was read before the merge The configuration: a line of archive guidance It is advice about how the work is done, and it is for this project.

The tool reports the schema valid and the trace blocked or ready. It does not check that the trace is true, or that the line in the apply instruction is followed, and it cannot find a scenario that nobody wrote. The first version's failure was a case that had no scenario until the second change added it, so the trace would have made the design's non-goal visible once the scenario existed, and the coverage review of chapter 6 remains the check that finds a scenario that is missing. The example is also a fork, with the cost that section 13.5 names.

13.7 What is outside of OpenSpec

The instruction file is the fourth place in which a rule can be written, and OpenSpec has no mechanism for it. The program's cleanup code treats two things as left by earlier versions: a managed openspec/AGENTS.md, and a block of text between two markers in the root AGENTS.md. In the scratch project, openspec init removed the managed file and the marked block from a project that still had them, and kept the rest of the root file as the person had written it. openspec update alone changed neither. The root file belongs to the project, and nothing in OpenSpec generates, reads or checks it. It is not the only such place: chapter 18 takes a text of the project's own, kept in the skills folder beside the generated skills, that OpenSpec does not generate or check either.

That is why it is not a row of the table. The last column of the table says what the tool checks, and a row that says "Nothing" about a file the tool does not know would suggest that the tool does something with it. It is better compared with the project configuration, which is the place nearest to it.

AGENTS.md The configuration's context and rules
Read by The agent, when a session opens The agent, added to the instruction of an OpenSpec artifact or operation
Applies to Every task in the project, OpenSpec or not Only the artifacts and operations OpenSpec instructs
What the tool checks Nothing The file's form, and nothing about what it says

A rule that every task must follow, such as the language of the project's files, belongs in the instruction file, as section 13.1 said. A rule written in both the instruction file and the configuration can disagree with itself, and nothing warns of it, so the person who writes both has to read them together. Section 3.5 gave the reason the rules live with the code. This chapter adds only that they live in two places, and that the tool knows one of them.

13.8 What the tool checks, and what it leaves out

The tool checks the form of a customization and never its effect, as the last column of the table in section 13.1 shows.

The effect is left to the reviewer, and it can fail in ways the checks do not see. A schema that validates can tell the agent something that does not produce the artifact the template holds. The default schema does this once already: section 7.7 shows that its instruction for the design names two parts the template lacks. The rules, the context and the guidance of section 13.3 are advice, and none of them is enforced. The order of the artifact list, and the wording of a fork's instruction, change what an agent does and are checked by nothing.

Each of these can happen to a change that passes every command, so a customization that reports well formed has shown that it is well formed, and no more.

13.9 Reviewing a customization

A customization is reviewed in the file first and then in what it produces, and the review has four passes. Placement asks whether the need is at the kind that reaches as far as it should. Form asks whether the tool accepts the customization. Instruction asks whether each instruction produces the part the template holds. Effect asks whether a change run through the schema produces what was meant. Placement and Effect matter most, because the tool can check Form and nothing else, and a customization at the wrong kind or with the wrong effect passes it.

The table is a memory aid, and no part of the tool reads it.

Check The customization has done its job when How it can fail
Placement The need is at the kind that reaches as far as it, and no further A rule for one artifact is in the instruction file, or a rule for every task is in one artifact's rules
The profile openspec config list shows the workflows the project needs The wrong configuration directory was used, and the global profile was read
The configuration openspec instructions returns the context and the rules for the artifact they were written for A rule is under an id that no artifact has
The schema's form openspec schema validate passes and openspec schema which names the intended source A user schema of the same name is shadowed by a project schema, or the reverse
The selection A new change records the schema that was meant A flag or a default is set that overrides it
The instruction Each instruction produces the part the template holds An instruction names a part the template does not have
The effect A change run through the schema produces the artifacts that were meant, and they are good The schema validates and the artifacts are wrong

13.10 Changing a customization

The cost of changing a customization depends on what has already been made with it. The table says what the revision covers at each stage.

What exists What the revision covers
Nothing has been made with it yet The file only. The next command that reads it sees the change.
Changes in progress A configuration edit is read the next time the instructions are fetched. A schema edited in place changes the open changes that use it at once: in the scratch project a change created with four artifacts reported five after the schema gained one, with the new one blocked. A change keeps the schema name it recorded, so a new default does not move it. A profile change reaches the skills only after openspec update.
Changes archived Nothing. The archive is a record and is not rewritten, as chapters 5 and 12 say. A change made under the old schema stays as it was made, and the next change uses the new one.

The row for changes in progress is the one to read twice. A schema is shared by every change that names it, so editing it moves them all, and a change that was half-written under one set of artifacts finds another. A person who wants a change to keep the old schema copies the schema under a new name before editing, and starts the new changes with the copy.

13.11 What customization hands on

Customization hands the project a harness that is its own. Each of its files is kept with the project or the machine, and each can be read, reviewed and revised like any other.

A customization is a choice of the kind that reaches as far as the need and no further, and the tool will confirm only that it was made well formed. The question to ask of any customization is where it was made and what is checked there.

14. A Customized Change, from Fork to Archive

The previous chapter said what can be customized and what the tool checks of each kind. This chapter shows it. It takes the vending machine's second change, refuse-without-exact-change, which chapter 4 quotes in full, and makes it again under a schema of its own, with-trace. The schema adds one artifact, a trace, between the design and the tasks. Every file that the customization adds or changes is shown, and so is the console input and the main output of each step. The proposal, the delta, the design and the tasks of the change are chapter 4's, and are pointed at and not repeated. The four needs of the example and the place where each is made are in the table of section 13.6.

The walkthrough ran in a scratch project on 26 November 2026. This chapter is the only one of the book that shows console blocks, because its claims are what the program printed and a reader can only check them by seeing it. A line that begins with $ is input, and what follows is the program's output. The project's folder is written as ., the program's own install folder as <package>, and a line of three dots marks output that is cut. No block shows the work of an agent. The files were written by hand in the scratch project.

14.1 Preparing the harness

The harness is prepared in four steps: a fork, a schema that differs from it, a template, and a configuration that names the fork. After each the program is asked what it now knows.

The scratch project holds the machine's own config.yaml, which names spec-driven, and a main specification of purchase that holds the first change's result, so the project is the example's second change waiting to be made. The first of the four steps is the fork. It copies the package's spec-driven into the project under a new name.

$ openspec schema fork spec-driven with-trace
Note: Schema commands are experimental and may change.
- Forking 'spec-driven' to 'with-trace'...
✔ Forked 'spec-driven' to 'with-trace'

Source: <package>/schemas/spec-driven (package)
Destination: ./openspec/schemas/with-trace

You can now customize the schema at:
  ./openspec/schemas/with-trace/schema.yaml

openspec schema which says where a schema comes from, and with --all it lists what the project can reach. The fork is a project schema, and spec-driven is still the package's.

$ openspec schema which with-trace
Note: Schema commands are experimental and may change.
Schema: with-trace
Source: project
Path: ./openspec/schemas/with-trace
$ openspec schema which --all
Note: Schema commands are experimental and may change.

Project schemas:
  with-trace

Package schemas:
  spec-driven

The second step is the edit of schema.yaml in the new folder. The file is the package's default of 273 lines, so it is shown as the difference from the fork. The diff has four changes. The description says what the fork is. A trace artifact is added after the design, requiring the specs and the design. The tasks gain trace in their requires. The apply block gains two lines. The lines of the default schema that the diff does not show are unchanged.

--- a/openspec/schemas/with-trace/schema.yaml
+++ b/openspec/schemas/with-trace/schema.yaml
@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@
 name: with-trace
 version: 1
-description: Default OpenSpec workflow - proposal → specs → design → tasks
+description: spec-driven with a trace between the design and the tasks
 artifacts:
   - id: proposal
     generates: proposal.md
@@ -196,6 +196,22 @@ artifacts:
     requires:
       - proposal

+  - id: trace
+    generates: trace.md
+    description: Which decision in the design satisfies each scenario
+    template: trace.md
+    instruction: |
+      Create the trace that names, for every scenario in the specs, the decision in
+      the design that satisfies it.
+
+      Write one row for each scenario, using the scenario's own name. Walk the
+      scenario's inputs through the design by hand. If the design has no decision
+      that covers the scenario, write "none" and record the scenario as not
+      satisfied; do not edit the design to hide the gap.
+    requires:
+      - specs
+      - design
+
   - id: tasks
     generates: tasks.md
     description: Implementation checklist with trackable tasks
@@ -264,6 +280,7 @@ artifacts:
     requires:
       - specs
       - design
+      - trace

 apply:
   requires: [ tasks ]
@@ -271,3 +288,5 @@ apply:
   instruction: |
     Read context files, work through pending tasks, mark complete as you go.
     Pause if you hit blockers or need clarification.
+    Before each task, read trace.md and stop if a scenario the task touches is
+    marked not satisfied.

The requires of the trace is what puts it between the design and the tasks, and the requires of the tasks is what makes it mandatory. The two lines of the apply block are the third of the example's four needs. The third step is the template that the trace's template: trace.md names, a new file, templates/trace.md, in the same folder. It is the whole file.

## Trace

<!-- One row for every scenario in the specs. Name the decision in the design that
     satisfies the scenario. A scenario with no decision is written as "none" and is
     not satisfied. -->

| Scenario | Decision in the design | Satisfied |
|---|---|---|
| <!-- scenario name --> | <!-- decision, or none --> | <!-- yes or no --> |

The fourth step is openspec/config.yaml. The configuration needs three changes. It names the fork as the default schema. It gains a rule for the design, which is the example's second need. And it gains a line of archive guidance, the fourth. The machine's own context and its rule for the tasks stay as they were.

--- a/openspec/config.yaml
+++ b/openspec/config.yaml
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
-schema: spec-driven
+schema: with-trace

 context: |
   This OpenSpec root holds one example for the book in
@@ -15,6 +15,13 @@ context: |
   is replaced rather than defended.

 rules:
+  design:
+    - State a case as a non-goal only if no scenario tests it.
   tasks:
     - Each task states how it is verified, by reading the artifacts or by running
       `openspec validate`.
+
+operations:
+  archive:
+    guidance:
+      - The archive summary says whether trace.md was read before the merge.

Then the program is asked whether the schema is well formed. This is the check that section 13.5 says it makes: the syntax, the template files, the ids and the cycles.

$ openspec schema validate with-trace
Note: Schema commands are experimental and may change.
✓ Schema 'with-trace' is valid

The answer says the schema is valid. It says nothing about the instruction of the trace, which is the new part that matters.

14.2 A new change takes the new default

A new change needs no flag, because the configuration now names the fork. The program says which schema it used, and writes it into the change's own file.

$ openspec new change refuse-without-exact-change
- Creating change 'refuse-without-exact-change' with schema 'with-trace'...
Created change 'refuse-without-exact-change' at openspec/changes/refuse-without-exact-change/
Schema: with-trace
Next: openspec status --change refuse-without-exact-change

The change's folder holds one file so far, .openspec.yaml, and it is the record that outranks the configuration's default from now on (section 13.4).

schema: with-trace
created: 2026-11-26

openspec status lists the artifacts and what blocks each. There are five, not four, and the trace is blocked until the specs and the design both exist.

$ openspec status --change refuse-without-exact-change
- Loading change status...
Change: refuse-without-exact-change
Schema: with-trace
Change root: ./openspec/changes/refuse-without-exact-change
Progress: 0/5 artifacts complete

[ ] proposal
[-] specs (blocked by: proposal)
[-] design (blocked by: proposal)
[-] trace (blocked by: specs, design)
[-] tasks (blocked by: specs, design, trace)

Next: openspec instructions proposal --change "refuse-without-exact-change" --json

The order of the first three artifacts is as chapters 3 and 4 gave it. What the customization changed is the end: the tasks, which waited for the specs and the design, now wait for the trace as well.

14.3 What the agent is told

The schema and the configuration decide what the agent is told when it asks for an artifact or an operation. The program shows it as JSON, and the three commands below are the ones that carry the customization. The output is long, and each block is cut to the field that the customization put there.

The design's instruction is the schema's, with the configuration's context, rules and template each in a field of its own. The rule for the design is the one the fourth step of section 14.1 wrote.

$ openspec instructions design --change refuse-without-exact-change --json
{
...
  "rules": [
    "State a case as a non-goal only if no scenario tests it."
  ],
...
}

The archive's guidance is a field of its own and is not a rule, as section 13.3 said.

$ openspec instructions archive --change refuse-without-exact-change --json
{
...
  "operationGuidance": [
    "The archive summary says whether trace.md was read before the merge."
  ],
...
}

The apply instruction is the schema's. It appears in the output once the change is ready, which section 14.6 reaches, and what it says is the two lines that the diff added. What the program prints is what the agent is told. Whether an agent follows it is not something the program shows.

14.4 The trace is the new file

The four default artifacts are written as chapter 4 quotes them. After the design the program says that the trace is next, and that the tasks wait for it alone.

$ openspec status --change refuse-without-exact-change
- Loading change status...
Change: refuse-without-exact-change
Schema: with-trace
Change root: ./openspec/changes/refuse-without-exact-change
Progress: 3/5 artifacts complete

[x] proposal
[x] specs
[x] design
[ ] trace
[-] tasks (blocked by: trace)

Next: openspec instructions trace --change "refuse-without-exact-change" --json

The trace is written from the design's Findings, where chapter 4 quotes Traces B, C and D. No archive holds this file, so it is written for the chapter, as the previous chapter's example was. Its three rows are the three scenarios of the delta, each with the decision in the design that satisfies it.

## Trace

| Scenario | Decision in the design | Satisfied |
|---|---|---|
| Change is given from stock | Work out the change before the product is released; 30 owed is 20 and 10 (Trace C) | yes |
| Exact payment gives no change | Nothing is owed, so the change is exact and no coin is returned (Trace D) | yes |
| Stock cannot make the change | If the change is not exact, refuse the purchase, release no product, and return the amount inserted (Trace B) | yes |

With the trace written the tasks are ready, and when they are written the program reports all five artifacts.

$ openspec status --change refuse-without-exact-change
- Loading change status...
Change: refuse-without-exact-change
Schema: with-trace
Change root: ./openspec/changes/refuse-without-exact-change
Progress: 5/5 artifacts complete

[x] proposal
[x] specs
[x] design
[x] trace
[x] tasks

All planning artifacts complete!
Next: openspec instructions apply --change "refuse-without-exact-change" --json

14.5 What the trace would have shown the first design

The trace was added because of what the first version failed to do. Chapter 4 told it: the design of give-exact-change set the stock case aside as a non-goal, the change passed validation and every task, and a walkthrough written afterwards found the case undecided. The question here is where the trace would have shown it.

A trace of the first design, against the three scenarios of the second change, is the file below. It is hypothetical, and it is written for this chapter. The machine did not write it, and the first change did not have the scenario it lists last. The first two rows follow the first design's own Findings, and the third follows its Non-Goals.

## Trace

| Scenario | Decision in the design | Satisfied |
|---|---|---|
| Change is given from stock | Work out the change greedily from the stock; 30 owed is 20 and 10 | yes |
| Exact payment gives no change | Nothing is owed, so no coin is returned | yes |
| Stock cannot make the change | none | no |

The third row has no decision, and the trace's instruction tells whoever writes it to say so and not to edit the design to hide the gap. The configuration's rule would have met the same row from the other side: the first design states exactly that case as a non-goal, while a scenario now tests it.

This is a limit as well as a finding. The row exists because the scenario exists. The first change had no scenario for the stock case, so a trace of it would have had two rows and both would have read yes. A trace finds a scenario that has no decision, and cannot find a scenario that nobody wrote. That is the coverage review of chapter 6, and the trace does not replace it. The trace does not prevent the failure either. It puts the failure where the review is cheapest, after the design and before the first task.

14.6 Apply, validate and archive

Apply reads the tasks, and with them unticked the program returns the schema's instruction. The boxes of chapter 4's tasks are ticked in the archive, so the scratch project's copy has them unticked, and ticks them after this command, as an apply would. The output is cut to the fields that matter.

$ openspec instructions apply --change refuse-without-exact-change --json
{
...
  "state": "ready",
  "instruction": "Read context files, work through pending tasks, mark complete as you go.\nPause if you hit blockers or need clarification.\nBefore each task, read trace.md and stop if a scenario the task touches is\nmarked not satisfied.",
...
}

With the boxes ticked, validate passes the change.

$ openspec validate refuse-without-exact-change --strict
Change 'refuse-without-exact-change' is valid

The command checks the structure of the specifications. It does not open the trace, and a trace that is a row of dashes passes it. The next block is a run and not advice: the trace is replaced by a one-row placeholder, and status and validate are run again.

## Trace

| Scenario | Decision in the design | Satisfied |
|---|---|---|
| - | - | - |

$ openspec status --change refuse-without-exact-change
- Loading change status...
Change: refuse-without-exact-change
Schema: with-trace
Change root: ./openspec/changes/refuse-without-exact-change
Progress: 5/5 artifacts complete
...
$ openspec validate refuse-without-exact-change --strict
Change 'refuse-without-exact-change' is valid

The program counts an artifact by its file. The placeholder is counted like the table of three rows, because the file is there. The original trace is restored and archive is run.

$ openspec archive refuse-without-exact-change --yes
Task status: ✓ Complete

Specs to update:
  purchase: update
Applying changes to openspec/specs/purchase/spec.md:
  ~ 1 modified
Totals: + 0, ~ 1, - 0, → 0
Specs updated successfully.
Change 'refuse-without-exact-change' archived as '2026-11-26-refuse-without-exact-change'.

The command moves the whole folder, as chapter 12 said, and the archived folder holds the trace beside the design.

$ ls openspec/changes/archive/2026-11-26-refuse-without-exact-change/
design.md
proposal.md
specs
tasks.md
trace.md

The guidance for the archive asked the summary to say whether the trace was read. The archive command writes no summary, and the output above has none. The archive workflow, which the agent runs, is where such a summary would be written, and nothing checks that it says it.

14.7 What the customization costs

The customization costs a fork and a file for every change. The fork is a copy of spec-driven as it was on the day it was made, and the project keeps it up to date by hand, or does not, because nothing flows from the package into it. Every change carries one more artifact, which is one more file to write after the design and to read before the first task.

What the tool counts is not what was reviewed. A design edited after the trace leaves the trace as it was. The next line is appended to the design of the scratch change, a decision that the trace does not mention, and status and validate are asked what they think.

**Decision**: refuse every purchase for which the stock holds fewer than three coins.

$ openspec status --change refuse-without-exact-change
- Loading change status...
Change: refuse-without-exact-change
Schema: with-trace
Change root: ./openspec/changes/refuse-without-exact-change
Progress: 5/5 artifacts complete
...
$ openspec validate refuse-without-exact-change --strict
Change 'refuse-without-exact-change' is valid

Five of five, and valid, after a decision the trace never traced. The trace is as good as the review that wrote it and the review that reads it, and the program does not know either.

A customized change is the default change with one more file. The program shows that the file exists, that the schema is well formed, and what each instruction says. It shows nothing about whether the trace is true, whether it was read before the tasks, or whether the summary at the archive said so, and those stay with the reviewer, as the previous chapter said of every customization.

15. The Workflows Outside the Table

Chapters 9 to 12 took seven workflows apart and one command, and gave each a card and a table of its stages. They are the six of the core profile and continue, and OpenSpec defines five more. This chapter takes all five in one place, with a short section for each in place of a card and a table. Each section answers the questions that chapter 9 asks of a workflow. A reader who wants the stages of a skill reads the skill, which is a text in the project's skills folder.

15.1 Five more workflows

The program holds a longer list than chapter 9, with twelve entries: propose, explore, new, continue, apply, update, ff, sync, archive, bulk-archive, verify and onboard.

A project whose profile names all twelve gets thirteen skills: one for each workflow, and the router. A scratch project showed this on 26 November 2026: openspec init --scope project with a global profile that listed all twelve installed thirteen skills in the project's skills folder. A profile that names the seven of chapter 9 gets eight. The table of chapter 9 is the table of those seven, and it is not wrong for being shorter than the program's list.

In a project whose profile names only those seven, the five have no skill, and the router offers each a shorter path instead: a section of its reference file without-skills.md. Each section lists the commands the work needs, or says what the agent should read, but it lacks the skill's checks and questions. For new and fast-forward, the section lists new change, status and instructions, and either stops after one artifact or carries on until the plan is complete. For verify, the agent reads the tasks and the specifications against the code and changes no file, and the section names none of the dimensions or severities of section 15.4. For bulk-archive, the agent archives one change at a time and never checks the deltas against each other, which is the very thing the skill does in section 15.5. For onboard, the agent follows the sections for explore, propose, apply and archive.

The table lists the five workflows outside it. Fast-forward is the name used in the text, and the program's name for it is ff.

Workflow Entry point What it does
New the skill openspec-new-change Create a change and show the template of its first artifact, then stop.
Fast-forward the skill openspec-ff-change Create all of a change's planning artifacts in one run.
Verify the skill openspec-verify-change Compare the implementation with the change's artifacts and report what does not match.
Bulk-archive the skill openspec-bulk-archive-change Archive several changes in one run, after checking their deltas against each other.
Onboard the skill openspec-onboard Walk the developer through one whole change, on a real task, with narration.

None of the five writes a kind of file that the workflows of the table do not write. New and fast-forward write the artifacts that propose and continue write. Verify writes nothing. Bulk-archive moves what archive moves. Onboard writes the artifacts, the code and the archive. What differs is how much is written or moved in one run, and how much the agent is told to ask.

15.2 New

The skill openspec-new-change starts a change and writes nothing into it. It asks what the developer wants to build if the request does not say, derives a name in lowercase with hyphens, creates the change, shows its status and the template of the first artifact, and stops. It is the first half of the path that chapter 10 describes, and continue is the second: new creates the place, and each run of continue fills one artifact.

The agent asks and runs commands, and the program creates the folder and reports the state. The skill passes no schema unless the developer names one or asks to see them, so the project's default is used. In a scratch project on the default schema, new change created a folder holding .openspec.yaml, which has the schema's name and the date of creation. status then showed zero of four artifacts complete, the proposal ready and the other three blocked.

The program refuses a name already in use, a name that is not in lowercase with hyphens, and a schema it does not have, each with an error and exit code 1. A request the agent cannot turn into a name, or a project with no root, stops it too.

A reviewer judges a run of new by what is missing: the folder holds .openspec.yaml and no artifact. The developer says what the change is for, names a schema if the default is not wanted, and decides when the first artifact is written and by which workflow.

15.3 Fast-forward

The skill openspec-ff-change creates a change and writes every artifact in its required set in one run. That is what propose does, and the two skills are close. Fast-forward has five numbered stages and propose has seven, and the loop that writes the artifacts is the same text in both, apart from a tick mark in the progress line and the word "critically" before "unclear". Section 10.2 gives propose's stages and what the program checks at each.

What fast-forward leaves out is what surrounds the loop: the clarifying of the request before anything is written, the loading of the project's context, and the choice of a schema. Three differences follow.

  • Fast-forward passes no schema, so another one can be chosen only in the request.
  • It asks only when the context is critically unclear and otherwise prefers reasonable decisions. Propose asks about an ambiguity that would change the scope, the observable behaviour, the compatibility or the acceptance criteria, and tells the agent to record a minor assumption in the artifacts. The skill of fast-forward has no sentence that tells the agent to record one.
  • Propose opens with a paragraph that says the request authorizes planning only and tells the agent to stop. Fast-forward has none. Both skills close with the same prompt, which calls the plan ready for review and offers to apply it when the developer asks.

The skill is silent on the boundary. That is a difference in text, and not a defect found in a run.

The agent writes, and the program supplies the build order and the template and instruction of each artifact. A reviewer reads a run as chapter 10 reads a run of propose: the required set exists or was reported as skipped, and nothing outside the change's folder was edited. The developer's part has two additions. Say in the request that the run is for planning and not for building, because the skill does not. And look for assumptions in the drafts, because nothing marks them and an unmarked assumption reads as a decision.

15.4 Verify

The skill openspec-verify-change compares the implementation with the change's artifacts and reports. It selects the change, asks the program for the status and for the apply instruction, which returns the artifact files, the tasks and the count of those done, and reads the artifacts. It then checks three dimensions:

  • Completeness counts the tasks and looks for each requirement in the code.
  • Correctness reads each requirement and each scenario of the delta and looks for an implementation and for a test.
  • Coherence compares the implementation with the decisions of the design and with the patterns of the project.

Each finding is critical, a warning or a suggestion, and the skill tells the agent to prefer the lower severity when it is uncertain. A removed requirement is checked by the inverse, so that finding no implementation is the expected result. A renamed requirement is checked for the behaviour it kept.

The skill marks a check that the schema does not define as not applicable, and a check whose evidence is missing as not verified. It never scores a skipped check as a pass, and it says "ready for archive" only when nothing is critical and no check was skipped.

The program contributes the files and the counts. The comparison is the agent's, by a search of the code for keywords and by reasoning. The skill describes a report and tells the agent not to implement tasks or archive the change while verifying. It names no file to write, and it says that the report is advisory and that archive keeps its own checks.

A reviewer judges a report by its evidence: each finding should name a file and a line, and a clean report is as good as its search. The developer reads the report as advice and decides what a finding means for the artifacts and for the code. What a green report shows, and what to do with a mismatch, is a question of its own, and this chapter does not answer it.

15.5 Bulk-archive

The skill openspec-bulk-archive-change archives several changes in one run. It lists the active changes and asks the developer to choose among them, with an option for all, and it never chooses for them. For each chosen change it gathers the status of the artifacts, the count of tasks, the delta files, and the name the archive folder would have. A change whose archive folder already exists is marked as blocked.

The skill then looks for a conflict, which is two chosen changes with deltas for the same capability. It settles a conflict by looking in the code for what each change implemented:

  • If only one is implemented, it syncs that one.
  • If both are, it applies them oldest first, so that the newer overwrites.
  • If neither is, it skips the sync and warns.

It shows one table of all the changes with their artifacts, tasks, deltas and conflicts, and asks one question, with the options to archive all, to archive only the ready ones, or to cancel. After a yes it fetches the specifications' rules, syncs each change's included deltas inline, checks the main specifications against the deltas, and only then moves the change's folder. A target that has appeared in the meantime fails that change and not the batch, and the skill reports every outcome at the end.

The agent does the merging and the moving, and the program supplies the lists, the statuses and the counts. This is the path of chapter 12 in which the agent merges, run over several changes.

The rule that settles a conflict asks for evidence in the code, so a project whose changes are prose has nothing for it to find. A reviewer should read how each conflict was settled and not take the table's word that it was. The developer chooses the changes, reads the table and gives the one confirmation. What a collision between two changes is, and what to do before the second archive, is a question of its own, and this chapter does not answer it. Chapter 16 takes up both questions, this one and the one at the end of section 15.4.

15.6 Onboard

The skill openspec-onboard is the longest of the twelve, 551 lines in the scratch project against 87 for new and 128 for fast-forward. Most of its text is not an instruction to the program. It is text for the agent to say, in a fixed order, while it does a whole change with the developer on a real task in the project.

It begins with a preflight, which runs openspec --version and stops if the program is missing. It goes on in eleven stages: a welcome, the choice of a task, a short exploration, the creation of the change, the proposal, the specification, the design and the tasks, then the implementation, the archive and a recap. It finds the task by scanning the code for comments that mark work to do, for errors that are swallowed, for functions without tests, for loose types, for debugging output and for user input that is not validated, and it shows the developer three or four suggestions.

The skill marks four pauses: after the exploration, after the proposal draft, after the tasks draft, and before the implementation. It shows the proposal and the tasks as drafts and saves each after approval. It marks no pause between the draft of the specification and the draft of the design. It implements in the codebase and archives with openspec archive and the flag --yes, which the skill says answers the confirmation prompts that it cannot answer from a tool call. If the developer says they need to stop, the skill tells the agent to say that the change is saved, to point at openspec status for where it stands, and to offer one next step from the workflows the session has.

The agent teaches and does the work, and the program answers the commands the skill calls. The skill's own words are that it does real work in the developer's codebase, and nothing in it makes the work a sandbox. The change is a change of the project, the code is its code and the archive is its archive.

A reviewer therefore judges onboard by what a project keeps: the diff of the code, the archived folder and the main specification, each one that the developer would have accepted without the tutorial. The developer chooses the task, approves the drafts at the pauses, confirms before the implementation, and says when to stop. In a repository whose rules say that a change writes the book and not the code, or the code and not the book, the tutorial's change has to fit those rules too, since the skill does not know them.

15.7 Judging the results, and correcting them

The program sees the same for all five: which files exist and how many tasks are counted. It does not see who asked for a write, which assumption a draft holds, whether a pause was kept, whether a conflict was settled rightly, or whether a verify report is right. The review of section 10.6 applies to each, and the evidence it adds is the table or the report the skill shows at its end.

The cost of a wrong result differs by workflow:

  • A change that new started holds nothing the developer wrote, so the cheapest correction is to remove the folder and start again.
  • A result of fast-forward is revised by the paths of section 10.7, and its usual defect is an unrecorded assumption.
  • A verify report changes no file, so a wrong report costs a second run and a closer reading.
  • A bulk-archive run that went wrong has moved folders and merged specifications, so the last row of the table of section 10.7 applies to each change it archived: the archive holds no revision, and the correction is a new change.
  • The same holds for onboard, whose code is corrected by the project's own means and whose change the archive keeps as it was. A developer who stopped onboard early has a change in flight that continue and apply can take up, and nothing to correct in the archive.

The five workflows outside the table add no kind of file and no check that the program makes, and differ only in how much one run writes or moves and how much the agent is told to ask. The program sees only that files exist and tasks are counted, so what separates a good run from a bad one is the same in all five, which is the developer's reading of what was written or moved, who asked for it, and what it assumed. Of the five, only bulk-archive and onboard change the record of the project beyond a plan, and a developer chooses either by what the project will keep.

16. What No Check Compares

Chapter 15 ended two of its sections on a question it did not answer. Section 15.4 left open what a green verify report shows and what to do with a mismatch. Section 15.5 left open what a collision between two changes is and what to do before the second archive. Both questions ask about a comparison, and in both cases the tool does not make it. The first compares the specification with the code. The second compares two changes with each other. This chapter takes the two together, because both turn on the same fact about the tool's checks. It does not introduce verify or bulk-archive again. Sections 15.4 and 15.5 do that, and this chapter adds only what they leave open.

16.1 Three statements

Three statements about a change are easy to take for one:

  • The change is well formed against the main specification.
  • Two changes that are open at the same time agree with each other.
  • The code does what a scenario of the specification says.

Chapters 11 and 12 showed how the first is checked. validate reads a change's delta and the main specifications, and archive checks the delta again before it merges. Nothing in those chapters checks the second or the third. The rest of this chapter shows why the first does not cover the other two, what the two workflows outside the table add, and what the developer does instead.

16.2 What every check compares

Every check the tool makes compares one change with the main specifications. A scratch project showed this on 26 November 2026. It had one main requirement with one scenario, and two changes modified the requirement's wording. One added the words "from its stock" and the other "and notes", and both carried every scenario the main specification had. Each change passed validate --strict on its own, and both passed validate --changes --strict in one run. list showed both as complete. No output named the overlap.

The other commands are the same. status takes one change by name, or all of them with --all, and has no option that relates two. A change's metadata file .openspec.yaml holds the schema, the date of creation and, in a change that declares no spec changes, skip_specs, and no field that names another change. So a pass says that a change is well formed against the main specification as it stands when the check runs. It says nothing about the main specification as it will stand after another change has been archived.

None of the checks reads code either. Chapter 11 says what validate reads and chapter 12 what archive reads, and neither is code. instructions apply counts the ticked boxes and, once every box is ticked, tells the agent to review or verify the change before archiving, as section 8.5 says. It leaves the comparison with the code to whoever does the verifying.

16.3 Between two changes, the order decides

When two open changes modify the same requirement, the change archived second decides what the main specification holds. A modified requirement replaces the requirement as a whole, as chapter 6 says. Whether the tool lets the second archive happen depends on whether the second change still carries every scenario of the main specification. The scratch project was run both ways.

The second change What the tool did in the runs What the main specification held afterwards
Carried every scenario the main specification had validate passed, and archive reported "Specs updated successfully." and nothing else The second change's wording only. The first change's wording was gone.
Omitted a scenario the first change had added validate failed, and archive stopped with "Aborted. No files were changed." The first change's requirement, unchanged, and the second change still open.

In the first run both changes were archived. The main requirement held the second change's wording and none of the first's. No output said so, and a modified block gives no reason why it should: it says what the requirement is and not what changed in it.

In the second run the first change added a scenario to the requirement, and the second change, drafted before that, did not carry it. While the first change was open, validate passed the second. Once the first was archived, validate failed with "MODIFIED … omits scenario(s) the current spec still has". Archive printed "Refresh the change spec before archiving to avoid dropping scenarios." and "Aborted. No files were changed.", exited with code 1, and left the second change open. The same change passed before an archive and was refused after it.

That refusal is the only one the runs produced. Both rows agree with chapter 12's row for MODIFIED, which says that a block must carry every scenario and that validate and archive reject one that drops it. What the runs add is that, because the check is made against the main specification as it stands, the order of archiving decides whether a change is refused.

16.4 What bulk-archive adds

Three details of bulk-archive bear on the question of this chapter.

The skill defines a conflict as two or more chosen changes with delta specs for the same capability path. The path is the unit and not the requirement, so two changes that modify different requirements of one capability count as a conflict too.

For two changes that are both implemented, the skill applies them oldest first, so that the newer overwrites. For two changes that modify the same requirement, that is the outcome of the first run in section 16.3: the main specification holds the second wording only.

The skill shows its resolution of each conflict in its table before it asks its one confirmation question. That table is where a developer can see which change will overwrite which, before anything is written.

16.5 What verify's evidence is

What section 15.4 leaves open about verify is what a report rests on, which is a matter of what the skill tells the agent to do.

  • For each added or modified requirement, the skill tells the agent to search the code for keywords related to it and to "assess if implementation likely exists".
  • For each scenario, it tells the agent to check whether the conditions are handled in the code and whether tests exist that cover it.
  • Its heuristics name the method for correctness as "keyword search, file path analysis, reasonable inference" and say not to require perfect certainty.

The skill does not tell the agent to run the code or to run a test. It asks whether a test exists, and not whether the test fails when the scenario is broken.

The skill also says what a report is not. A check marked "Not verified" describes a limit of the report, in the skill's words, and is not a new condition for archive, which keeps its own checks. Two things can stop the skill. Before the first step that writes anything, a shared project-root guard checks that the project has an OpenSpec root, and stops and asks when it has none. When the change to verify is vague or ambiguous, the skill asks the user to choose one.

Verify is not one of the seven workflows of chapter 9. In a project whose profile names only those seven, a request for verify reaches the router's shorter path of section 15.1, not this skill. This chapter rests on the skill text and says nothing about how well an agent carries it out.

16.6 The scenario as the unit of a check

A scenario is the unit that can be carried from the specification into a check. Chapter 6 writes it with a WHEN and a THEN that can be observed, and an observable THEN is something a test, a command or a procedure can confirm or refute. Section 8.5 asks the same of a task's evidence, that it could have come out the other way.

The tool holds no link between a scenario and a check. A specification has requirements and scenarios and no field for the check that covers a scenario, and a change's metadata has none either. Where the link exists, it exists in the project's tests and in the tasks that name them.

16.7 Making the two comparisons

Before an archive, the developer makes the two comparisons that the tool does not. Each has a routine, in the manner of chapters 11 and 12.

Before a second archive

  1. Before archiving any change, list the open changes and find those whose deltas name the same capability. openspec show <change> --json --deltas-only prints each delta's spec, operation, requirement name, text and scenarios.
  2. Decide which change archives first, and write the reason down in the second change's design. The order decides whose wording the main specification holds.
  3. Archive the first change, or sync it as chapter 12 describes, so that the main specification is current.
  4. For each change still open that modifies the same requirement, copy the requirement from the main specification as it now stands, with its scenarios and with the first change's wording, and apply that change's edit to the copy.
  5. Run validate on the second change.
  6. After the second archive, read the requirement in the main specification whole, and not only the diff.

Step 4 is more than the refusal asks for. In a third run of the scratch project, the second change from section 16.3 was given only the scenario it had omitted. It then validated and archived, and the main requirement held its wording: the first change's words "from its stock" were gone, although the first change's scenario was kept. The refusal protects a scenario and not a wording, so the wording is kept only when the first change's text is carried over as well.

Before archiving a change with code

  1. Take the delta's scenarios one at a time.
  2. For each, name the check that would fail if the scenario were broken: a test, a command or a procedure.
  3. If there is no such check, write a note that says so.
  4. Run the checks.
  5. Record each result in the task that names the check, as chapter 8 describes.

16.8 Changing the result

When a comparison finds that something is wrong, the correction depends on where the error is and how far the change has gone.

After a wrong second archive, the main specification holds a requirement that has lost the first change's wording. The archive is not edited. The lost wording is restored by a new change that modifies the requirement, by the path of chapter 12.

After a mismatch between the code and the specification, the skill's recommendations name the ways out, worded as follows:

  • for a requirement with no implementation: "Implement requirement X: <description>";
  • for a scenario that is not covered: "Add test or implementation for scenario: <description>";
  • for a design decision the code does not follow: "Update implementation or revise design.md to match reality".

The recommendations name the code first, and only the design decision has the artifact as a way out. Which side was wrong is the developer's decision. A requirement the code does not meet may be a missing implementation, or a requirement that was not right. When the artifact is at fault and the change is open, it is revised in the change, as section 11.5 says. When the requirement is archived, it is corrected by a new change, as after a wrong second archive.

16.9 What the example shows

The example shows a correction and neither of the two cases. The vending machine has two archived changes, give-exact-change and refuse-without-exact-change. They were never open together. The second modified a requirement of the first after the first had been archived, so no order decided anything and nothing was refused. The example holds no code, so it shows no mismatch between code and specification and no verify report.

The tool checks one change's text against the main specification as it stands on the day of the check. It refuses a modified requirement that has lost a scenario, it passes one that has lost another change's wording, and it reads no code. Two changes can each pass and still leave a main specification that says what only one of them meant, and a change can pass with code that does something else. Whether two changes agree, and whether the code does what a scenario says, is therefore the developer's reading: of the requirement in the main specification after the second archive, and of each scenario against the check that would fail if it were broken.

17. The Commands No Workflow Calls

Chapters 9 to 16 took the workflows apart, and with them the commands that their skills tell the agent to run. The program has more commands than that. Some of them a developer runs by hand, some a script runs, and some nobody needs until something goes wrong. This chapter takes the ones that no workflow skill runs and no earlier chapter explains. It asks of each group the questions that chapter 9 asks of a workflow: who acts, what is read and written, what can stop it, how a reviewer judges what it did, and what happens when its result is wrong. A command has no stages, so each group gets a table that fits it, in the form chapter 15 used for the workflows outside the table.

17.1 The commands outside the workflow skills

openspec --help lists 24 commands. The twelve workflow skills tell the agent to run twelve of them: init, update, context, schemas, new change, status, instructions, list, show, validate, archive, and store list as the one form of store. The workflow chapters described those. Two more are run by no workflow skill and explained in chapter 13: config, which holds the profile, and schema, with which chapter 14 forked one. The others have no chapter yet, and the table sorts them into four groups.

Command What it does Group
view Prints one dashboard of the specifications and the changes in flight. Reading the record
show --diff Shows a change with a diff of each modified requirement. Reading the record
spec, change Older forms of show, list and validate, by noun. Reading the record
templates Says where each artifact's template comes from. Checking the harness
doctor Reports the health of the root, its store and its references. Checking the harness
store Creates, registers and removes stores. Working across repositories
workset Saves named sets of folders on the machine. Working across repositories
version, install Report the program's release, and install the standalone program. The program itself
completion, feedback Add shell completion, and send feedback to the OpenSpec project. The program itself

The router names four of these commands, and config profile, in a line each. Its file of answers offers view, templates and config profile as answers to a developer's questions, tells the agent to run doctor when something seems wrong, and lets it send feedback only once the user has approved the message. It never says what any of their results mean, so the groups of the table still hold.

show is named in chapters 10 and 16 for other forms. --diff is the one form no chapter has used, and it belongs with the commands that read.

17.2 Reading the record

The first group reads. The developer runs each command, the program prints, and no file changes.

Command Reads Writes Can stop it
view The main specifications and the changes in flight. Nothing. No root.
show <change> --diff The change's proposal and deltas, and the main specification each delta names. Nothing. A name that is no change.
spec show, spec list, spec validate The main specifications. Nothing. Nothing for list: with no root it prints "No items found" and succeeds.
change show, change list, change validate The changes in flight. Nothing. The same as spec.

view prints a dashboard: a summary of the specifications and their requirements, the changes in progress and completed, and the task progress; below it each change with a progress bar and the state of its artifacts, and each specification with its count of requirements. Without a terminal it prints once and ends. It is the shortest way to see the state of a project, and it says nothing that list and status do not.

show <change> --diff prints the proposal and then, under "Specifications Changed (diffs)", a unified diff of each modified requirement against the main specification. Chapter 6 said that a reader of a modified block has to set it beside the main specification to see what moved. This form does that, for the text as it stands when the command runs. It does not say that the change is right.

spec and change are the older form of the same reading, with the noun first. Each of them prints a warning that the commands are deprecated and names the verb-first command to use instead, openspec show, openspec list or openspec validate. The verdicts of spec validate and change validate are those of validate. A script that still calls them works and warns. A new one has no reason to use them.

For the developer, these commands are a way to read without opening files, and the review is the reading itself. A dashboard full of ticks says that files exist, as status does in chapter 10.

17.3 Checking the harness

The second group checks where things come from. It reads the harness and writes nothing.

Command Reads Reports What fails it
templates The schema in use and its template files. Each artifact's template path and its source: the package, the project or the user's directory. A schema that cannot be resolved.
doctor The root, a declared store, and each entry of references in openspec/config.yaml. Whether each is found and healthy, with a fix for each problem. Not a missing reference: that is a warning.
store doctor <id> One registered store. Its location, its OpenSpec root, its metadata and its Git state. A store that is not registered.

templates answers the question that chapter 13 asked of a schema with openspec schema which, for the files below it. In a project that has not forked its schema, every template comes from the package. In a project with a fork, the same command names the project as the source.

doctor looks at relations, not at content. With nothing declared it reports the root and says that no references are declared. A reference whose store is not registered on the machine is reported as such, with the command that would register it, and the command still exits with status 0. A warning is printed and not counted. A script that runs doctor and checks only its exit status learns that the command ran; it has to read the --json output to learn what it found.

For the developer, the two commands are the answer when an agent was told something other than expected. A rule that does not appear, a template that does not match, or a reference that adds nothing to the instructions has its cause in one of the places these commands name.

17.4 Working across repositories

The third group writes, and it writes on the machine. Chapter 3 said that the program keeps stores and the user's own state outside the repository. These are the commands that make it. OpenSpec's guide calls stores and worksets a beta and says that their commands, flags and file formats may change between releases.

A store is a standalone OpenSpec repository registered on the machine under an id. It takes the openspec/ folder out of a code repository and gives it a repository of its own, so that several code repositories can share one set of specifications. Any command that reads or writes specifications and changes takes --store <id> and then works on the store instead of the nearest openspec/ folder, and its output begins with "Using OpenSpec root:" and the store's id.

Command Writes Can stop it
store setup <id> --path <folder> The folder, with openspec/, an .openspec-store/store.yaml file, a Git repository and a first commit; and the store's entry in the machine's registry. No Git identity, unless told to skip Git.
store register <path> The entry in the registry, for a store that already exists. A folder without an openspec/ root.
store unregister <id> Removes the entry. The files stay. An id that is not registered.
store remove <id> --yes Removes the entry and deletes the folder. No --yes with no one to ask.
workset create <name> --member <folder> A named list of folders, in the user's data directory. No member.
workset remove <name> --yes Removes the list. The member folders are not touched. No --yes with no one to ask.

store setup writes in two places: the store's folder, and its entry in the machine's registry, which lives in the user's data directory beside the list of projects the program knows. store unregister removes only the entry and leaves the files where they are. store remove deletes the folder as well, and with no one to ask it does so only when --yes is given.

A project points at a store in two ways. A store key in its configuration makes the store the root when the project's own openspec/ holds no specifications or changes; when it holds them, the key is ignored with a warning. A references list leaves the root alone and adds an index of each store's specifications to every instruction, in a block marked "Read-only upstream context", with each specification's Purpose and the command to fetch it in full. The agent is told the store exists. It is not told to obey it, and nothing checks whether it read it.

Where a command works is settled in a fixed order, and the first rule that applies wins: --store on the command; the project's own openspec/, when it holds specifications or changes; the store key; and a defaultStore in the global configuration, which config sets. When none applies, the command fails and lists the registered stores. It does not pick a store by its name, even one that matches the repository's.

In a store the workflows run as they always do, and only the place changes. A change started from a code repository that uses a store is written into the store's folder, with all its artifacts and, at the end, its archive. The code it describes stays in the code repository.
