The two are committed and pushed separately, and no check compares them.

The skills follow the same rule. Each workflow skill of chapters 9 to 12 carries a paragraph on store selection. When the developer names a store, or the work lives in one, the agent runs store list --json for the registered ids and adds --store <id> to every command that reads or writes specifications and changes, for the rest of the workflow. When the project declares a store that this machine cannot resolve, the agent stops before writing and shows the error and its fix, instead of treating the project as one without OpenSpec. That is why store list is the one form of store a skill runs.

A workset is a name for several folders, kept on the machine. workset open writes a workspace file and opens the folders in one editor window; the guide says that the openers for two editors are built in and that those for terminal agents are disabled for now. workset remove removes the list and leaves the member folders untouched. A workset does not change which openspec/ folder a command uses.

For the developer, the review of this group is of the machine. The registry and the worksets are files outside every repository. OpenSpec never clones, pulls or pushes a store: a teammate clones it with Git and registers it on each machine, and a checkout that was not pulled shows old specifications until it is pulled. A teammate who clones only the project does not have the store, which is why doctor reports a reference as unregistered on a new machine.

17.5 The program itself

The fourth group is about the program and reaches furthest: most of its forms change the machine or send something off it.

Command Reaches
version Nothing outside the program.
version --check The package registry, for a newer release.
install [version] The project's GitHub releases, for the standalone program.
completion generate <shell> Nothing; it prints a script.
completion install <shell> The shell's own setup files.
feedback <message> GitHub, as a public issue on the OpenSpec project.

version prints the release, the package manager and the scope of the install, and its --json form adds the folder of the install. That is the line chapter 3 points at when it says the release is named in the README. version --check asks the registry whether a newer release exists, and so does update when it offers an upgrade.

install fetches the standalone program, which runs without Node.js, from the project's GitHub release, together with its checksums, and puts it in ~/.local/bin unless told otherwise. It then says which copy comes first on the path, and prints the command that removes the package-manager copy. Until one of the two is removed, the machine has two programs, and version says which one ran.

completion generate <shell> prints a completion script for the shell. completion install writes such a script into the shell's setup, and completion uninstall takes it out.

feedback sends a message to the OpenSpec project. It files an issue on the project's GitHub repository through the gh program when that is installed and signed in, with the release, the platform and the time added below the message. Without gh it prints a prefilled address for the issue form instead. An issue on a public repository is public.

For the developer, this group is the one whose effect is outside the project. Before a run, the question is where it reaches: the shell, the install, or a public tracker.

17.6 Judging the result, and correcting it

The program checks none of these commands' effects. It reads, it reports and it writes what it is told, and the earlier chapters' checks of form are the only checks there are. What a wrong run costs depends on what it wrote:

  • A reading or checking command changes no file, so a wrong run costs a second run with the right name or form.
  • store unregister and workset remove are undone by registering the store or creating the workset again, because their files were left in place.
  • store remove --yes deletes the folder. Only a copy elsewhere, such as a pushed remote, brings it back.
  • A store checkout that was not pulled shows old specifications, and the agent works against them until it is pulled with Git.
  • install leaves two copies of the program until one is removed, and the path decides which runs.
  • A feedback issue is public once it is filed, and correcting it is a matter for the tracker, not for the program.

Before a command of the third or fourth group, the developer can say in one sentence what it will write and where, and run git status and the matching list afterwards: store list, workset list or version.

The commands that no workflow calls read the record, check the harness, connect repositories and maintain the program, and none of them judges a change. Reading and checking leave the project as it was, and say nothing that validate, list and status do not. Connecting writes the machine's state, which no clone carries and which doctor can find missing. Maintaining reaches the shell, the install and a public tracker. So the developer's review of these commands is not of a change, but of the machine they wrote to and of what left it.

18. A Customization Beyond the Documented Means, and What It Rests On

Chapters 13 and 14 customized OpenSpec through the files it documents: the profile, the project configuration and the schema. This chapter takes a need that none of those files meets, and a customization that a project built for it anyway. It asks which documented means were tried and why each fell short, what was used instead, on what each part of it rests, and why it is still there after openspec update. The example is a customization made for one use case, and the chapter shows it as far as the reader needs it to follow, and no further.

18.1 A state that outlives the conversation

Explore keeps what it finds in the conversation. The skill openspec-explore says so in one of its rules: "Track decisions in the conversation, not in files." Section 10.1 showed the consequence: explore leaves nothing unless the developer asks for it to be captured as a change.

That is enough for an exploration that ends in one sitting. It is not enough for one that is carried out over several sittings, or that moves to a new session, because a new session begins without the conversation of the last one. What was decided, what is still open and what was rejected are then held by the developer's memory, or by nobody.

The customization keeps that state in a file. The file holds the latest state of one topic: its decisions, its open questions, the options it rejected and its next step. It is not a transcript, and it is not an artifact of a change. It exists before any change does, and it is removed once the change it led to has been proposed.

18.2 What the documented means cannot reach

The first question of section 13.1 is which kind a need belongs at. For this need the answer is none of them, and the table says why for each means that was considered.

Means What it reaches Why it cannot carry the rule
An edit to the generated skill openspec-explore The text the agent reads in explore openspec update writes the skill back. In the scratch project, a line added to it was gone after the update, which reported that the "skill files differ from the generated content".
operations in the configuration Advice for apply and archive The documentation names operations.apply.guidance and operations.archive.guidance, and nothing for explore. A run showed that an entry for explore is ignored with a warning.
rules in the configuration The instruction of the artifact whose id matches Explore writes no artifact while it explores, so no rule is ever read for it.
A schema, or a fork of one The artifacts of a change, their order, and what the agent is told when it writes each A schema has no place for an instruction that holds while a conversation goes on.
The profile Which workflows are installed It selects workflows and changes none.

Of the five, the schema needs a closer look, because chapters 13 and 14 used one to add a file to every change, and that seems the obvious way to add a file here too.

A schema describes a change: which files it has, in which order they are written, and what the agent is told when it writes each one. Explore comes into contact with a schema only where there is a change. When the developer explores a change that already exists, the schema tells explore which files to read. When the developer asks for the exploration to be captured as a new change, the schema tells explore what to write.

The log is needed earlier than either. It is written while the developer and the agent are still talking, before any change exists, and at that point explore reads nothing from a schema. A fork would come too late. It could also only add a file to a change, and that file would stay in the change and go into the archive with it, which is the opposite of a note that is removed once a change has been proposed.

Chapter 14's trace shows the difference. The trace belongs to a change and is meant to be kept in the archive, so a fork was the right way to add it. The log belongs to the conversation before there is a change, so a fork is the wrong way, and the cost of keeping one up to date, which sections 13.5 and 14.7 describe, would buy nothing.

18.3 The configuration's context, and a text of the project's own

Two things carry the customization. The rule reaches explore through context in openspec/config.yaml, and the procedure is held in a text that the project wrote itself.

The documentation says that context "appears in ALL artifacts", and section 13.3 showed it returned with every instruction the agent asks for. That is the documented part. Explore is not an artifact, and the documentation does not say that explore reads context. The generated skill does: at its start it reads the project's openspec/config.yaml and treats context and rules as constraints to follow and not to copy. So the rule reaches explore because of what the skill does, not because of what the documentation promises.

This is the paragraph of context in the project's openspec/config.yaml, as the change add-explore-log left it. It is shown without its indentation, with its lines broken anew and split into paragraphs; the wording is unchanged.

Explore log (owner, 27 November 2026): during an explore session, follow
the project skill explore-log (`.agents/skills/explore-log/SKILL.md`).

At the start of a new session, read the matching log before the first
checkpoint.

Keep the current state in openspec/.explore/log-<topic>.md, one file per
topic, written at checkpoints by a subagent.

This log write is the one explore write allowed without asking; every
other write keeps the confirmation rule.

The directory is ignored by git.

A standalone openspec-propose run deletes the matching log; ask when the
match is ambiguous. Explore's own capture leaves it in place.

The paragraph calls the text a project skill. The name says where the text is kept and what form it has: it is a SKILL.md in a folder of its own under .agents/skills/, beside the skills OpenSpec generates, and like them it begins with front matter that gives a name and a description. In this book a skill is the text through which OpenSpec delivers one workflow, as section 9.2 describes, or the router, which section 9.3 describes as the one skill that picks among the workflows instead. This text is neither. It delivers no workflow of its own; it adds rules to explore, which the generated skill openspec-explore delivers. OpenSpec does not generate it, and no documentation names such a text as a means of customization. This chapter therefore calls it the project's own text.

The project's own text holds what the paragraph only names: when to write, how the topic of a file is chosen, what a new session does first, and what the file contains. The file has the same sections every time.

# Explore log: <topic>

Last updated: <YYYY-MM-DD>

## Topic

## Current state

## Confirmed decisions

## Open questions

## Rejected options

## Next step

The text also says how the write is handed to a second agent in each coding tool the project uses. Those lines name the tools and are left out here.

18.4 The log, and the read its first version lacked

Each rule of the log answers one way in which a resumed session could start from the wrong state.

Rule What it prevents
One file per topic, under openspec/.explore/ and outside openspec/changes/ A log read as a change: in a run, openspec list did not show it.
A topic suffix chosen at the first checkpoint and kept for the session; a new file only after the developer agrees One topic's log overwritten by another's.
The whole file replaced at each write, never appended to A file that keeps decisions which were later reversed.
A write at a checkpoint only: a decision confirmed, an open question opened or closed, a change of direction, the end of the session, or the developer's request A write after every turn, which costs time and races the conversation.
The write handed to a second agent The conversation stopping for a file. Whether it waits for the write depends on the coding tool.
The log write the one write explore makes without asking A yes or no at every checkpoint, which the generated skill would otherwise require.
The standalone propose workflow removes the matching log; explore's own capture leaves it A log that outlives the change it led to, or one removed while explore still needs it.

The first version had every rule of the table and no rule for reading. It said when to write and how, and nowhere that a new session should look at what was already there. Its own checks passed, and it validated. Reading the rules against the use case, before the change was archived, showed the gap: a new session that chose the same suffix would replace the earlier state with its own at its first checkpoint, and a session that chose another would leave two logs for one topic. Either way, the case the customization was made for was the case it failed. The rule that closed it says that a new session lists openspec/.explore/, reads the log that matches its topic, and starts from that state before its first checkpoint. In a later run, a new session read a log seeded with a confirmed decision and wrote one that kept it.

A hook of the coding tool that runs when a session starts was considered as a way to make the read certain, and rejected. It runs before the developer has said what the session is about, so it cannot know which log matches, and it would have needed one implementation for each coding tool.

18.5 What survives an update, and on what grounds

openspec update rewrites the files it generates and leaves the rest. In the scratch project, created with openspec init --scope project, three things were changed by hand before the update: a line was added to the generated explore skill, a folder of the project's own was added to the skills folder, and a context entry was added to openspec/config.yaml. After the update, the line in the generated skill was gone, and the folder and the entry were as they had been.

That is why the customization was built from those two files and not from an edit to the generated skill. How far it can be relied on differs for each part.

Part What it rests on What a later release could change
The context entry, and that it is returned with every instruction The documentation, and the configuration being the project's file Nothing that the documentation does not announce.
That explore reads context The text of the generated explore skill The skill is rewritten at every update, and a new text may read the configuration differently or not at all.
That update leaves a folder of the project's own in the skills folder One run, on one release Nothing promises it. The documentation says nothing about files that update does not manage.

Only the first row is a promise. The other two are behaviour, and behaviour is checked again after each update rather than assumed. The project has a check program of its own for that, outside OpenSpec, which confirms after an update that the text is in place, that context still names the log's path and that the log's folder is still ignored by git. It confirms that the parts exist, which is the form of section 13.8, and not that explore still reads them.

18.6 What it costs, and where it stops

The customization has costs that no check reports. The context paragraph is returned with every instruction, so it is read when a proposal, a design or a task list is written, and at every apply and archive, where it has nothing to do. It also says again part of what the project's text says, so the same rule is written twice and the two can drift apart, which nothing would report. Whether the agent reads the log at the start of a new session depends on the model following the text, and a run shows that it did once, not that it always will.

It stops at one person. The log is ignored by git, so it exists only in one working copy, and another person on another machine never sees it. Two people exploring one topic in the same working copy would each replace the whole file. An exploration shared between people would need a log under version control, a rule for who commits it and when, and a way to merge two states of one topic, and the customization was kept to one person rather than take those on.

A need that no documented means meets can be met by pairing the one documented channel that reaches the workflow, the configuration's context, with a text of the project's own, and the pair survives an update because the update rewrites only what it generated. It survives only as far as its grounds go. What the documentation states holds; that explore reads the configuration and that the update leaves a foreign folder alone is behaviour, to be checked again at every update, and no check of the project's or of OpenSpec's says whether the customization still meets its use case. That was shown once already, when every check passed on a version that did not read its own log, and only trying the use case against the rules found it.

19. What the Book Describes, and What It Leaves Open

The book has followed one tool from its conventions to the commands that no workflow calls, and to a customization that goes beyond what it documents. This last chapter says what kind of book that makes it, what it found, and which questions it leaves for the reader to take further. It adds nothing about the tool that an earlier chapter did not establish.

19.1 What kind of book this is

The first two chapters are about the method, not the tool. Chapter 1 argued that work done with a model needs a record that outlives the conversation, and that the record has a cost that has to be earned. Chapter 2 named the cornerstones such a record must satisfy. OpenSpec appeared there as one implementation, and section 1.6 said that it is replaceable in the argument.

From chapter 3 on, the book is a technical description of one tool, OpenSpec, as one release of it behaves. It describes what the tool writes, what it reads, what it checks and what it leaves to the developer, and it describes it in the order a change meets it.

Chapters What they describe
3 How OpenSpec's conventions carry the cornerstones, and where they stop.
4 to 8 One change from request to archive, and each of its four artifacts: the proposal, the specification, the design and the tasks.
9 to 12 Seven of the twelve workflows, and the validate command, by who does the work in each.
13 and 14 Customizing the harness, and one customized change from fork to archive.
15 to 17 The five workflows outside the table, the two comparisons no check makes, and the commands no workflow calls.
18 A customization that no documented means carries, and on what it rests through an update.

It is not a manual of every option the tool has. Nor is it a guide to practice. It says how the tool behaves when a developer uses it, and not how a team should organize its work around it.

19.2 The one finding

Chapter after chapter reached the same place. validate checks the form of a delta and the main specifications, and not whether the behaviour is the right one. The tasks are counted and not read, so a ticked box is a claim. No check opens the proposal or the design. The planning workflows are visible to the program only as files that exist. A customization is confirmed as well formed, and its effect is not. No check compares two changes with each other or a scenario with the code. The commands that no workflow calls read, check, connect and maintain, and none of them judges a change.

That is one finding, seen from every side: the program checks form and counts, and the developer judges content. Chapter 9 gave it the shape of a division of work, in which the agent writes, the program reports and checks, and the developer decides and reviews. Chapter 3 gave it its reason: human control is the one cornerstone the conventions cannot carry, because a tool can hold a decision and cannot make one. Everything the book said about reviewing an artifact, a workflow or a command is an application of that division to one part of the tool.

19.3 What the book leaves open

The questions below follow from what the book showed. Each names the chapter whose finding it extends, and none is answered here, because the book has no evidence to answer it with.

Large projects

  • Where does a capability end? The example has one capability, and section 5.5 showed how a proposal names the capability it changes. A system with dozens of them needs a rule for cutting behaviour into capabilities. The book has none to offer.
  • Who reads two changes against each other? Chapter 16 showed that no check compares two changes that are open at the same time, and that the comparison is a reading of the main specification after the second archive. With one writer that reading is a habit. With many changes in flight it is a duty that someone has to own, at a time the process has to fix. The book does not say who, or when.
  • How is a specification shared? Section 17.4 described stores: a repository of specifications that several code repositories can use, registered on each machine, never synchronized by OpenSpec, and marked as beta. It described the commands, not a practice. How a store is kept current, who may change it, and how a change to it is coordinated with the code it describes are not shown.
  • Who owns the record? Chapter 5 said that a proposal is drafted by an agent and owned by a person. Sections 1.7 and 2.7 said that a team must settle what earns a record. The book has one owner throughout, and it does not show how a team settles either question.
  • How does a change meet a branch and a review? The book never relates a change folder to a branch, a pull request or a code review, beyond the remark in section 3.4 that an abandoned change leaves no half-finished branch behind. Whether a change lives in one branch, who approves its artifacts and in which order they are reviewed against the code are not described.
  • What does automation check? Chapter 11 showed what validate checks, and section 17.3 that doctor exits with status 0 on a warning. Whether either should stop a merge, and what a pipeline would need to read to stop it, are not described.

Introducing and keeping it

  • How does a system without specifications get them? Section 15.6 showed onboard doing one change on a real task in an existing project. Writing the main specifications of a system that has none, from code that already runs, is not shown.
  • How does a project move between releases? While it was written, the book moved twice to a newer release. At each move it repeated its runs and noted the differences where they mattered, in sections 3.1, 9.2, 9.3 and 15.1. It does not show how a project with many changes carries its artifacts and its skills through a release.
  • How fast does a specification drift? Section 2.6 said that a specification must be maintained, and section 3.7 that nothing checks afterwards whether the specification and the code still agree. The book observed no project for long enough to see drift happen.
  • What does it cost, and what does it return? Sections 1.7 and 1.8 described the shape of the cost and said that the size of the return is not established. The book measured neither.

Comparisons

  • Would another spec-driven tool behave differently? Section 1.6 said that another tool may use different names, different artifacts and a different workflow, and chapter 3 that a different tool could arrange the same material and still serve the same principles. The book describes how OpenSpec divides the work between the agent, the program and the developer, and it does not show how another tool divides it.
  • Would another spec-driven tool check more? The book compares OpenSpec with nothing. The finding of section 19.2 is a finding about the release the book describes, and whether another tool closes any part of it is open.

None of these questions is a defect found in the tool. Where OpenSpec has a mechanism for one of them, as it has stores for shared specifications, the book has described the mechanism. What it has not done is use the mechanism where many people, many changes and many months meet, and that is where these questions are decided.

The book has shown, for one release, what OpenSpec writes, what it checks and what it leaves to the developer, and the answer was the same in every chapter: the program checks form and counts, and the content is the developer's to judge. At that scale the book does not say what happens, and it hands the reader the questions that follow from its finding instead: who reads, who owns, what is shared, and what is checked. The tool will not answer them, because each turns on a reading of content, and that reading is the part of the work that stays with the developer.
